sections.Statement:
Assume Countable Choice as in [[pthm-td-constant-conductivity-neumann-existence]]. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^3(0,L_i)$, let $c,k>0$, and let $T_b>\epsilon/30>0$, where $T_b$ and $\epsilon$ are in kelvins. For $r\in[0,1]$ set $h(r)=r^2(1-r)^2-1/30$ and prescribe
$$g(x)=T_b+\epsilon h(x_1/L_1)\qquad(x\in\overline\Omega).$$
Use its even $2L_i$-periodic extension in each coordinate as the initial datum on $\mathbb R^3$. The unique insulated heat solution has constant spatial mean $T_b$ and satisfies
$$\int_\Omega|T(x,t)-T_b|^2\,dx\le \frac{\epsilon^2|\Omega|}{2100}e^{-2(k/c)t/C_\Omega},\qquad C_\Omega=\frac32\max_iL_i^2.$$
This gives an exactly computed initial variance and the conditional relaxation estimate of the model.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** Countable Choice, $L_i>0$, $c,k>0$, $T_b>\epsilon/30>0$, the profile $h(r)=r^2(1-r)^2-1/30$, and the field $g(x)=T_b+\epsilon h(x_1/L_1)$.

[A1] Countable Choice is the explicit hypothesis used by the heat-evolution supplier [[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] [[pthm-td-constant-conductivity-neumann-existence]]: the even-periodic compatible initial field has the unique Gaussian-convolution heat solution with positive bounds and homogeneous Neumann faces.

[F2] [[pthm-td-neumann-heat-relaxation]]: for this solution, the mean is conserved and $E(t)\le e^{-2(k/c)t/C_\Omega}E(0)$.
sections.Example: The function $h$ is dimensionless, and $g$ has units of kelvins. The extension uses even reflection at each face and period $2L_i$; the initial field is nonconstant but compatible with insulated walls.
sections.Verification:
1.1 Write $q(r)=r^2(1-r)^2$. Then $q'(r)=2r(1-r)(1-2r)$, so $q'(0)=q'(1)=0$, and $q''(0)=q''(1)=2$. Also $0\le q\le1/16$ on $[0,1]$. The constant and first two derivatives therefore match across the even-reflection and periodic seams; the extension is $C^2$, with bounded uniformly continuous derivatives. Since $h=q-1/30$, its values lie in $[-1/30,7/240]$, so $g\ge T_b-\epsilon/30>0$. [given, algebra]

1.2 Expand $q(r)=r^2-2r^3+r^4$, so $\int_0^1q(r)\,dr=1/3-1/2+1/5=1/30$. Also $q(r)^2=r^4-4r^5+6r^6-4r^7+r^8$, whence
$$\int_0^1q(r)^2\,dr=\frac15-\frac46+\frac67-\frac48+\frac19=\frac1{630}.$$
Therefore $\int_0^1h(r)\,dr=0$ and
$$\int_0^1h(r)^2\,dr=\int_0^1(q-1/30)^2\,dr=\frac1{630}-\frac1{900}=\frac1{2100}.$$
Integrating over the other two coordinates now gives $\overline g=T_b$ and $E(0)=\epsilon^2L_2L_3L_1/2100=\epsilon^2|\Omega|/2100$. [given, algebra]

2.1 The profile satisfies every initial-data hypothesis of [F1]; its vanishing normal derivative follows from $q'(0)=q'(1)=0$. Apply [F1] for existence and [F2] with the computed $E(0)$ to obtain the stated conserved mean and decay bound. This is a deduction within the adopted continuum model. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

**Given:** Countable Choice, $L_i>0$, $c,k>0$, $T_b>\epsilon/30>0$, the profile $h(r)=r^2(1-r)^2-1/30$, and the field $g(x)=T_b+\epsilon h(x_1/L_1)$.

[F1] [[pthm-td-constant-conductivity-neumann-existence]]: the even-periodic compatible initial field has the unique Gaussian-convolution heat solution with positive bounds and homogeneous Neumann faces.

The function $h$ is dimensionless, and $g$ has units of kelvins. The extension uses even reflection at each face and period $2L_i$; the initial field is nonconstant but compatible with insulated walls.

sections.Example:

$$S(U,V)=a\ln(U/U_0)+b\ln(V/V_0).$$

Applying the definitions on this chart gives

$$T=U/a,\qquad p=bT/V,\qquad C_V=a,\qquad C_p=a+b,\qquad \kappa_T=1/p,\qquad \alpha_p=1/T.$$

sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** $U,V,U_0,V_0>0$ with units $\mathrm J,\mathrm{m^3},\mathrm J,\mathrm{m^3}$ respectively; $a,b>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$; fixed composition; the displayed function is stipulated on this chart.

sections.Verification:

fm.title: An identity dynamics leaves a noncanonical finite preparation unchanged
fm.physical_scope: A two-state finite model with explicitly frozen identity dynamics; it shows that a canonical preparation rule alone supplies no relaxation dynamics and is not an empirical statement.

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, complete lecture notes, §1.3
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, §§4.4–4.6

sections.Example: Let $\Omega=\{a,b\}$ with energies $E_a=0$, $E_b=\varepsilon>0$, and fix $T>0$. The separately adopted canonical law has probabilities proportional to $(1,e^{-\beta\varepsilon})$. For the dynamical comparison, stipulate the identity transition map $\Phi_t(a)=a$, $\Phi_t(b)=b$ for all $t\ge0$ and start with the point mass $\delta_a$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** A two-state energy model, positive temperature, the canonical preparation rule, and the explicitly stipulated identity dynamics.

[F1] [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]: the two microstates and their fixed finite energies define an admissible finite statistical model.

[F2] [[post-td-canonical-sampling]]: the canonical probabilities are the normalized weights $e^{-\beta E_x}$; this is an adopted preparation rule and includes no time-evolution equation.

[A1] The comparison dynamics is the deterministic identity map $\Phi_t$ for every $t\ge0$, and the initial law for that comparison is $\delta_a$.
sections.Verification:
**Given:** $\varepsilon>0$, $T>0$, and the stipulated dynamics.

1.1 Put $q=e^{-\beta\varepsilon}$, so $0<q<1$. The canonical law is $P_\beta(a)=1/(1+q)$ and $P_\beta(b)=q/(1+q)$; in particular it is not $\delta_a$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The identity map preserves the initial point mass at every time: $(\Phi_t)_*\delta_a=\delta_a$. Hence the time-evolved law does not converge to the canonical law, whose probability of $b$ is strictly positive. This is a counterexample to deriving equilibration from the sampling rule alone. [A1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

fm.title: Two minimizers in a reduced coexistence model
fm.physical_scope: A dimensionless coarse-grained order-parameter example illustrating a possible failure of a singleton variational-minimizer assumption; it is not a continuum Gibbs-potential calculation.

sections.Example: Consider the reduced coarse-grained variational model with scalar dimensionless order parameter $m\in[-1,1]$ and dimensionless free-energy function $g(m)=(m^2-1)^2$. Its global minimizers are $m=-1$ and $m=1$. This model shows why uniqueness must be stated as a parameter-specific assumption. It does not identify these two minimizers with Gibbs measures of a continuum pair potential.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
[F1] [[post-td-grand-variational-phase-uniqueness]]: the selected continuum conclusion is licensed only when the relevant grand variational minimizer set is a singleton.

[A1] Adopt the stated toy variational function $g(m)=(m^2-1)^2$ on the closed interval $[-1,1]$; $m$ and $g$ are dimensionless.
sections.Verification:
**Given:** The domain $[-1,1]$, the explicit function $g$, and the limited illustrative scope.

1.1 For every $m\in[-1,1]$, $g(m)=(1-m^2)^2\geq0$. Equality holds exactly when $m^2=1$, namely at $m=-1$ or $m=1$. [given, A1, algebra]

2.1 The two equality points are distinct, so the set of global minimizers has two elements and is not a singleton. Thus the uniqueness premise [F1] fails for this toy model; no continuum phase claim follows. [given, F1, step 1.1] ∎

fm.title: Nonzero pressure work around a closed model cycle
fm.physical_scope: Constructed smooth concave positive-temperature chart and an idealized quasistatic piston cycle at fixed composition; the work and heat values are model calculations, not reported observations.

references.title: Daniel Arovas, Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, §2.7
Jeremy Tatum, Heat and Thermodynamics, §12.5, Summary, Maxwell Relations, and Gibbs-Helmholtz Relations

sections.Example:
Fix a material constitution and amount $n$ and stipulate, on $U>0$ and $0<V<1/b$, the entropy chart

$$S(U,V)=C\ln(U/U_*)+aV-\frac{ab}{2}V^2+S_0,$$

where $C>0$ is in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, $U_*>0$ is in joules, $a>0$ is in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$, $b>0$ is in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, and $S_0$ is in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. Consider a piecewise-C1 quasistatic cycle with isotherms $T_1>T_2>0$ and volumes $0<V_1<V_2<1/b$, joined by isochoric legs. The ideal frictionless piston load tracks the equilibrium pressure, controlled heat exchange is permitted along the path, and no other work coordinate acts. The calculation shows that the pressure-work integral is not an endpoint increment.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The stipulated local entropy chart, constants and SI units in the Example, and an admitted ideal quasistatic frictionless constant-area piston protocol along the four stated legs, with the load tracking the equilibrium pressure and controlled heat exchange permitted. No empirical realization is claimed.

[F1] [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and [[def-td-si-quantities]]: The chart uses positive physical energy and volume in joules and cubic metres; entropy is in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$.

[F2] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: $\ln$ is defined on positive arguments and has derivative $1/x$.

[F3] [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]: $T=1/S_U$ and $p=T S_V$ on a positive-temperature chart.

[F4] [[post-td-mechanical-conjugate-identification]]: On the admitted quasistatic frictionless piston path, work on the system is $\delta W_{\mathrm{on}}=-p\,dV$.

[F5] [[post-td-first-law-energy]] and [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]: For the admitted closed cycle, $\Delta U=Q+W_{\mathrm{on}}$ with heat positive into and work positive on the system.

[L1] [[def-piecewise-c1-path-operations-and-oriented-reparametrizations]] and [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]: For a piecewise-C1 path $\gamma$ in the $(T,V)$ chart, $\int_\gamma (0,p)\cdot d(T,V)$ is the Riemann line integral $\int p\,dV$.

[L2] [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]] and [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: Continuous integrands on each compact segment are Riemann integrable and their polynomial antiderivatives give the segment integrals.

[L3] [[thm-gradient-theorem-for-line-integrals]]: The integral of a gradient along a closed piecewise-C1 path is zero.

[L4] [[thm-chain-sum-product-and-composition-rules-for-banach-derivatives]]: The derivative of a product of differentiable scalar maps is the sum of the two product terms.
sections.Verification:
1.1 By [F2] and [L4], the entropy derivatives are $S_U=C/U$ and $S_V=a(1-bV)$. Thus [F3] gives $T=U/C>0$ and $p=aT(1-bV)>0$ on the stated domain. The Hessian is diagonal with entries $-C/U^2$ and $-ab$, so the chart is C2 and concave. [given, F1, F2, F3, L4, algebra]

2.1 On each isotherm the vector field in [L1] is continuous, so [L2] gives $\int_{V_1}^{V_2}p(T_1,V)\,dV=aT_1[(V_2-V_1)-\tfrac b2(V_2^2-V_1^2)]$; the reverse isotherm contributes the negative of the same bracket multiplied by $aT_2$, and the isochoric legs contribute zero. [given, L1, L2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Summing the four legs yields $\oint p\,dV=a(T_1-T_2)(V_2-V_1)[1-\tfrac b2(V_1+V_2)]>0$, since $T_1>T_2$ and $V_1,V_2<1/b$. Thus $W_{\mathrm{on}}=-\oint p\,dV<0$ by [F4]. [given, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The cycle returns to the same $U$, so [F5] gives $Q=-W_{\mathrm{on}}=\oint p\,dV>0$. If $p\,dV$ were an exact differential on a neighborhood containing this loop, [L3] would force its closed integral to be zero, contradicting step 3.1. Hence pressure work here is a process functional, not a state-function increment. [F5, L3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

fm.title: One component in two phases has one regular equation-set degree of freedom
fm.physical_scope: A constructed pair of smooth one-component Gibbs charts; the example verifies the regular equation-set rank and dimension only, and does not assert a stable or realized coexistence endpoint.

sections.Example:
Let $C=1$, $P=2$, and $R=0$. Fix $T_0=300\,\mathrm K$ and $p_0=10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$, and take a common open chart around $(T_0,p_0)$. On it define the branch Gibbs potentials per mole
$$

$$
where $g_0$ is in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $s_0,c>0$ are in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, $v_1,v_2>0$ are distinct molar volumes in $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, and $\kappa>0$ is in $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}Pa^{-1}}$. [F2] [[pthm-td-regular-gibbs-phase-rule]]: In the thermodynamic application, the same rank formula is conditional on an attained stable endpoint and the stated exchange hypotheses; this example verifies only the equation-map part.

sections.Verification:

fm.title: A boundary reaction minimum with a one-sided extent
fm.physical_scope: A constructed two-species, one-reaction fixed-temperature and fixed-pressure model with a smooth Gibbs-potential extension to a zero-amount boundary; no empirical reaction data are claimed.

references.title: Konstantin K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Statistical Mechanics, §4.1 First-order phase transitions

sections.Example:
Use species $A,B$, one reaction column $\nu=(-1,1)^{\mathsf T}$, and starting amounts $n_A^0=0$ mol, $n_B^0=1$ mol. The admissible extents are $\xi\in[-1,0]$ mol because $n_A(\xi)=-\xi$ and $n_B(\xi)=1\,\mathrm{mol}+\xi$ must both be nonnegative. At fixed $T_0,p_0$, take the smooth extended constrained potential
$$
\Phi(\xi)=\Phi_0-(1\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}})\xi .
$$
At $\xi_*=0$ mol, let the boundary chemical potentials be $\mu_A=0$ and $\mu_B=-1\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. No positive-mole thermodynamic chart at $n_A=0$ is asserted; these are the explicitly extended local model data.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The stoichiometric column, initial amounts, feasible interval, the C1 extension to a neighborhood of $\xi_*$, and the values of $\mu_A,\mu_B$. The extension is a model premise.

[F1] [[pthm-td-reaction-boundary-equilibrium]]: At an active-species boundary, feasible tangent directions satisfy $(\nu h)_j\ge0$ for active $j$, and a local minimum requires $(\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu)\cdot h\ge0$ for every such direction.
sections.Verification:
1.1 Here species $A$ is active because $n_A(\xi_*)=0$. A tangent extent $h$ must satisfy $(
u h)_A=-h\ge0$, so $h\le0$. The affinity vector is the scalar $
u^{\mathsf T}\mu=-\mu_A+\mu_B=-1\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. Hence $(
u^{\mathsf T}\mu)h\ge0$ for every feasible tangent extent $h\le0$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Directly, $\Phi(\xi)-\Phi(0)=-(1\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}})\xi\ge0$ for every feasible $\xi\in[-1,0]$ mol, so the boundary point is a global minimum on this interval. It need not satisfy the interior equality $
u^{\mathsf T}\mu=0$. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

references.title: Daniel Arovas, Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, §2.10.5

sections.Example:

fm.title: Two indistinguishable hard-core particles in an interval
fm.physical_scope: A finite one-dimensional positional toy model with two classical identical particles and a hard-core exclusion; it is a model calculation, not a reported measurement.

sections.Example:
Take a dimensionless interval $\Lambda=[0,L]$ with $0<a<L$, two identical particles, and the hard-core pair potential $\varphi(r)=+\infty$ for $|r|<a$ and $0$ otherwise. At any positive temperature the configurational canonical partition function is independent of $T$ and equals
$$Z_{\Lambda,2}=\frac12(L-a)^2.$$
The factor $1/2$ is the adopted indistinguishable positional measure. This finite-volume calculation has no momentum variables or experimental data.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
[F1] [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]: for two positions the hard-core pair energy is infinite precisely on forbidden separations $|x_1-x_2|<a$.

[A1] [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]]: integrate symmetric positional weights with $d\mu_{\Lambda,2}=\frac12dx_1dx_2$.

[A2] [[post-td-equilibrium-ensemble-sampling]]: at exact $N=2$, the canonical positional partition is the integral of $e^{-\beta H_2}$ against $\mu_{\Lambda,2}$.
sections.Verification:
**Given:** The interval, hard-core radius, exact particle number, and the adopted positional measure.

1.1 The allowed labelled pairs form two disjoint triangles, $x_2\geq x_1+a$ and $x_1\geq x_2+a$. The first has area $\int_0^{L-a}(L-a-x_1)\,dx_1=(L-a)^2/2$, and the second has the same area by exchanging coordinates. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Their total allowed area is $(L-a)^2$. On it $e^{-\beta H_2}=1$; on the excluded band it is zero because $H_2=+\infty$. Multiplying the allowed area by the measure factor $1/2$ from [A1] gives $Z_{\Lambda,2}=(L-a)^2/2$, as asserted. [given, A1, A2, step 1.1] ∎

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, complete lecture notes, §§1.3.1 and 3.6
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, §§4.3–4.4 and §5.7

sections.Example: Take two noninteracting two-level sites with states $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, single-site energies $0,\varepsilon$, and total Hamiltonian $H=\varepsilon(n_1+n_2)$. sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The finite product energy model, the assigned positive temperature, the unitary evolution postulate, and the stated initial state.

[F1] [[pthm-td-independent-factorization]]: for two explicitly independent finite systems with additive energy, the canonical joint law is the product of the single-site canonical laws.

[F2] [[pthm-td-finite-mode-occupation-and-trace-formulas]]: a fermionic two-level site with $q=e^{-\beta\varepsilon}$ has excited probability $q/(1+q)$ under the adopted quantum Gibbs preparation.

**Given:** $q=1/2$, the product model, and the closed-system evolution.

## Example

Take two noninteracting two-level sites with states $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, single-site energies $0,\varepsilon$, and total Hamiltonian $H=\varepsilon(n_1+n_2)$. Fix $T>0$ and $\varepsilon=k_{\mathrm B}T\log2$. Start in $\rho_0=|00\rangle\langle00|$ and adopt the closed-system unitary evolution generated by $H$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite product energy model, the assigned positive temperature, the unitary evolution postulate, and the stated initial state.

[F1] [[pthm-td-independent-factorization]]: for two explicitly independent finite systems with additive energy, the canonical joint law is the product of the single-site canonical laws.

[F2] [[pthm-td-finite-mode-occupation-and-trace-formulas]]: a fermionic two-level site with $q=e^{-\beta\varepsilon}$ has excited probability $q/(1+q)$ under the adopted quantum Gibbs preparation.

[F3] [[post-nrqm-framework-autonomous-dynamics]] and [[def-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-framework-evolution]]: closed-system evolution is $\rho(t)=U_t\rho_0U_t^*$ with $U_t=e^{-itH/\hbar}$.

[A1] Each site has $q=1/2$, and the initial vector is the ground energy eigenvector $|00\rangle$ of $H$.

## Verification

**Given:** $q=1/2$, the product model, and the closed-system evolution.

1.1 By [F1]–[F2], the finite-temperature Gibbs probabilities on $(00,01,10,11)$ are $(4/9,2/9,2/9,1/9)$. In particular the Gibbs probability of $|11\rangle$ is $1/9>0$. [F1, F2, A1, algebra]

2.1 Since $H|00\rangle=0$, $U_t|00\rangle=|00\rangle$ for every $t$; thus $\rho(t)=|00\rangle\langle00|$. Its probability for the projector $|11\rangle\langle11|$ is zero at every time, unlike the Gibbs value $1/9$. The state therefore never reaches this Gibbs density under the declared unitary evolution. [F3, A1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

fm.title: Two independent two-level sites give a product thermal law
fm.physical_scope: A calculated two-site finite product model with additive energy and no interaction; it is not an observation or a claim about interacting sites.

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, complete lecture notes, §1.3.1
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, §§4.4.1 and 4.6

sections.Example: Let each site have states $0,1$ with energies $0,\varepsilon$, and take $T>0$ with $\varepsilon=k_{\mathrm B}T\log 2$. The composite has states $(n_1,n_2)\in\{0,1\}^2$ and additive energy $E=\varepsilon(n_1+n_2)$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** Two finite sites, additive energy, common positive temperature, and canonical sampling.

[F1] [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]: the composite state set is the Cartesian product and additivity of energy is explicit model data.

[F2] [[pthm-td-finite-canonical-identities]]: each finite canonical law has probabilities proportional to $e^{-\beta E}$.

[F3] [[pthm-td-independent-factorization]]: under the explicit product and additive-energy assumptions, partition sums factor and the joint canonical law is the product of the two subsystem laws.

[A1] Set $\beta\varepsilon=\log 2$, hence the single-site excited-state weight is $q=1/2$.
sections.Verification:
**Given:** The model data and $q=1/2$.

1.1 Each site has $Z_1=1+q=3/2$ and probabilities $(2/3,1/3)$. By [F3], $Z_{12}=Z_1^2=9/4$ and the joint probabilities of $(00,01,10,11)$ are $(4/9,2/9,2/9,1/9)$. [F1, F2, F3, A1, algebra]

2.1 The expected total occupation is the sum of the two marginal means, $1/3+1/3=2/3$, so the mean energy is $2\varepsilon/3$. This conclusion follows for the declared noninteracting product model only. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

fm.title: A positive-slope segment in the reduced van der Waals model
fm.physical_scope: An exact derivative calculation in the dimensionless reduced van der Waals model below its model critical temperature; no real-fluid measurement or universal equation of state is asserted.

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, author-hosted complete lecture notes, §5.1.1
Konstantin K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Statistical Mechanics, §4.1 First-order phase transitions

sections.Example:
Adopt the reduced van der Waals equation as a phenomenological model:
$$
p(v,t)=\frac{8t}{3v-1}-\frac{3}{v^2},\qquad v>\frac13,\quad t>0,
$$
where $p=P/P_c$, $v=V/V_c$, and $t=T/T_c$ use positive model scales $P_c,V_c,T_c$. The equation is a model premise; its extension to liquid-like densities is not a universal physical law.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The reduced model and domain in the Example, with $P_c,V_c,T_c>0$.

[A1] The isothermal local mechanical-stability criterion for this model is not needed for the calculation below. The claimed result is only the sign of the model derivative.

[F1] [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]]: A phase branch and its chart are model-specified; a branch equation is not asserted to be universal.
sections.Verification:
1.1 At fixed $t$, differentiating the rational equation gives
$$
\frac{\partial p}{\partial v}=-\frac{24t}{(3v-1)^2}+\frac{6}{v^3}.
$$
At $t=0.9$ and $v=1$, this derivative is $-24(0.9)/4+6=0.6>0$. [given, algebra]

2.1 The derivative is continuous near $(t,v)=(0.9,1)$ because $3v-1\ne0$ there. Hence it remains positive on some open neighborhood within $v>1/3$. Since $P=P_cp$ and $V=V_cv$ with positive scales, $(\partial P/\partial V)_T=(P_c/V_c)(\partial p/\partial v)_t>0$ there as well. This verifies a positive-slope branch of this phenomenological model only. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

fm.title: A volume-filling field changes ideal-gas pressure
fm.physical_scope: A finite-dimensional classical ideal positional gas with a constant per-particle external energy throughout the volume; it is excluded from the fixed uniformly tempered exterior class.

sections.Example: For the ideal positional gas $\varphi=0$ in a region of dimensionless volume $V$, the grand partition is $\Xi_V(z,\beta)=e^{zV}$. Now impose an external energy $c$ joules per particle at every point of the volume. The new grand partition is $\Xi_V^{(c)}=e^{ze^{-\beta c}V}$, so the dimensionless pressure rate changes from $z$ to $ze^{-\beta c}$ when $c\neq0$. This exact volume-filling external preparation is not a member of the deterministic exterior class used by [[pthm-td-qualified-van-hove-and-exterior-limit]].
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
[F1] [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]: $V$ is dimensionless reference volume, $\beta$ is inverse energy, and the ideal model has $H_N=0$.

[A1] [[post-td-equilibrium-ensemble-sampling]]: $\Xi_V=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_{V,N}$ with the indistinguishable positional factor $1/N!$.

[F2] [[def-td-admissible-van-hove-and-tempered-exterior]]: the qualified exterior theorem restricts deterministic exterior configurations by one fixed square-count bound $t$ and does not include an energy field applied throughout $\Lambda$.

[L1] [[pthm-td-qualified-van-hove-and-exterior-limit]]: its current conditional statement treats exterior energy only as $W_n(\omega,\zeta)$ for a fixed $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$ and expressly excludes a volume-filling external field; the theorem is draft and remains conditional on its mathematical suppliers.
sections.Verification:
**Given:** The finite-volume grand weight, an ideal gas, and the uniform per-particle shift $c$ over the entire region.

1.1 Since $H_N=0$, the finite-volume canonical positional integral is $Z_{V,N}=V^N/N!$. Summing the adopted grand weights gives $\Xi_V=\sum_{N\geq0}(zV)^N/N!=e^{zV}$. [given, F1, A1, algebra]

2.1 Adding $cN$ to the energy multiplies the $N$-particle weight by $e^{-\beta cN}$, so $\Xi_V^{(c)}=\sum_{N\geq0}(ze^{-\beta c}V)^N/N!=e^{ze^{-\beta c}V}$. For $c\neq0$ this has a different log-partition rate. [given, A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The perturbation is a potential on every point of $\Lambda$, whereas [F2] and [L1] restrict the boundary result to free walls or the interaction with one fixed uniformly tempered exterior configuration. Therefore this example lies outside those hypotheses and contradicts no qualified boundary conclusion. [given, F2, L1, step 2.1] ∎

fm.title: The close-packing endpoint can have zero canonical weight

references.title: D. Dereudre, Introduction to the theory of Gibbs point processes
references.locator: Section 1.3, PDF pp.10–12: canonical positional normalization; the one-dimensional hard-rod integral is calculated here.

sections.Example:
In one dimension, let the pair potential be infinite when the separation is less than $a>0$, and zero otherwise. For $N\geq1$ labeled rods in $[0,L]$, with canonical positional normalization $1/N!$, write $S=L-(N-1)a$. If $S>0$, translating the ordered coordinates by $y_i=x_i-(i-1)a$ gives
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac{S^N}{N!}=\frac{(L-(N-1)a)^N}{N!},\qquad \beta>0.$$
If $S=0$, the allowed configuration set has zero Lebesgue measure and $Z(L,N;\beta)=0$. Along $N\to\infty$ with $L=(N-1)a$, the density $N/L\to1/a$ while every finite-volume partition is zero. Thus the thermodynamic close-packing endpoint is approached by a sequence of zero-weight finite systems; it is not realized by a positive canonical partition. The interior canonical limit theorem makes no assertion at that endpoint.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** Hard-core distance $a>0$ and inverse temperature $\beta>0$.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]: the canonical positional partition integrates over labeled coordinates and divides by $N!$.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-canonical-interior-density-limit]]: its canonical limit assertion is restricted to interior attainable densities.

[F3] [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], and [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: product Lebesgue measure assigns volume $S^N$ to the cube $[0,S]^N$ and permits iterated integration.

[F4] [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]: the coordinate-order partition has $N!$ permutation chambers and the canonical normalization divides by $N!$.

[F5] [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]: translating a Lebesgue-measurable set preserves its Lebesgue measure.
sections.Verification:
**Given:** $N\geq1$ and $L\geq(N-1)a$.

1.1 Order the coordinates $0\leq x_1<\cdots<x_N\leq L$. The exclusion constraints are $x_{i+1}-x_i\geq a$. Apply the coordinatewise translation $x_i\mapsto y_i=x_i-(i-1)a$; each one-coordinate translation preserves Lebesgue measure [F5], so product measure is preserved. The ordered region becomes $0\leq y_1\leq\cdots\leq y_N\leq S$, where $S=L-(N-1)a$. The cube $[0,S]^N$ splits, up to equality sets of zero product measure, into $N!$ coordinate-order regions. Product-measure uniqueness makes these permutation chambers equal in measure, so the ordered region has volume $S^N/N!$. The full labeled allowed volume is $N!$ times this, and canonical division by $N!$ gives $Z(L,N;\beta)=S^N/N!$. [F1, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 If $L=(N-1)a$, then $S=0$ and the transformed region is a null set; its integral is zero. If $L>(N-1)a$, then $S>0$ and the ordered region has positive product volume. Thus the maximal-density endpoint does not carry a positive canonical partition at exact close packing; the interior-only theorem [F2] makes no contrary assertion. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

In one dimension, let the pair potential be infinite when the separation is less than $a>0$, and zero otherwise. For $N\geq1$ labeled rods in $[0,L]$, with canonical positional normalization $1/N!$, write $S=L-(N-1)a$. If $S>0$, translating the ordered coordinates by $y_i=x_i-(i-1)a$ gives
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac{S^N}{N!}=\frac{(L-(N-1)a)^N}{N!},\qquad \beta>0.$$
If $S=0$, the allowed configuration set has zero Lebesgue measure and $Z(L,N;\beta)=0$. Along $N\to\infty$ with $L=(N-1)a$, the density $N/L\to1/a$ while every finite-volume partition is zero. Thus the thermodynamic close-packing endpoint is approached by a sequence of zero-weight finite systems; it is not realized by a positive canonical partition. The interior canonical limit theorem makes no assertion at that endpoint.
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Hard-core distance $a>0$ and inverse temperature $\beta>0$.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]: the canonical positional partition integrates over labeled coordinates and divides by $N!$.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-canonical-interior-density-limit]]: its canonical limit assertion is restricted to interior attainable densities.

[F3] [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], and [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: product Lebesgue measure assigns volume $S^N$ to the cube $[0,S]^N$ and permits iterated integration.

[F5] [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]: translating a Lebesgue-measurable set preserves its Lebesgue measure.

**Given:** $N\geq1$ and $L\geq(N-1)a$.

1.1 Order the coordinates $0\leq x_1<\cdots<x_N\leq L$. The exclusion constraints are $x_{i+1}-x_i\geq a$. Apply the coordinatewise translation $x_i\mapsto y_i=x_i-(i-1)a$; each one-coordinate translation preserves Lebesgue measure [F5], so product measure is preserved. The ordered region becomes $0\leq y_1\leq\cdots\leq y_N\leq S$, where $S=L-(N-1)a$. The cube $[0,S]^N$ splits, up to equality sets of zero product measure, into $N!$ coordinate-order regions. Product-measure uniqueness makes these permutation chambers equal in measure, so the ordered region has volume $S^N/N!$. The full labeled allowed volume is $N!$ times this, and canonical division by $N!$ gives $Z(L,N;\beta)=S^N/N!$. [F1, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 If $L=(N-1)a$, then $S=0$ and the transformed region is a null set; its integral is zero. If $L>(N-1)a$, then $S>0$ and the ordered region has positive product volume. fm.title: A flat exposed face with many Fenchel minimizers

references.title: R. T. Rockafellar, Convex Analysis, §23

sections.Example: Let $f$ be the indicator of $[-1,1]$. The zero tilt $f(y)-0\cdot y$ has every point of the interval as a minimizer, and $f^*(0)=0$ is attained at every such point. Equivalently, $0\in\partial f(x)$ for every $x\in[-1,1]$. Thus the supporting face at slope zero is the whole interval, and coercive Fenchel attainment need not be unique.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The indicator $f(x)=0$ for $x\in[-1,1]$ and $f(x)=+\infty$ otherwise.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]: the indicator of a nonempty closed convex set is proper, closed, and convex in the given conventions.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-fenchel-transform-and-subgradient]]: $f^*(p)$ is the supremum of $py-f(y)$ over $y\in\operatorname{dom}f$, and $p\in\partial f(x)$ means $f(y)\ge f(x)+p(y-x)$ for all $y$.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-extended-convex-epigraph-equivalence]]: a proper indicator with a closed convex epigraph is closed and convex in the local extended-real conventions.

[L1] [[lem-tdmath-fenchel-young-equality]]: equality in Fenchel's inequality at a finite point is equivalent to the subgradient condition and attainment of the conjugate supremum.

[L2] [[thm-tdmath-fenchel-attainment]]: if the closed proper convex tilt is coercive, it has a finite global minimum and the conjugate supremum is attained, without a uniqueness conclusion.
sections.Verification:
**Proof technique:** direct calculation.

1.1 The epigraph is $[-1,1]\times[0,\infty)$, a nonempty closed convex rectangle, and the domain $[-1,1]$ is nonempty; hence the indicator is proper, closed, and convex by [F1, F3]. At slope $p=0$, every $y\in[-1,1]$ contributes $0$ to the conjugate supremum, and no other $y$ is in the effective domain, so $f^*(0)=0$ and every point of the interval attains this supremum. [F1, F2, F3, given]

2.1 Fix any $x\in[-1,1]$. For every $y\in\mathbb R$, $f(y)\ge0=f(x)+0(y-x)$: equality holds on the interval and the left side is $+\infty$ outside it. Hence $0\in\partial f(x)$; [L1] also gives $f^*(0)=0=0\cdot x-f(x)$ at each such $x$. [F2, L1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The zero tilt is $g=f$. It is coercive as an extended-real function: for any $M\in\mathbb R$, choosing $R=2$ ensures $|x|\ge R$ implies $g(x)=+\infty>M$. sections.Example: Suppose $J(P)=I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z$ has two distinct stationary minimizers $P_0\ne P_1$ with equal finite value $m$. sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** Two distinct stationary minimizers $P_0,P_1$ with finite equal minimum $m$.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-continuum-variational-pressure]]: $\Phi(P)$ is the limit of normalized finite-volume expected energies, and $\rho(P)$ is expected unit-cell count.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-specific-entropy-density]]: $I(P)$ is the large-cube limit of relative entropies against the unit-intensity Poisson reference.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-relative-entropy-variational-and-chain-rules]]: relative entropy obeys the mixture-label chain rule and is nonnegative.

**Given:** The assumptions above.

1.1 Let $P,R$ be stationary laws of finite specific entropy and let $P_\theta=\theta P+(1-\theta)R$. sections.Example:
For intensity $z>0$, let $P=Q_z$ be the translation-invariant Poisson law from [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], compared with the unit-intensity reference $Q=Q_1$. Its specific relative entropy is
$$I(Q_z)=1-z+z\log z.$$
The parameter $z$ is a mathematical intensity relative to the chosen reference; no physical preparation is asserted.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** $d\geq1$, $z>0$, and $P=Q_z$ with reference $Q=Q_1$.

[F1] The cell count under $Q_\lambda$ is Poisson with mean $\lambda$, conditional positions have the same uniform law for all $\lambda$, and disjoint cells are independent ([[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], [[thm-tdmath-poisson-reference-count-properties]]).

[F2] Finite-region relative entropy is computed from a Radon–Nikodym density, and the specific entropy is the normalized cube limit ([[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]], [[thm-tdmath-specific-entropy-density]]).

[F3] $e^x e^y=e^{x+y}$, $n!=n(n-1)!$ for $n\geq1$, and $e^x=\sum_{n\geq0}x^n/n!$ ([[thm-exponential-addition-formula]], [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]).

**Given:** The hypotheses and the laws in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 In one unit cell, the conditional distribution of point positions given the count is identical for $Q_z$ and $Q_1$. The ratio of their count probabilities at $n$ is $$\frac{e^{-z}z^n/n!}{e^{-1}/n!}=e^{1-z}z^n.$$ Thus this is the Radon–Nikodym density on that cell. [F1, algebra]

2.1 The cube $\Lambda_m=[0,m)^d$ is the disjoint union of $m^d$ unit cells. Independence in [F1] makes the finite-cube density the product of the cell densities: $$h_m(\omega)=e^{(1-z)m^d}z^{N_{\Lambda_m}(\omega)}.$$ [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The count $N_{\Lambda_m}$ is Poisson with mean $zm^d$ by [F1]. Directly from its mass function and the exponential series, $$E_PN_{\Lambda_m}=e^{-zm^d}\sum_{n\geq1}n\frac{(zm^d)^n}{n!}=zm^d e^{-zm^d}\sum_{k\geq0}\frac{(zm^d)^k}{k!}=zm^d.$$ Therefore [F2] gives $$\frac{D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})}{m^d}=\frac{E_P\log h_m}{m^d}=1-z+z\log z$$ for every positive integer $m$. 4.1 Taking the cube limit in [F2] yields $I(Q_z)=1-z+z\log z$. At $z=1$ the value is zero, the reference-law baseline. [F2, step 3.1] ∎

**Given:** [A1] and $a,b$ as distinct tags.

fm.title: A singular two-phase equation map with a four-dimensional solution set

references.title: Faye Jackson, MATH 395 notes, Implicit Function Theorem, pp. 99–106 and 127–132

sections.Example: Take $C=2$ components and $P=2$ phases on the open coordinate domain $U=(0,\infty)^2\times(0,1)^2\subset\mathbb R^4$. Set all four chemical-potential coordinate functions $\mu_i^\alpha$ identically equal to zero. The two coexistence equations then vanish identically, so the solution set is all of $U$ and has local dimension four. The regular formula would give $C-P+2=2$, but its nonsingular-minor hypothesis fails because the equation Jacobian is zero.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The stated component and phase counts, open domain, and constant coordinate functions.

[L1] [[thm-tdmath-phase-dimension]]: the dimension $C-P+2$ is conditional on an invertible square derivative minor for the coexistence equation map.
sections.Verification:
**Proof technique:** direct calculation.

1.1 For $C=P=2$, there are $n=2+2(2-1)=4$ coordinates and $q=2(2-1)=2$ equations. Since each $\mu_i^\alpha$ is identically zero, both differences $\mu_i^2-\mu_i^1$ equal zero at every point of $U$. Thus the zero set is exactly the open set $U$, which is locally parameterized by its four original coordinates. [given, algebra]

2.1 The derivative of each identically zero equation is the zero covector, so the equation Jacobian has rank zero and no $2\times2$ minor is invertible. Therefore [L1] does not apply; the example does not contradict its regular dimension count, and it shows why equation count alone does not determine local dimension. [L1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

fm.title: A Superlinear Count Test Is Not Local-Tame

sections.Example: For the unit cell $C_0=[0,1)^d$, the observable $f(\omega)=N_{C_0}(\omega)^2$ is local but is not one of the tests defining the local-tame topology.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The unit-cell configuration space and the definition of local-tame observables.

[F1] Every cell configuration is finite, and $N_{C_0}$ is measurable with respect to the restriction to $C_0$ ([[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]).

[F2] A local-tame observable supported in $C_0$ must satisfy $|f(\omega)|\leq b(1+N_{C_0}(\omega))$ for one finite constant $b$ ([[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]]).
sections.Verification:
**Given:** $f(\omega)=N_{C_0}(\omega)^2$.

1.1 By [F1], $N_{C_0}$ is finite and measurable from the restriction to $C_0$, so its square is a measurable local observable. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Fix any finite $b\geq0$ and choose an integer $n>b+1$. The cell configuration space contains configurations with exactly $n$ distinct points in $C_0$. On each such configuration, $f=n^2>b(1+n)$, so the tame growth bound in [F2] fails for this $b$. Since $b$ was arbitrary, $f$ is not tame. [given, F1, F2, construct, algebra] ∎

fm.title: A vertical separator and biconjugation outside the domain

references.title: R. T. Rockafellar, Convex Analysis, §12, Theorems 12.1–12.2

sections.Example: Let $f:\mathbb R\to\{0,+\infty\}$ be the indicator of $[0,\infty)$: $f(y)=0$ for $y\ge0$ and $f(y)=+\infty$ for $y<0$. At $z=(-1,0)$, the epigraph is separated by a vertical hyperplane (one whose coefficient of the epigraph-height coordinate is zero). The conjugate is $f^*(p)=0$ for $p\le0$ and $+\infty$ for $p>0$, so $f^{**}(-1)=+\infty=f(-1)$. The affine minorants $\ell_k(y)=-ky$, $k\ge0$, display the unbounded dual values at $y=-1$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The indicator function just defined and the Euclidean coordinates $(y,s)$ on its epigraph.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]: properness, convexity, lower semicontinuity, and the epigraph use the stated extended-real conventions.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-fenchel-transform-and-subgradient]]: $f^*(p)=\sup_{y\in\operatorname{dom}f}(py-f(y))$ and $f^{**}(x)$ is the supremum over $p$ with finite $f^*(p)$.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-extended-convex-epigraph-equivalence]]: convexity and lower semicontinuity are equivalent to convexity and closedness of the epigraph.

[L1] [[lem-tdmath-closed-convex-separation]]: a point outside a nonempty closed convex Euclidean set has a strict linear separator.

[L2] [[thm-tdmath-finite-dimensional-biconjugation]]: a proper closed convex extended-real function on finite-dimensional Euclidean space equals its biconjugate.
sections.Verification:
**Proof technique:** direct calculation.

1.1 The domain is $[0,\infty)$, so it is nonempty and $f$ is proper. Its epigraph is $E=\{(y,s):y\ge0,\ s\ge0\}$, a nonempty closed convex set; [F3] therefore makes $f$ closed and convex. The point $(-1,0)$ lies outside $E$. With $u=(-1,0)$ and $c=0$, every $(y,s)\in E$ satisfies $\langle u,(y,s)\rangle=-y\le0<1=\langle u,(-1,0)\rangle$, so this is the strict vertical separator; its height coefficient is zero. [F1, F3, L1, given, algebra]

sections.Example: For the reaction $2\,\mathrm{H_2}+\mathrm{O_2}\to2\,\mathrm{H_2O}$, let extent $\xi$ and species amounts use moles. The dimensionless stoichiometric column is $\nu=(-2,-1,2)^{\mathsf T}$ in the species order $(\mathrm{H_2},\mathrm{O_2},\mathrm{H_2O})$, and take $n^0=(2,1,0)^{\mathsf T}$. Then the feasible extent interval is $[0,1]$, and at $\xi=0$ the tangent cone permits only forward directions $h\ge0$. The matrix of hydrogen and oxygen atom counts annihilates $\nu$. For the explicitly mathematical objective $\Phi(n)=n_{\mathrm{H_2O}}$, the induced extent function is $f(\xi)=2\xi$ and has a boundary minimum at zero. This is a stoichiometric calculation, not a claim about chemical equilibrium or a measured system.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The reaction vector, initial amounts, extent convention, and linear objective in the Example.

[L1] [[lem-tdmath-stoichiometric-tangent-cone]]: the feasible tangent cone is determined by nonnegative changes in species whose amounts are zero at the point; the extent derivative is $\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu$ for a differentiable potential.
sections.Verification:
**Proof technique:** direct calculation.

1.1 The species-amount vector is $n(\xi)=n^0+\nu\xi=(2-2\xi,1-\xi,2\xi)^{\mathsf T}$. Nonnegativity of its third component requires $\xi\ge0$, and nonnegativity of its first two components requires $\xi\le1$; hence the feasible set is exactly $[0,1]$. [given, algebra]

1.2 The elemental count matrix is $D=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&2\\0&2&1\end{pmatrix}$, with first row counting hydrogen atoms and second row oxygen atoms per molecule. Direct multiplication gives $D\nu=(-4+4,-2+2)^{\mathsf T}=(0,0)^{\mathsf T}$, so every change $n(\xi)-n^0=\nu\xi$ preserves both atom totals. [given, algebra]

2.1 At $\xi_*=0$, only the water component is zero. Its directional change is $(\nu h)_3=2h$, so [L1] gives $T_{\mathcal F}(0)=\{h:2h\ge0\}=[0,\infty)$. A negative direction is infeasible because it would make the water amount $2\xi$ negative. [L1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $\Phi(n)=n_3$, the induced function is $f(\xi)=\Phi(n(\xi))=2\xi$. Its derivative at $0$ is $Df(0)h=2h\ge0$ for every feasible tangent $h\ge0$, and $f(\xi)\ge f(0)$ for every $\xi\in[0,1]$. This verifies the boundary first-order condition and minimum directly for this chosen mathematical objective. [L1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

fm.title: Mean-zero Poincare inequality on a rectangle

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations, §4.4
references.locator: Official chapter PDF retrieved; §4.4, Theorem 4.9, Poincare inequalities.

sections.Statement:
Let $d\ge1$, let $L_1,\ldots,L_d>0$, and let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^d(0,L_i)$. If $w\in C^1(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$ has zero mean, then
$$\int_\Omega |w(x)|^2\,dx\le \frac d2\sum_{i=1}^d L_i^2\int_\Omega |\partial_iw(x)|^2\,dx\le C_\Omega\int_\Omega |\nabla w(x)|^2\,dx,$$
where $C_\Omega=\frac d2\max_iL_i^2$. All integrals are the multidimensional Riemann integrals of continuous functions on the indicated closed rectangles, with the usual extension to their interiors.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** A dimension $d\ge1$, positive side lengths $L_i$, the open rectangle $\Omega=\prod_i(0,L_i)$, and $w\in C^1(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$ with $\int_\Omega w=0$.

[A1] The zero-mean condition is $\int_\Omega w(x)\,dx=0$.

[F1] [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]: if $G$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and its interior derivative has a Riemann-integrable extension $f$, then $\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a)$.

[F2] [[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]]: for a Riemann-integrable function on a product of nondegenerate closed rectangles, each section integral is integrable and the iterated integrals equal the multiple integral.
sections.Proof:
1.1 Expand the square in the product integral and use [A1]: $\int_\Omega\int_\Omega(w(x)-w(y))^2\,dy\,dx=2|\Omega|\int_\Omega w^2-2(\int_\Omega w)^2=2|\Omega|\int_\Omega w^2$. The integrand is continuous, so [F2] justifies the repeated integrals. [A1, F2, algebra]

1.2 For $x,y\in\Omega$, define $z^{(0)}=x$ and $z^{(i)}=(y_1,\ldots,y_i,x_{i+1},\ldots,x_d)$ for $1\le i\le d$, and set $\delta_i=w(z^{(i-1)})-w(z^{(i)})$. Then $w(x)-w(y)=\sum_i\delta_i$ and $d\sum_i\delta_i^2-(\sum_i\delta_i)^2=\sum_{i<j}(\delta_i-\delta_j)^2\ge0$. [given, algebra]

1.3 Fix $i$ and the other coordinates. By [F1], $\delta_i$ is the integral of $h=\partial_iw$ over the interval between $x_i$ and $y_i$. If the endpoints differ, let $\bar h$ be the average of $h$ on that interval. Nonnegativity of $\int(h-\bar h)^2$ gives $(\int h)^2\le |x_i-y_i|\int h^2$; if they agree, $\delta_i=0$. Since $|x_i-y_i|\le L_i$, in both cases $\delta_i^2\le L_i\int_0^{L_i}|\partial_iw(z_1,\ldots,z_{i-1},s,z_{i+1},\ldots,z_d)|^2\,ds$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Integrate the last bound over $x,y$. The $x_i,y_i$ integrations contribute $L_i^2$, the displayed segment bound contributes $L_i$, each unused variable from a pair $x_j,y_j$ with $j\ne i$ contributes $L_j$, and the remaining variables and $s$ give $\int_\Omega|\partial_iw|^2$. By [F2], this yields $\int_\Omega\int_\Omega\delta_i^2\,dy\,dx\le |\Omega|L_i^2\int_\Omega|\partial_iw|^2$. [F2, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 By step 1.2 and the finite squared-sum inequality, the double integral in step 1.1 is at most $d\sum_i\int_\Omega\int_\Omega\delta_i^2\,dy\,dx$. Apply step 2.1, divide by $2|\Omega|>0$, and use $\sum_iL_i^2|\partial_iw|^2\le(\max_iL_i^2)|\nabla w|^2$ pointwise. This gives both stated inequalities with the displayed $C_\Omega$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

references.locator: Complete 635-page PDF retrieved; ensembles and traces §§4.2–4.6 pp.192–217; Bose/Fermi models §§5.6–5.7 pp.277–303; 1D Ising §6.2.2 pp.330–333.

sections.Statement: For $q\in(0,1)$, the bosonic geometric law on $n\in\mathbb N_0$ with weights $(1-q)q^n$ has mean $q/(1-q)$ and variance $q/(1-q)^2=\mathbb E[n](1+\mathbb E[n])$; its relative standard deviation tends to $1$ as $q\uparrow1$. The fermionic two-state law on $n\in\{0,1\}$ with weights $1/(1+q)$ and $q/(1+q)$ has mean $q/(1+q)$ and variance $q/(1+q)^2=\mathbb E[n](1-\mathbb E[n])$. Here Bose and Fermi name these explicitly specified counting laws; no claim about a physical preparation is made.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The geometric and two-state laws with $q\in(0,1)$.

[A1] The bosonic states are $\mathbb N_0$ with weights proportional to $q^n$; the fermionic states are $\{0,1\}$ with weights proportional to $q^n$.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]] and [[thm-tdmath-summable-canonical-differentiation]]: countable canonical weights normalize when the partition sum is finite, and under the envelope the mean and variance follow from derivatives of $Z$.

[F2] [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]], [[def-expectation-on-a-finite-probability-space]], and [[def-variance-and-covariance]]: finite laws normalize and define means and variances by finite sums.

[F3] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[def-natural-logarithm]], and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: every $q\in(0,1)$ has the form $e^{-\gamma}$ with $\gamma=-\log q>0$.

[F4] [[thm-chain-rule]]: derivatives of the parameterized exponential and logarithm compositions obey the chain rule.

[F5] [[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]]: $n^k e^{-bn}\to0$ for each fixed integer $k$ and $b>0$.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The geometric and two-state laws with $q\in(0,1)$.

1.1 Let $S_N=\sum_{n=0}^Nq^n$. Multiplying this finite sum by $1-q$ gives $(1-q)S_N=1-q^{N+1}$. Since $q=e^{-\gamma}$ for $\gamma>0$, [F5] gives $q^{N+1}\to0$; hence $Z=(1-q)^{-1}$ and the weights $(1-q)q^n$ sum to one. On a compact $\gamma$-interval $[b,B]\subset(0,\infty)$, set $a_n=(1+n^2)e^{-bn}$. Then $a_{n+1}/a_n=e^{-b}(1+(n+1)^2)/(1+n^2)\to e^{-b}<1$. Choose $c$ with $e^{-b}<c<1$; for all sufficiently large $n$, $a_{n+1}\le ca_n$, so the tail is bounded by a convergent geometric series. Thus $\sum_n(1+n^2)e^{-\gamma n}\le\sum_na_n<\infty$, which is the local envelope required by [F1]. [A1, F1, F3, F5, algebra]

1.2 The fermionic partition sum is $1+q$; its two probabilities are $1/(1+q)$ and $q/(1+q)$. Their finite weighted sums give mean $q/(1+q)$ and variance $q/(1+q)^2$, equal to the mean times one minus the mean. [A1, F2, F3]

2.1 With $Z(\gamma)=(1-e^{-\gamma})^{-1}$, [F1] gives $\mathbb E n=-\partial_\gamma\log Z=q/(1-q)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(n)=\partial_\gamma^2\log Z=q/(1-q)^2$. Substitution $q=e^{-\gamma}$ and [F4] justify the parameter derivatives. Therefore $\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(n)}/\mathbb E n=1/\sqrt q\to1$ as $q\uparrow1$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 These are calculations for the two specified probability laws only; no independence, physical preparation, or measured fluctuation claim is used. [A1, step 2.1, step 1.2] ∎

      locator: "Complete 635-page PDF retrieved; ensembles and traces §§4.2–4.6 pp.192–217; Bose/Fermi models §§5.6–5.7 pp.277–303; 1D Ising §6.2.2 pp.330–333."

## Statement

For $q\in(0,1)$, the bosonic geometric law on $n\in\mathbb N_0$ with weights $(1-q)q^n$ has mean $q/(1-q)$ and variance $q/(1-q)^2=\mathbb E[n](1+\mathbb E[n])$; its relative standard deviation tends to $1$ as $q\uparrow1$. The fermionic two-state law on $n\in\{0,1\}$ with weights $1/(1+q)$ and $q/(1+q)$ has mean $q/(1+q)$ and variance $q/(1+q)^2=\mathbb E[n](1-\mathbb E[n])$. Here Bose and Fermi name these explicitly specified counting laws; no claim about a physical preparation is made.

## Facts & Assumptions


**Given:** The geometric and two-state laws with $q\in(0,1)$.

[A1] The bosonic states are $\mathbb N_0$ with weights proportional to $q^n$; the fermionic states are $\{0,1\}$ with weights proportional to $q^n$.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]] and [[thm-tdmath-summable-canonical-differentiation]]: countable canonical weights normalize when the partition sum is finite, and under the envelope the mean and variance follow from derivatives of $Z$.

[F2] [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]], [[def-expectation-on-a-finite-probability-space]], and [[def-variance-and-covariance]]: finite laws normalize and define means and variances by finite sums.

[F3] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[def-natural-logarithm]], and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: every $q\in(0,1)$ has the form $e^{-\gamma}$ with $\gamma=-\log q>0$.

[F4] [[thm-chain-rule]]: derivatives of the parameterized exponential and logarithm compositions obey the chain rule.

[F5] [[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]]: $n^k e^{-bn}\to0$ for each fixed integer $k$ and $b>0$.



## Proof

**Given:** The geometric and two-state laws with $q\in(0,1)$.

1.1 Let $S_N=\sum_{n=0}^Nq^n$. Multiplying this finite sum by $1-q$ gives $(1-q)S_N=1-q^{N+1}$. Since $q=e^{-\gamma}$ for $\gamma>0$, [F5] gives $q^{N+1}\to0$; hence $Z=(1-q)^{-1}$ and the weights $(1-q)q^n$ sum to one. On a compact $\gamma$-interval $[b,B]\subset(0,\infty)$, set $a_n=(1+n^2)e^{-bn}$. Then $a_{n+1}/a_n=e^{-b}(1+(n+1)^2)/(1+n^2)\to e^{-b}<1$. Choose $c$ with $e^{-b}<c<1$; for all sufficiently large $n$, $a_{n+1}\le ca_n$, so the tail is bounded by a convergent geometric series. Thus $\sum_n(1+n^2)e^{-\gamma n}\le\sum_na_n<\infty$, which is the local envelope required by [F1]. [A1, F1, F3, F5, algebra]

1.2 The fermionic partition sum is $1+q$; its two probabilities are $1/(1+q)$ and $q/(1+q)$. Their finite weighted sums give mean $q/(1+q)$ and variance $q/(1+q)^2$, equal to the mean times one minus the mean. [A1, F2, F3]

2.1 With $Z(\gamma)=(1-e^{-\gamma})^{-1}$, [F1] gives $\mathbb E n=-\partial_\gamma\log Z=q/(1-q)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(n)=\partial_\gamma^2\log Z=q/(1-q)^2$. Substitution $q=e^{-\gamma}$ and [F4] justify the parameter derivatives. Therefore $\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(n)}/\mathbb E n=1/\sqrt q\to1$ as $q\uparrow1$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 These are calculations for the two specified probability laws only; no independence, physical preparation, or measured fluctuation claim is used. [A1, step 2.1, step 1.2] ∎

sections.Statement:
Let $\beta,z>0$, let $\rho>0$ be an interior attainable density, and choose $\alpha=\log z$ supporting the free canonical rate $F_\beta$ at $\rho$. For either free or periodic boundary condition $b$, let $C^b_{L,N_L}$ be the exact-$N_L$ canonical law and $G^b_{L,z,\beta}$ the grand-canonical law using the same finite-volume energy, where $N_L/L^d\to\rho$. Assume
$$L^{-d}\log Z_b(L,N_L;\beta)\longrightarrow F_\beta(\rho).$$
Let $R_{L,\omega}$ be the periodized empirical field of [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]], and let
$$\mathcal M_{z,\beta}:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
Then for every open $\tau_L$ neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$ there is $c_U>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log C^b_{L,N_L}\{\,\omega:R_{L,\omega}\notin U\,\}\leq-c_U.$$
If $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}=\{P_*\}$, then $R_{L,\omega}\to P_*$ in probability in $\tau_L$ under $C^b_{L,N_L}$. This is a statement about spatially averaged local observables through the empirical field, not about the raw finite-box law at a fixed origin.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** A superstable regular interaction, $\beta,z>0$, an interior density $\rho$, exact particle numbers $N_L/L^d\to\rho$, the displayed canonical rate limit, and the same finite-volume boundary condition in the canonical and grand-canonical laws.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]: the canonical and Poisson-normalized partition conventions satisfy $Z_{Q,b}(L,N;\beta)=e^{-L^d}Z_b(L,N;\beta)$ for either boundary condition.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-canonical-grand-duality]]: a supporting $\alpha=\log z$ gives physical pressure $P(\alpha,\beta)=F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho$.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-continuum-variational-pressure]]: the normalized grand pressure is $p_Q(z,\beta)=P(\alpha,\beta)-1=-\min_P\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}$, and its minimizer set is nonempty and compact in $\tau_L$.

[F4] [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]] and [[lem-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field-stationary-density]]: $R_{L,\omega}$ is the stationary empirical field used by the grand empirical-field large-deviation principle.

[L1] Georgii's Theorem 2 (1994, Sections 3–5) gives, for superstable regular interactions, a good large-deviation principle in $\tau_L$ for these periodized empirical fields under both free and periodic grand-canonical Gibbs laws, with rate $I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z+p_Q(z,\beta)$. The complete proof was read; the chosen $b$ must be one of the two stated boundary conditions.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 The canonical law is the grand law conditioned on $N=N_L$, since the grand weight on the $N_L$ sector differs from the canonical density only by the constant activity factor $z^{N_L}$. Its conditioning probability is $$G^b_{L,z,\beta}(N=N_L)=\frac{z^{N_L}e^{-L^d}Z_b(L,N_L;\beta)}{Z_{Q,b}(L;z,\beta)}.$$ Divide the logarithm by $L^d$. The numerator terms tend to $\rho\log z+F_\beta(\rho)-1$ by the assumed canonical rate and [F1]; the denominator tends to $p_Q(z,\beta)$. By [F2]–[F3], $p_Q(z,\beta)=F_\beta(\rho)+\rho\log z-1$, so $$L^{-d}\log G^b_{L,z,\beta}(N=N_L)\longrightarrow0.$$ Thus the exact-number conditioning event has subexponential, positive grand probability for all sufficiently large $L$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Let $U$ be an open $\tau_L$ neighborhood of $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$ and set $F=U^c$. The good rate in [L1] has zero set exactly $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$. Its infimum on the closed set $F$ is strictly positive: otherwise a sequence in $F$ with rates tending to zero would lie in a compact rate sublevel, have a limit in $F$, and by lower semicontinuity that limit would be a zero of the rate outside $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$. The large-deviation upper bound therefore gives some $c>0$ with $$\limsup_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log G^b_{L,z,\beta}\{R_{L,\omega}\in F\}\leq-c.$$ [F3, F4, L1, algebra]

2.1 Conditioning on $N=N_L$ yields $$C^b_{L,N_L}\{R_{L,\omega}\notin U\}\leq \frac{G^b_{L,z,\beta}\{R_{L,\omega}\in F\}}{G^b_{L,z,\beta}(N=N_L)}.$$ The numerator decays exponentially by step 1.2 and the denominator has zero exponential rate by step 1.1, so the ratio tends to zero. This proves concentration on every neighborhood of $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$. If the minimizer is unique, these neighborhood bounds are exactly convergence in probability in $\tau_L$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

fm.title: Compound mass is well-defined and additive

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §§II.A.1–II.A.2

sections.Statement: For every tagged scalable compound $c$, the mass in [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] is independent of the finite summation set used. For any compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; $m(0)=0$. For every $x\in X$, the unit-state compound $e_x$ has $m(e_x)=1$. A compound has zero mass if and only if it is the empty compound.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
[F1] [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]: compounds are nonnegative finite-support functions, and mass is defined by a finite sum over support.

[F2] [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]] supplies bijective reindexing and splitting over disjoint finite sets. Enumerating a finite set expresses its real sum using [[def-finite-sum]]; additivity and scalar linearity then follow from clauses 1 and 2 of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. In particular, its sum of zero terms is zero, so disjoint splitting shows that adjoining zero terms leaves a sum unchanged. Clause 4 of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] gives nonnegativity of a sum of nonnegative terms and says that a zero sum forces each term to be zero.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** [F1] and [F2].

1.1 Let $E$ be any finite subset of $X$ containing $\operatorname{supp}(c)$. On $E\setminus\operatorname{supp}(c)$ the function is zero, so the finite sum over $E$ equals the finite sum over $\operatorname{supp}(c)$ by [F2]. If $E$ and $E'$ both contain the support, compare each sum to the sum over the finite union $E\cup E'$; hence the value is independent of the chosen finite summation set. [F1, F2]

2.1 The support of $c+d$ is contained in the finite union of the supports of $c$ and $d$. Sum over that union; distributivity in [F2] gives $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$, since zero terms outside each individual support contribute nothing by step 1.1. The support of $tc$ equals that of $c$ for $t>0$, and scalar linearity of the finite sum gives $m(tc)=t m(c)$. For $t=0$, $tc=0$ and both $m(tc)$ and $t m(c)$ are zero. The empty sum is zero, so $m(0)=0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 The support of $e_x$ is the singleton $\{x\}$, whose one summand is $1$, so the recursion in [F2] gives $m(e_x)=0+1=1$. If $m(c)=0$, sum its nonnegative coefficients over its finite support. Clause 4 in [F2] forces every summand to be zero; coefficients off the support are also zero, hence $c=0$. Conversely $c=0$ has zero mass by step 2.1. Thus all the claimed mass identities hold, including the empty and unit-state cases. [F1, F2, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

For every tagged scalable compound $c$, the mass in [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] is independent of the finite summation set used. For any compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; $m(0)=0$. For every $x\in X$, the unit-state compound $e_x$ has $m(e_x)=1$. A compound has zero mass if and only if it is the empty compound.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]: compounds are nonnegative finite-support functions, and mass is defined by a finite sum over support.

[F2] [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]] supplies bijective reindexing and splitting over disjoint finite sets. Enumerating a finite set expresses its real sum using [[def-finite-sum]]; additivity and scalar linearity then follow from clauses 1 and 2 of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. In particular, its sum of zero terms is zero, so disjoint splitting shows that adjoining zero terms leaves a sum unchanged. Clause 4 of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] gives nonnegativity of a sum of nonnegative terms and says that a zero sum forces each term to be zero.

## Proof

**Given:** [F1] and [F2].

1.1 Let $E$ be any finite subset of $X$ containing $\operatorname{supp}(c)$. On $E\setminus\operatorname{supp}(c)$ the function is zero, so the finite sum over $E$ equals the finite sum over $\operatorname{supp}(c)$ by [F2]. If $E$ and $E'$ both contain the support, compare each sum to the sum over the finite union $E\cup E'$; hence the value is independent of the chosen finite summation set. [F1, F2]

2.1 The support of $c+d$ is contained in the finite union of the supports of $c$ and $d$. Sum over that union; distributivity in [F2] gives $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$, since zero terms outside each individual support contribute nothing by step 1.1. The support of $tc$ equals that of $c$ for $t>0$, and scalar linearity of the finite sum gives $m(tc)=t m(c)$. For $t=0$, $tc=0$ and both $m(tc)$ and $t m(c)$ are zero. The empty sum is zero, so $m(0)=0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 The support of $e_x$ is the singleton $\{x\}$, whose one summand is $1$, so the recursion in [F2] gives $m(e_x)=0+1=1$. If $m(c)=0$, sum its nonnegative coefficients over its finite support. Clause 4 in [F2] forces every summand to be zero; coefficients off the support are also zero, hence $c=0$. Conversely $c=0$ has zero mass by step 2.1. Thus all the claimed mass identities hold, including the empty and unit-state cases. [F1, F2, step 2.1] ∎

fm.title: Conditional Log-Density Convergence for the Poisson Reference

references.title: \"X.X. Nguyen and H. Zessin, Ergodic theorems for spatial processes\"
references.locator: \"Section 6, Theorem 6.6 and proof, printed pp.149–150 / PDF pp.16–17, directed $L^1$ convergence of conditional log densities\"

references.title: \"H.-O. Georgii and H. Zessin, Large deviations and the maximum entropy principle for marked point random fields\"
references.locator: \"Section 2.3, printed p.184 / PDF p.7, specific Poisson-relative entropy and variational formula\"

sections.Statement:
Assume AC. Let $P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$, as defined in [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]], have finite specific relative entropy $I(P)=\gamma<\infty$ relative to the unit-intensity reference $Q$ of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. Let $C=[0,1)^d$ be the reference cell and order the other unit cells lexicographically; $F_+$ is the set of cells preceding $C$. For each finite $A\subset F_+$ let $k_A$ be the conditional density of the configuration in $C$ given the configuration in $A$, relative to $Q_C$, as supplied by [[thm-conditional-density-formula]]. Then
$$g(A):=E_P[\log k_A]=D(P_{A\cup C}\Vert Q_{A\cup C})-D(P_A\Vert Q_A)$$
is finite, nonnegative, and increasing with finite $A$, with $\sup\{g(A):A\subset F_+\text{ finite}\}=\gamma$. For any increasing finite exhaustion $A_m\uparrow F_+$, the densities $k_{A_m}$ converge in $L^1(P_{F_+}\otimes Q_C)$ to a density $k_\infty$ of $P_{F_+\cup C}$ relative to $P_{F_+}\otimes Q_C$, and
$$\log k_{A_m}\longrightarrow\log k_\infty\quad\text{in }L^1(P).$$
The logarithmic convergence is directed: for every $\varepsilon>0$ some finite $A_m$ satisfies $\sup_{B\supseteq A_m,\ B\subset F_+\text{ finite}}E_P|\log k_B-\log k_\infty|<\varepsilon$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** AC, dimension $d\geq1$, a stationary law $P$ with $I(P)=\gamma<\infty$, the cell partition and its lexicographic order.

[A1] AC is inherited from the Poisson reference construction and used by the conditional density and uniformly integrable martingale suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], [[thm-conditional-density-formula]], [[thm-uniformly-integrable-martingale-convergence]]).

[F1] For $P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$, finite specific entropy implies every bounded-region restriction has finite relative entropy; its normalized cube entropies converge to $\gamma$ ([[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]], [[thm-tdmath-specific-entropy-density]]).

[F2] Independent Poisson reference increments, the conditional entropy chain rule, its variational form, and monotonicity under added conditioning ([[thm-tdmath-poisson-reference-count-properties]], [[lem-tdmath-relative-entropy-variational-and-chain-rules]]).

[F3] A nonnegative uniformly integrable martingale converges almost surely and in $L^1$ ([[thm-uniformly-integrable-martingale-convergence]]).

[F4] On a probability space, uniform integrability plus convergence in probability implies $L^1$ convergence ([[thm-uniform-integrability-plus-probability-convergence-implies-l1-convergence]]).

[F5] Monotone convergence and Fatou apply to the nonnegative truncations and entropy densities used below ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[thm-fatou-lemma]]).

[F6] Agreement of finite measures on a generating pi-system implies agreement on the generated sigma-algebra ([[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]).
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Let $A\subset F_+$ be finite. By [F1], $D(P_{A\cup C}\Vert Q_{A\cup C})$ is finite, so the joint density $h_{A,C}$ relative to $Q_A\otimes Q_C$ exists. The marginal density $h_A$ is its $Q_C$ integral. On $0<h_A<\infty$, [F2] gives the conditional density $k_A=h_{A,C}/h_A$ relative to $Q_C$; the exceptional fibers have $P_A$-measure zero. The chain rule in [F2] gives $g(A)=E_P D(P_{C|A}\Vert Q_C)=D(P_{A\cup C}\Vert Q_{A\cup C})-D(P_A\Vert Q_A)$, so $g(A)$ is finite and nonnegative. [A1, F1, F2, construct]

sections.Statement: Let $M$ and $R$ take values in finite sets under a joint probability law $p(m,r)\ge0$ with $\sum_{m,r}p(m,r)=1$. For any finite random variable $Y$ with law $p_Y$, define its Shannon entropy by $H(Y):=-\sum_{y:p_Y(y)>0}p_Y(y)\log p_Y(y)$; for a pair, $H(M,R)$ means this definition applied to its joint law. sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** As stated in the item.

[A1] $M,R$ take values in finite sets under the joint probability law $p(m,r)$.

**Given:** A finite joint probability law for $M$ and $R$.

1.1 For every $r$ with $a_r>0$, the numbers $q(m|r)$ are nonnegative and sum to one. sections.Statement: Let a family of simple domains satisfy [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], and suppose every pair has an admitted simple thermal join satisfying T1 and T2 of [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Then the fixed-work orientation signs from [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]] agree throughout the family. One common affine proof-coordinate convention $u'=\varepsilon u$, $\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, therefore makes each fixed-work accessibility order increase with $u'$ and preserves the energy-sum formula for joins. This is a mathematical coordinate convention; it does not change a physical energy quantity or assert a sign of a measured temperature.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: the component charts are open, represented states have their positive type weights, and the relation is composition-consistent and transitive.

[A2] [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]: T1 sends every admissible split to its join; T2 supplies, for each join state, at least one admissible split accessible in both directions to that join state, at the same summed energy and work coordinates.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]]: each component domain has a constant sign $\varepsilon_\Gamma$ with fixed-work comparison equivalent to $\varepsilon_\Gamma(u_y-u_x)\ge0$.

sections.Statement: Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be finite and convex. For every $x_0\in U$, there are a neighborhood $V$ of $x_0$ and $L<\infty$ such that $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|$ for all $x,y\in V$. The same conclusion holds for finite concave functions by applying the result to $-f$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The open convex domain, finite-valued function, and Euclidean norm.

[F1] [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]: line segments and finite convex combinations of points in a convex set remain in that set.
sections.Proof:
1.1 Choose a closed cube centered at $x_0$ whose concentric dilation by factor $2$ lies in $U$. Every point of the cube is a convex combination of its finitely many vertices, so [F1] and convexity bound $f$ above there by the largest vertex value $M$. If $x$ lies in the cube, then $2x_0-x$ lies in the dilated cube; convexity gives $f(x_0)\le(f(x)+f(2x_0-x))/2$, hence $f(x)\ge2f(x_0)-M'$, where $M'$ is the finite upper bound on the dilated cube. Thus $f$ is bounded above and below on a ball about $x_0$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Choose concentric balls $B(x_0,r)\subset B(x_0,2r)\subset U$ on which $m\le f\le M$. For distinct $x,y\in B(x_0,r/2)$, extend the segment from $x$ through $y$ to $z=y+(r/2)(y-x)/\|y-x\|$, which lies in $B(x_0,2r)$. Put $\theta=\|y-x\|/(r/2+\|y-x\|)$, so $y=(1-\theta)x+\theta z$. Convexity yields $f(y)-f(x)\le\theta(M-m)\le(2(M-m)/r)\|y-x\|$. Repeating with $x,y$ interchanged gives the reverse bound. Negation proves the concave case. [step 1.1, F1, algebra] ∎

sections.Statement: Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for every simple state $x$, the forward sector $A_x=\{y\in\Gamma_i:x\prec y\}$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$. For collinear $y=tx+(1-t)z$, $0<t<1$, $y\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$, and $x\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** A1–A7 and S1–S3 on a nonempty open convex domain $\Gamma_i$.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: A1–A7 include consistency, scaling, splitting, convex-combination access, and stability for positive spectators.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-relative-interior-segment]]: a nonempty convex set has nonempty relative interior, and segments from a relative-interior point to a closure point, excluding the closure endpoint, remain in the relative interior.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellation]]: any finite common spectator cancels when the two bases have equal mass, under A1–A6 without CH.
sections.Proof:
1.1 If $x\prec y$ and $x\prec z$, splitting gives $x\sim(tx,(1-t)x)$. Consistency, positive scaling, and transitivity then give $(tx,(1-t)x)\prec(ty,(1-t)z)$. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] gives $(ty,(1-t)z)\prec ty+(1-t)z$, so the convex combination belongs to $A_x$. [A1, algebra]

1.2 Let $y=tx+(1-t)z$ with $0<t<1$. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] gives $(tx,(1-t)z)\prec y$. Splitting gives $y\sim(ty,(1-t)y)$. If $y\prec z$, scaling by $1-t$ and adding $ty$ gives $(ty,(1-t)y)\prec(ty,(1-t)z)$. Compose and cancel the common $(1-t)z$ by [F2], then scale by $1/t$, to get $x\prec y$. If instead $x\prec z$, scaling by $1-t$ and adding $tx$ gives $(tx,(1-t)x)\prec(tx,(1-t)z)\prec y$; recombination gives $x\prec y$. [A1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Take $y\in\overline{A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$. If $y\in A_x$, the claim is immediate. Otherwise choose $w\in\operatorname{ri} A_x$ by [F1]. Because $\Gamma_i$ is open, choose $z=w+(1+\eta)(y-w)\in\Gamma_i$ for some $\eta>0$. For every integer $n>1+\eta$, $y_n=(1+1/n)y-z/n=w+(1-\eta/n)(y-w)$ lies in $\operatorname{ri}A_x$ by [F1], so $x\prec y_n$. Also $y=\frac{n}{n+1}y_n+\frac1{n+1}z$. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] gives $(\frac n{n+1}y_n,\frac1{n+1}z)\prec y$; scaling by $(n+1)/n$ and using the reversible split of $y$ gives $(y_n,z/n)\prec(y,y/n)$. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Consistency adds the same spectator $z/n$ to $x\prec y_n$, and transitivity with step 2.1 gives $(x,z/n)\prec(y,y/n)$ for every $n>1+\eta$. Apply the stability hypothesis in [A1] to bases $x,y$, fixed positive equal-mass represented spectators $z,y$, and the tail sequence $\epsilon_m=1/(m+n_0)$ with $n_0>1+\eta$. It follows that $x\prec y$. Thus every relative closure point belongs to $A_x$. [A1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §VI.B, pp. 76–79

sections.Statement: For the construction in [[def-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space]], $\approx_0$ is an equivalence compatible with product and positive scaling; $V_F$ is a real vector space and its displayed operations are representative-independent.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The decorated cost algebra, type composition and scaling, and the formal pair relation in the Definition.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space]]: types are identified at zero cost in both directions, and a pair difference is identified after adding a common catalyst type.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-decorated-cost-algebra]]: costs satisfy nonnegative closed-cycle bounds, triangle inequalities, translation invariance, and positive homogeneity.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: reversible splitting and recombination are allowed for every positive scaled amount.
sections.Proof:
1.1 The relation $\approx_0$ is reflexive because $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$, and symmetric by definition. Suppose $\Gamma\approx_0\Gamma'$ and $\Gamma'\approx_0\Gamma''$. The triangle inequality gives both directed costs between $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma''$ at most zero. For any $\epsilon>0$, choose a finite reverse witness of cost $d<\epsilon$; such witnesses exist because the reverse infimum is zero. Every forward witness of cost $c$ closes with it, so [F2] gives $c+d\ge0$, hence $c>-\epsilon$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ shows every forward witness has nonnegative cost and its infimum is at least zero; the same argument reverses the direction. Both infima are therefore zero, proving transitivity. The same argument proves product compatibility: subadditivity makes both product costs at most zero, and any finite reverse witness bounds every forward product witness below by a quantity tending to zero. Positive homogeneity gives scaling compatibility directly. Thus $\approx_0$ is an equivalence compatible with product and positive scaling, and the quotient is a commutative monoid. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Reversible splitting [A1] gives accessible transitions in both directions between $(s+t)\Gamma$ and $s\Gamma\times t\Gamma$. Extensivity makes each such edge have zero entropy cost. Any reverse witness bounds all forward costs below by [F2]'s closed-cycle inequality, so both infima are zero. Hence $(s+t)\Gamma\approx_0 s\Gamma\times t\Gamma$. The empty type $1$ is an identity under composition; its reassociation and permutation identifications have zero cost by the type conventions. [A1, F1, F2]

2.1 The pair relation $\equiv$ is reflexive using unit catalyst $1$ and symmetric by swapping the two sides. Suppose $(A,B)\equiv(A',B')$ via catalyst $C$, and $(A',B')\equiv(A'',B'')$ via catalyst $D$. Their witnesses are
$A\times B'\times C\approx_0 A'\times B\times C,\qquad
A'\times B''\times D\approx_0 A''\times B'\times D.$
Multiply the first equivalence by $B''\times D$, the second by $B\times C$, and compose. Reassociating and permuting gives
$A\times B''\times(B'\times C\times D)\approx_0 A''\times B\times(B'\times C\times D),$
which witnesses $(A,B)\equiv(A'',B'')$. Hence $\equiv$ is an equivalence relation. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $(A,B)\equiv(A',B')$ via $C$, so $A\times B'\times C\approx_0 A'\times B\times C$. For an arbitrary pair $(D,E)$, multiply this witness by $D\times E$. Reassociation gives $(A\times D)\times(B'\times E)\times C\approx_0(A'\times D)\times(B\times E)\times C$, exactly the witness for $(A\times D,B\times E)\equiv(A'\times D,B'\times E)$. Apply the same argument to a change of representative of $(D,E)$ and use transitivity; addition is representative-independent. Scaling a catalyst witness by $t>0$ and using product compatibility from step 1.1 proves that positive scalar multiplication is representative-independent. Product commutativity and associativity give the additive laws, and the empty type gives $(A\times1,B\times1)=(A,B)$. Swapping a pair gives an inverse: its sum with $(A,B)$ is $(A\times B,B\times A)$, equivalent to $(1,1)$ with unit catalyst because the two product types agree up to permutation and have zero cost in both directions. Thus the classes form an abelian group with zero $[(1,1)]$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 For $t>0$, the displayed operation $t(A,B)=(tA,tB)$ satisfies $t(v+w)=tv+tw$ because scaling distributes over type composition, and $t(sv)=(ts)v$ for $s>0$ by associativity of type scaling. Also $1v=v$. The scalar-addition law for positive $s,t$ follows from step 1.2:
$(s+t)[A,B]=[(s+t)A,(s+t)B]=[sA\times tA,sB\times tB]=s[A,B]+t[A,B].$
The zero scalar is defined as the additive identity, and $(-t)v$ is defined as $t(-v)$, where $-v$ swaps the pair. [F1, step 1.2, step 3.1]

5.1 The positive scalar laws extend to negative scalars by swapping pairs. For the scalar-addition law with opposite signs, write $s-t$ with $s,t\ge0$. If $s\ge t$, positive scalar addition gives $sv=(s-t)v+tv$, so cancellation in the additive group gives $(s-t)v=sv-tv$; if $t>s$, apply the same identity to $t=(t-s)+s$ and negate. Cases with zero are immediate. For scalar composition, write each nonzero scalar as its sign times a positive magnitude; the defined action swaps the pair once for each negative sign and scales by the product of magnitudes, so $(rs)v=r(sv)$, with zero cases immediate. For distributivity over vector addition, positive scalars distribute by step 4.1 and a negative scalar distributes by taking the additive inverse of that identity. Together with the abelian-group laws in step 3.1, these are all real-vector-space axioms. [F1, step 4.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
