1.1 The relation $\approx_0$ is reflexive because $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$, and symmetric by definition. Suppose $\Gamma\approx_0\Gamma'$ and $\Gamma'\approx_0\Gamma''$. The triangle inequality gives both directed costs between $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma''$ at most zero. For any $\epsilon>0$, choose a finite reverse witness of cost $d<\epsilon$; such witnesses exist because the reverse infimum is zero. Every forward witness of cost $c$ closes with it, so [F2] gives $c+d\ge0$, hence $c>-\epsilon$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ shows every forward witness has nonnegative cost and its infimum is at least zero; the same argument reverses the direction. Both infima are therefore zero, proving transitivity. The same argument proves product compatibility: subadditivity makes both product costs at most zero, and any finite reverse witness bounds every forward product witness below by a quantity tending to zero. Positive homogeneity gives scaling compatibility directly. Thus $\approx_0$ is an equivalence compatible with product and positive scaling, and the quotient is a commutative monoid. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Reversible splitting [A1] gives accessible transitions in both directions between $(s+t)\Gamma$ and $s\Gamma\times t\Gamma$. Extensivity makes each such edge have zero entropy cost. Any reverse witness bounds all forward costs below by [F2]'s closed-cycle inequality, so both infima are zero. Hence $(s+t)\Gamma\approx_0 s\Gamma\times t\Gamma$. The empty type $1$ is an identity under composition; its reassociation and permutation identifications have zero cost by the type conventions. [A1, F1, F2]

$A\times B'\times C\approx_0 A'\times B\times C,\qquad
A'\times B''\times D\approx_0 A''\times B'\times D.$
Multiply the first equivalence by $B''\times D$, the second by $B\times C$, and compose. Reassociating and permuting gives
$A\times B''\times(B'\times C\times D)\approx_0 A''\times B\times(B'\times C\times D),$

Product commutativity and associativity give the additive laws, and the empty type gives $(A\times1,B\times1)=(A,B)$. $(s+t)[A,B]=[(s+t)A,(s+t)B]=[sA\times tA,sB\times tB]=s[A,B]+t[A,B].$
The zero scalar is defined as the additive identity, and $(-t)v$ is defined as $t(-v)$, where $-v$ swaps the pair. [F1, step 1.2, step 3.1]

Cases with zero are immediate. For scalar composition, write each nonzero scalar as its sign times a positive magnitude; the defined action swaps the pair once for each negative sign and scales by the product of magnitudes, so $(rs)v=r(sv)$, with zero cases immediate. sections.Statement:

For each Borel $B\subseteq C$, let $N_B(\eta)=\#(\eta\cap B)$. Then

sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The finite simple configurations and sorted-list Borel structure in the Statement.

[F1] Finite products carry the product sigma-algebra generated by measurable rectangles, and finite products of standard Borel spaces are standard Borel ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-standard-borel-space]], [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

[F2] A pi-system generating a sigma-algebra determines every lambda-system containing it ([[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]).

[F3] The half-open dyadic intervals of side $2^{-m}$ form a finite Borel partition of $[0,1)$ at each $m\in\mathbb N$; integer exponents and the natural-number index use their stated domains ([[def-half-open-box]], [[def-natural-numbers]], [[def-integers]], [[def-integer-power]]).
sections.Proof:
**Given:** $d\geq1$ and the finite configurations in the Statement.

1.1 On the component of configurations with exactly $n$ points, $N_B(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{j=1}^n\mathbf1_B(x_j)$ is Borel for every Borel $B\subseteq C$. The count of $C$ identifies the component $n$, so every count map is Borel on the full disjoint union. Thus the count-generated sigma-algebra is contained in the sorted-list Borel sigma-algebra. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Let $(T,\mathcal T)$ be any measurable space. For $H\in\mathcal B(C)\otimes\mathcal T$, define $M_H(\eta,t)=\sum_{x\in\eta}\mathbf1_H(x,t)$. The class of such $H$ for which $M_H$ is measurable with respect to the count sigma-algebra times $\mathcal T$ contains every rectangle $A\times D$, since $M_{A\times D}(\eta,t)=N_A(\eta)\mathbf1_D(t)$. It is closed under relative complements because $M_{(C\times T)\setminus H}=N_C-M_H$, and under disjoint countable unions by pointwise convergence of finite partial sums. Rectangles form a generating pi-system, so [F2] proves measurability for every product-measurable $H$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Fix a component with $n$ distinct points and an index $k\leq n$. Recover the coordinates of the $k$th lexicographic point recursively. Initially the selected prefix is empty and its rank is $r=k$. At coordinate $j$, with measurable prefix $p=(a_1,\ldots,a_{j-1})$, use step 2.1 on the Borel set $H_j=\{(x,p,t):x_\ell=p_\ell\ (\ell<j),\ x_j<t\}$, where $t\in[0,1]$. The count of matching points with $x_j<a_j$ is $M_{H_j}(\eta,p,a_j)$, measurable by step 2.1 after composition with the measurable prefix and $a_j$. Subtracting it from $r$ gives the positive rank among points with the extended prefix. [F3, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The recursive choice in step 3.1 is the usual lexicographic ordering rule: among points with a fixed prefix, sort by the next coordinate, retain the value at the current rank, then subtract the points strictly below it to obtain the rank among ties. sections.Statement: For the cost $F$ of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]], $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$, $F$ is positively homogeneous, invariant under adding the same catalyst to both endpoints, and satisfies the triangle inequality whenever the extended-real sum on its right is defined. It is subadditive under composition whenever $F(\Gamma_1,\Gamma'_1)+F(\Gamma_2,\Gamma'_2)$ is defined. Every pair of actual forward and reverse decorated-chain witnesses has nonnegative total cost. A finite reverse witness therefore bounds all forward costs below; $F=-\infty$ can occur only when the reverse direction has no witness.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** A1–A6 on accessible finite compounds, the additive extensive entropy $\sigma$, and the decorated-chain definition.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: accessibility is reflexive, transitive, consistent under common spectators, and positively scalable; stability is available.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]]: each chain has a finite real cost, and $F$ is its infimum, with empty infimum $+\infty$.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-arbitrary-family-calibration]]: $\sigma$ is additive and extensive on every separated finite compound and represents same-type comparisons.
sections.Proof:
1.1 A reflexive identity edge from any nonempty state of $\Gamma$ to itself has cost zero, so $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)\le0$. For a decorated closed chain, start with the compound containing every edge input $a_0,\ldots,a_{N-1}$. Apply the edge $a_0\prec b_1$ with all other edge inputs as spectators, then apply $a_1\prec b_2$ with the already produced $b_1$ and all still-unused inputs as spectators, and continue through $a_{N-1}\prec b_N$. Consistency and transitivity give $\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}a_k\prec\sum_{k=1}^{N}b_k$. Since $T_N=T_0$ and the intermediate types occur once on each side, these two compounds have the same total type up to the declared reassociation and permutation. Their entropy difference is exactly the chain cost. The same-type entropy representation [F2] makes this difference nonnegative. Hence every closed-chain witness costs at least zero and $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$. [A1, F1, F2, construct]

1.2 Take finite witnesses for $(\Gamma_1,\Gamma'_1)$ and $(\Gamma_2,\Gamma'_2)$. Run the first chain with a fixed state of $\Gamma_2$ and its second catalyst as spectators; then run the second chain with the first chain's output state and first catalyst as spectators. Consistency allows both sequences, and each fixed spectator contributes zero entropy difference. The resulting witness from $\Gamma_1\times\Gamma_2$ to $\Gamma'_1\times\Gamma'_2$ has the sum of the two costs. If both infima are finite real numbers, choose witnesses within $\epsilon/2$ of each infimum and let $\epsilon\downarrow0$. If one infimum is $-\infty$ and the other is finite, use a fixed finite witness for the latter and arbitrarily negative witnesses for the former; the product costs are unbounded below. If both are $-\infty$, choose both costs arbitrarily negative, so the product infimum is $-\infty$. If either is $+\infty$ and the other is not $-\infty$, the right side is $+\infty$ and the inequality is automatic. The mixed extended sum $+\infty+(-\infty)$ is undefined and is excluded by the Statement. [A1, F1, F2, construct]

1.3 A witness for $F(\Gamma\times C_0,\Gamma'\times C_0)$ is a witness for $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$ with enlarged catalyst $C_0\times C$, so $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')\le F(\Gamma\times C_0,\Gamma'\times C_0)$. Conversely, add one fixed state of the nonempty catalyst $C_0$ to every edge of an arbitrary witness for $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$. Its cost is unchanged, proving the reverse inequality. Thus $F(\Gamma\times C_0,\Gamma'\times C_0)=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$. [A1, F1, F2]

2.1 Scaling every state, type, and catalyst in a witness by $t>0$ multiplies its cost by $t$ because $\sigma_{tT}(ta)=t\sigma_T(a)$. This gives $F(t\Gamma,t\Gamma')\le tF(\Gamma,\Gamma')$; applying the same argument with scale $1/t$ gives equality, including the extended values. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Concatenate a witness from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma'$ with one from $\Gamma'$ to $\Gamma''$, adding the other chain's fixed catalyst state as spectator to each edge. The result is a witness from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma''$ whose cost is the sum. Taking finite approximations proves the triangle inequality when both costs are finite; an unbounded-below term with a finite witness in the other direction gives the corresponding $-\infty$ case; if a term is $+\infty$ and the sum is defined, the inequality is automatic. For an actual forward witness and an actual reverse witness with possibly different catalysts, add the reverse catalyst's fixed state to every forward edge and the forward catalyst's fixed state to every reverse edge. Consistency supplies these padded edges, and additivity makes each edge cost unchanged. The padded chains now have the same catalyst, so concatenate them into a closed chain; step 1.1 gives $c+d\ge0$. Thus any fixed finite reverse witness of cost $d$ bounds every forward witness below by $-d$. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct] ∎

sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** As stated in the item.

references.title: Daniel Arovas, Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, §2.7

sections.Statement:
Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Suppose that for every $x\in C$ there is a nondegenerate interval $J_x\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $1$ such that $\lambda x\in C$ and $f(\lambda x)=\lambda f(x)$ for every $\lambda\in J_x$. Here nondegenerate means that $J_x$ contains a point different from $1$; $1$ may be an endpoint. Then

$$f(x)=Df(x)[x]=\sum_{j=1}^d x_j\,\partial_j f(x)\qquad(x\in C).$$

The radial identity need only hold on one side of $1$: openness of $C$ and $C^1$ regularity supply an ambient derivative, and the interval makes $1$ a nonisolated point at which that derivative is determined by the radial identity. This uses the same function on the same domain; it asserts nothing about a family of functions on different tagged domains.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The open domain $C$, the $C^1$ function $f$, and for each $x\in C$ the stated radial homogeneity on a nondegenerate interval containing $\lambda=1$.

[F1] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: If $f$ and $g$ are totally differentiable at the relevant points, then $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$.
sections.Proof:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $x\in C$. Openness of $C$ and continuity of $\lambda\mapsto\lambda x$ give an open interval $K_x\subset(0,\infty)$ around $1$ with $\lambda x\in C$ for $\lambda\in K_x$. Define $g:K_x\to\mathbb R$ by $g(\lambda)=f(\lambda x)$. By [F1], $g'(1)=Df(x)[x]$. This ambient derivative exists even if $1$ is an endpoint of the interval $J_x$ on which homogeneity is assumed. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Since $J_x$ is a nondegenerate interval containing $1$, it contains points $\lambda\ne1$ arbitrarily close to $1$, also lying in $K_x$. For these points, homogeneity and $g(1)=f(x)$ give $(g(\lambda)-g(1))/(\lambda-1)=f(x)$. The ambient derivative in step 1.1 exists, so its limit along this possibly one-sided set is $g'(1)=f(x)$. Therefore $f(x)=Df(x)[x]$, and writing the total derivative in Euclidean coordinates gives $Df(x)[x]=\sum_{j=1}^d x_j\partial_j f(x)$. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

sections.Statement: Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable. Then $\int\liminf_{n\to\infty} f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** As stated in the item.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]: nonnegative integrals are monotone and the integral of a nonnegative measurable function is defined by simple minorants.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-monotone-convergence]]: integrals commute with increasing pointwise limits, including infinite values.

[A1] The sequence $f_n$ is nonnegative and measurable on the stated measure space.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** A measure space and measurable $f_n\ge0$.

1.1 Set $h_k:=\inf_{n\ge k}f_n$. For each real $a$, $\{h_k<a\}=\bigcup_{n\ge k}\{f_n<a\}$, so $h_k$ is measurable by the sigma-algebra closure in [F1]. The sequence $h_k$ is increasing and its pointwise limit is $\liminf_n f_n$, which is measurable since $\{\lim_kh_k>a\}=\bigcup_k\{h_k>a\}$. [F1, A1]

2.1 For every $n\ge k$, monotonicity gives $\int h_k\le\int f_n$, so $\int h_k\le\inf_{n\ge k}\int f_n$. Taking $k\to\infty$ and applying monotone convergence to $h_k$ yields $\int\liminf f_n=\lim_k\int h_k\le\lim_k\inf_{n\ge k}\int f_n=\liminf_n\int f_n$. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

**Given:** A measure space and measurable $f_n\ge0$.

sections.Statement: Let a finite canonical model have energies $E_i$, ground energy $E_0$, and exactly $g\ge1$ states at $E_0$, with every other energy strictly larger. As $\beta\to+\infty$, each ground-state probability tends to $1/g$, each excited-state probability tends to zero, and the Shannon entropy $-\sum_i p_i(\beta)\log p_i(\beta)$ tends to $\log g$. This is a finite-model statement only.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** As stated in the item.

[A1] The state set is finite and nonempty, $E_0=\min_iE_i$, exactly $g$ states attain it, and every remaining gap $E_i-E_0$ is positive.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]: finite canonical weights are $p_i=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$ and Shannon entropy uses natural logarithms.

[F2] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[def-natural-logarithm]], and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: exponential is positive; logarithms convert products to sums and are continuous on positive reals.

[F3] [[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]]: $\beta e^{-\beta\Delta}\to0$ for every fixed $\Delta>0$.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** A finite energy list with ground energy $E_0$, degeneracy $g\ge1$, and positive gaps for all other states.

1.1 Factor $e^{-\beta E_0}$ from the partition sum to obtain $Z=e^{-\beta E_0}(g+\sum_{i:E_i>E_0}e^{-\beta(E_i-E_0)})$. Every gap is positive, and there are finitely many, so the parenthesized sum tends to $g$. Thus each ground probability tends to $1/g$ and every excited probability tends to zero. [A1, F1, F2]

2.1 Ground-state entropy terms tend to $-g(1/g)\log(1/g)=\log g$. For an excited state with gap $\Delta_i>0$, step 1.1 gives $p_i=O(e^{-\beta\Delta_i})$ and $\log p_i=-\beta\Delta_i-\log D(\beta)$, where $D(\beta):=g+\sum_{j:E_j>E_0}e^{-\beta(E_j-E_0)}\to g>0$ by step 1.1, so $\log D(\beta)$ is bounded by continuity of $\log$; hence $|p_i\log p_i|=O((1+\beta)e^{-\beta\Delta_i})\to0$ by [F3]. The excited sum is finite, so its limit is zero and the total entropy tends to $\log g$. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

sections.Statement: Under A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for compounds $A,B$ with $m(A)=m(B)$ and every finite spectator compound $C$, $A+C\prec B+C$ if and only if $A\prec B$. Consequently, for finite-support signed maps $u,v$ of equal total coefficient, define $u\preceq_s v$ by $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$. This relation is well-defined, agrees with $\prec$ on nonnegative maps, is invariant under adding a common signed map, is transitive, and is closed under addition of two comparisons. No comparison hypothesis is used.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** Finite-support nonnegative compound maps, equal-mass comparisons, and A1–A6.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: the compound relation is reflexive and transitive, composition-consistent, positively scale-invariant, admits splitting/recombination, and satisfies the stated fixed-spectator stability axiom. It does not assume CH.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]: compounds are finite-support nonnegative maps; their total coefficient masses add under composition and scale under nonnegative dilation. [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]] also proves that zero mass is equivalent to the empty map; the spectator need not have the same mass as either base.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-forward-signed-comparison]]: for equal-total finite-support maps $u,v$, $u\preceq_s v$ means $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$, with common signed translation leaving the difference unchanged.
sections.Proof:
1.1 Assume $A+C\prec B+C$ and $m(C)>0$. Scaling by $1/n$ gives $A/n+C/n\prec B/n+C/n$. Define $E_j=(n-j)A/n+jB/n+C/n$ for $j=0,\ldots,n$. For $j<n$, add the common spectator $(n-j-1)A/n+jB/n$ to the scaled comparison to obtain $E_j\prec E_{j+1}$. Transitivity yields $A+C/n=E_0\prec E_n=B+C/n$. Stability with bases $A,B$, fixed positive spectators $C,C$, and $\epsilon_n=1/n$ gives $A\prec B$. If $m(C)=0$, nonnegativity gives $C=0$ and the implication is immediate. Conversely, consistency gives $A+C\prec B+C$ from $A\prec B$. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 For equal-total signed maps $u,v$, the difference $d=v-u$ has finite support and total coefficient zero, so $m(d^+)=m(d^-)$. If $u,v$ are nonnegative, their pointwise common part $k(x)=\min\{u(x),v(x)\}$ gives $u=k+d^-$ and $v=k+d^+$. Cancellation in step 1.1 proves $u\prec v$ exactly when $d^-\prec d^+$, which by [F2] is $u\preceq_s v$; adding a common signed map leaves $d$ unchanged by [F2]. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 If $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s w$, [F2] identifies these with comparisons of $(v-u)^-$ to $(v-u)^+$ and $(w-v)^-$ to $(w-v)^+$. Consistency combines them. Their pointwise common minimum cancels by step 1.1, leaving $(w-u)^-\prec(w-u)^+$, which [F2] identifies as $u\preceq_s w$. ## Statement

Under A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for compounds $A,B$ with $m(A)=m(B)$ and every finite spectator compound $C$, $A+C\prec B+C$ if and only if $A\prec B$. Consequently, for finite-support signed maps $u,v$ of equal total coefficient, define $u\preceq_s v$ by $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$. This relation is well-defined, agrees with $\prec$ on nonnegative maps, is invariant under adding a common signed map, is transitive, and is closed under addition of two comparisons. No comparison hypothesis is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Finite-support nonnegative compound maps, equal-mass comparisons, and A1–A6.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: the compound relation is reflexive and transitive, composition-consistent, positively scale-invariant, admits splitting/recombination, and satisfies the stated fixed-spectator stability axiom. It does not assume CH.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]: compounds are finite-support nonnegative maps; their total coefficient masses add under composition and scale under nonnegative dilation. [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]] also proves that zero mass is equivalent to the empty map; the spectator need not have the same mass as either base.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-forward-signed-comparison]]: for equal-total finite-support maps $u,v$, $u\preceq_s v$ means $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$, with common signed translation leaving the difference unchanged.

## Proof

1.1 Assume $A+C\prec B+C$ and $m(C)>0$. Scaling by $1/n$ gives $A/n+C/n\prec B/n+C/n$. Define $E_j=(n-j)A/n+jB/n+C/n$ for $j=0,\ldots,n$. For $j<n$, add the common spectator $(n-j-1)A/n+jB/n$ to the scaled comparison to obtain $E_j\prec E_{j+1}$. Transitivity yields $A+C/n=E_0\prec E_n=B+C/n$. Stability with bases $A,B$, fixed positive spectators $C,C$, and $\epsilon_n=1/n$ gives $A\prec B$. If $m(C)=0$, nonnegativity gives $C=0$ and the implication is immediate. Conversely, consistency gives $A+C\prec B+C$ from $A\prec B$. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 For equal-total signed maps $u,v$, the difference $d=v-u$ has finite support and total coefficient zero, so $m(d^+)=m(d^-)$. If $u,v$ are nonnegative, their pointwise common part $k(x)=\min\{u(x),v(x)\}$ gives $u=k+d^-$ and $v=k+d^+$. Cancellation in step 1.1 proves $u\prec v$ exactly when $d^-\prec d^+$, which by [F2] is $u\preceq_s v$; adding a common signed map leaves $d$ unchanged by [F2]. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 If $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s w$, [F2] identifies these with comparisons of $(v-u)^-$ to $(v-u)^+$ and $(w-v)^-$ to $(w-v)^+$. Consistency combines them. Their pointwise common minimum cancels by step 1.1, leaving $(w-u)^-\prec(w-u)^+$, which [F2] identifies as $u\preceq_s w$. The same finite-sum argument proves closure under addition; reflexivity follows from reflexivity of the zero compound. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

sections.Statement:
Let $d\geq1$ and let $\phi$ be a regular potential with a nonnegative nonincreasing envelope $\psi:[R_0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, where $R_0<\infty$ and $\int_{R_0}^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr<\infty$. Thus $|\phi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ for $|x|_\infty\geq R_0$. For $g>2R_0$ set
$$\eta(g)=g^d\psi(g)+\int_g^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr.$$
Then $\eta(g)\to0$ and
$$\sum_{m=1}^\infty m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq 2^{d-1}g^{-d}\eta(g).$$
Moreover, there is a choice $g(\ell)>0$, for all sufficiently large real $\ell$, such that $g(\ell)\to\infty$, $g(\ell)/\ell\to0$, and
$$\left(\frac{\ell}{g(\ell)}\right)^d\eta(g(\ell))\longrightarrow0.$$
For every fixed finite configuration and all sufficiently large periods $L$, the noncoincident periodic-image tail $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d,\ |k|_\infty\geq K_0}|\phi(x-y+Lk)|$ is absolutely convergent. The tail of the cell envelope $\psi(|j|_\infty-1)$ over all sufficiently large integer offsets is summable. This lemma is a deterministic tail estimate; it uses no superstability or thermodynamic-limit conclusion.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** $d,R_0,\psi$ as in the Statement.

[F1] The lower regularity convention in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]] supplies a nonnegative nonincreasing tail envelope with finite weighted integral.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The hypotheses and notation above.

1.1 Since $\psi$ is nonincreasing, $0\leq g^d\psi(g)\leq \frac{d}{1-2^{-d}}\int_{g/2}^{g}r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr$ for $g>2R_0$: on $[g/2,g]$, $\psi(r)\geq\psi(g)$, and integration of $r^{d-1}$ gives the displayed coefficient. Both the interval integral and the tail integral in $\eta(g)$ tend to zero as $g\to\infty$, so $\eta(g)\to0$. [F1, algebra]

1.2 For $m\geq2$ and $r\in[(m-1)g,mg]$, monotonicity gives $\psi(r)\geq\psi(mg)$ and $r^{d-1}\geq((m-1)g)^{d-1}$. Hence $$ \int_{(m-1)g}^{mg}r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr\geq g^d(m-1)^{d-1}\psi(mg). $$ Since $m^{d-1}\leq2^{d-1}(m-1)^{d-1}$, summing over disjoint intervals yields $\sum_{m\geq2}m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq2^{d-1}g^{-d}\int_g^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr$. The $m=1$ term equals $g^{-d}g^d\psi(g)$, so adding it proves the stated bound because $2^{d-1}\geq1$. [F1, algebra]

1.3 For integer $m\geq\lceil R_0+3\rceil$, monotonicity gives $\psi(r)\geq\psi(m-1)$ on $[m-2,m-1]$, so $\int_{m-2}^{m-1}r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr\geq(m-2)^{d-1}\psi(m-1)$. Since $m^{d-1}\leq c_d(m-2)^{d-1}$ for these $m$, summing over disjoint unit intervals proves $\sum_{m\geq\lceil R_0+3\rceil} m^{d-1}\psi(m-1)<\infty$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 For each integer $k\geq1$, let $G_k$ be the least integer greater than $2R_0$ such that $\eta(g)\leq k^{-2d}$ for every $g\geq G_k$; it exists by step 1.1 and the well-ordering of the positive integers. Choose a strictly increasing sequence $L_k$ with $L_k\geq kG_k$ and $L_k\geq k^2$. For $\ell\geq L_1$, let $k(\ell)=\max\{k:L_k\leq\ell\}$ and $g(\ell)=\ell/k(\ell)$. Then $k(\ell)\to\infty$, $g(\ell)\geq G_{k(\ell)}$ and $g(\ell)\geq k(\ell)$, while $g(\ell)/\ell=1/k(\ell)$. 3.1 Fix distinct points $x,y$ in a finite configuration and a period $L>0$. Grouping lattice indices by $m=|k|_\infty$ and applying the sum bound of step 1.2 with gap $g=L/2$ shows $\sum_k|\phi(x-y+Lk)|<\infty$ whenever $L/2>2R_0$. There are finitely many remaining images; any $+\infty$ term makes the periodic energy $+\infty$ by definition, while otherwise their finite sum is well-defined. This proves the periodic-image convention used in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]] for all sufficiently large $L$. [F1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

sections.Statement: Let $L\ge0$, $T>0$, and let $f:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous. If $f(t)\le L\int_0^t f(s)\,ds$ for every $t\in[0,T]$, then $f(t)=0$ for every $t\in[0,T]$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** A nonnegative continuous function and the stated integral inequality.

[F1] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: a continuous function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable.

[F2] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]], and [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: the product rule, chain rule, and mean value theorem apply to the displayed differentiable real functions.

[F3] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: $(e^x)'=e^x$ for every real $x$.
sections.Proof:
1.1 By [F1], the integral defining $h(t)=\int_0^t f(s)\,ds$ exists. Continuity of $f$ gives $h'(t)=f(t)$ on $(0,T)$: the difference quotient error is bounded by $\sup_{|s-t|\le|r|}|f(s)-f(t)|$, which tends to zero as $r\to0$. Also $h$ is continuous on $[0,T]$. The hypothesis gives $h'\le Lh$, so [F2]–[F3] yield $g'(t)\le0$ for $g(t)=e^{-Lt}h(t)$ on $(0,T)$. The mean value theorem makes $g$ nonincreasing; since $g(0)=0$ and $g\ge0$, $g\equiv0$ and $h\equiv0$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 For any $t>0$, the nonnegative continuous function $f$ has integral $h(t)=0$. If $f(t_0)>0$ at any $t_0>0$, continuity gives a positive lower bound on a nonempty subinterval of $[0,t_0]$, contradicting $h(t_0)=0$. At $t=0$ the assumed inequality gives $f(0)\le0$; nonnegativity gives $f(0)=0$. Hence $f\equiv0$. [step 1.1, given] ∎

sections.Statement: For finite random variables $M,R$ with joint law $p(m,r)$ and marginals $p_M,p_R$, use the entropy definition $H(Y)$ of [[lem-tdmath-conditional-memory-entropy]] for $Y=M,R,(M,R)$. Define $I(M;R):=\sum_{p(m,r)>0}p(m,r)\log\frac{p(m,r)}{p_M(m)p_R(r)}$. Then $I(M;R)=H(M)+H(R)-H(M,R)=H(M)-H(M|R)\ge0$, with equality exactly when $p(m,r)=p_M(m)p_R(r)$ for every pair.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** As stated in the item.

[A1] $p(m,r)$ is a joint probability law on finite sets and $p_M,p_R$ are its marginal laws.

[F1] [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]] and [[def-finite-sum]]: the joint and marginal probabilities are finite normalized sums, and if $p(m,r)>0$ then both marginals are positive.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-conditional-memory-entropy]]: finite Shannon entropies are defined there and satisfy $H(M,R)=H(R)+H(M|R)$.

[F3] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: $\log t$ is differentiable for $t>0$ with derivative $1/t$.

[F4] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: derivative signs determine monotonicity on an interval.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** A finite joint law $p(m,r)$ and its two marginals.

1.1 Define $\phi(t):=t-1-\log t$ for $t>0$. Its derivative is $1-1/t$, nonpositive on $(0,1]$ and nonnegative on $[1,\infty)$; the mean-value theorem [F4] gives $\phi(t)\ge\phi(1)=0$, with equality only at $t=1$. Thus $-\log t\ge1-t$, strictly unless $t=1$. [F3, F4]

1.2 Expanding the finite logarithmic sum gives $I(M;R)=H(M)+H(R)-H(M,R)$; applying [F2] rewrites it as $H(M)-H(M|R)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Put $q(m,r):=p_M(m)p_R(r)$. For $p(m,r)>0$, $q(m,r)>0$ by [F1], and step 1.1 with $t=q/p$ gives $p\log(p/q)\ge p-q$. Summing over the support of $p$ yields $I(M;R)\ge1-\sum_{p>0}q\ge0$. Equality forces $q=p$ on the support and no $q$-mass outside it, hence equality at every pair; conversely independence makes each positive logarithm zero. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

For finite random variables $M,R$ with joint law $p(m,r)$ and marginals $p_M,p_R$, use the entropy definition $H(Y)$ of [[lem-tdmath-conditional-memory-entropy]] for $Y=M,R,(M,R)$. Define $I(M;R):=\sum_{p(m,r)>0}p(m,r)\log\frac{p(m,r)}{p_M(m)p_R(r)}$. Then $I(M;R)=H(M)+H(R)-H(M,R)=H(M)-H(M|R)\ge0$, with equality exactly when $p(m,r)=p_M(m)p_R(r)$ for every pair.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** As stated in the item.

[A1] $p(m,r)$ is a joint probability law on finite sets and $p_M,p_R$ are its marginal laws.

[F1] [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]] and [[def-finite-sum]]: the joint and marginal probabilities are finite normalized sums, and if $p(m,r)>0$ then both marginals are positive.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-conditional-memory-entropy]]: finite Shannon entropies are defined there and satisfy $H(M,R)=H(R)+H(M|R)$.

[F3] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: $\log t$ is differentiable for $t>0$ with derivative $1/t$.

[F4] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: derivative signs determine monotonicity on an interval.

## Proof

**Given:** A finite joint law $p(m,r)$ and its two marginals.

1.1 Define $\phi(t):=t-1-\log t$ for $t>0$. Its derivative is $1-1/t$, nonpositive on $(0,1]$ and nonnegative on $[1,\infty)$; the mean-value theorem [F4] gives $\phi(t)\ge\phi(1)=0$, with equality only at $t=1$. Thus $-\log t\ge1-t$, strictly unless $t=1$. [F3, F4]

1.2 Expanding the finite logarithmic sum gives $I(M;R)=H(M)+H(R)-H(M,R)$; applying [F2] rewrites it as $H(M)-H(M|R)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Put $q(m,r):=p_M(m)p_R(r)$. For $p(m,r)>0$, $q(m,r)>0$ by [F1], and step 1.1 with $t=q/p$ gives $p\log(p/q)\ge p-q$. Summing over the support of $p$ yields $I(M;R)\ge1-\sum_{p>0}q\ge0$. Equality forces $q=p$ on the support and no $q$-mass outside it, hence equality at every pair; conversely independence makes each positive logarithm zero. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

sections.Statement:

([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $d\ge1$, let $\phi$ be a stable pair

$$Z_{L,N}:=\frac{a^N}{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta U_N(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}\,d\lambda_d^{\otimes N},$$
where $\lambda_d$ is Lebesgue measure restricted to the Borel subsets of
$\mathbb R^d$, $\lambda_d^{\otimes N}$ is its $N$-fold product measure. The
integrand uses the ordinary real exponential when $U_N<+\infty$ and is defined
to be $0$ when $U_N=+\infty$. Also,
$\int_{\Lambda_L^N}f\,d\lambda_d^{\otimes N}$ abbreviates the nonnegative
integral of $f\mathbf1_{\Lambda_L^N}$ on the full product space, using
[[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]. Set $Z_{L,0}=1$.
Define $\Xi_L:=\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}Z_{L,N}$ as the nonnegative extended sum of
[[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]. For $L\ge1$ put
$Q:=a e^{\beta B}$. Choose any real $K>eQ+1$ and set
$$n_L:=\lfloor K L^d\rfloor+1.$$
which satisfies $K L^d<n_L\le K L^d+1$ by the integer-part lemma
[[lem-integer-part]]. Let
$\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}:=\sum_{N=0}^{n_L}Z_{L,N}$. Then
$$1\le\Xi_L\le e^{Q L^d},\qquad \sum_{N>n_L}Z_{L,N}\le e^{-L^d},\qquad \Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge(1-e^{-L^d})\Xi_L.$$
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a dimension $d\ge1$, the model in
[[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]], its stability constant
$B$, $a,\beta>0$, and $L\ge1$.

[A1] Stability means $U_N\ge-BN$ for every finite configuration and every
$N\ge1$ ([[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]]).

[L1] [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] defines the nonnegative integral as the
supremum of simple minorants. This current batch-11 definition is draft text;
its exact interface is inspected in the batch dependency evidence.

[F1] [[def-countable-choice]] states $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; the standard
Lebesgue measure and box suppliers used here state this assumption explicitly.

[F2] [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]] defines
$\lambda_d$ as Lebesgue measure on its measurable sets; restricting it to
Borel sets gives a measure. [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]] gives
$\lambda_d([0,L]^d)=L^d$ under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$;
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]] gives
the rectangle formula for finite products of sigma-finite measures.

[F3] [[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]
ensures the Lebesgue factors are sigma-finite, so the finite product measures
in the Definition exist.

[F4] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] defines
$e^x=\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}x^N/N!$, with integer powers as in
[[def-integer-power]]; [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]] proves
convergence for every real $x$.

[F5] [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]] gives $e^xe^y=e^{x+y}$, and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]] gives monotonicity of $e^x$.

[F6] [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]] defines $0!=1$ and the ordinary
factorial recursion; [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]] defines the series
sum as the supremum of its nonnegative partial sums, allowing $+\infty$.

[F7] [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]] identifies
the finite product Borel sigma-algebra, and extended-real measurability means
measurability of preimages of extended-real Borel sets
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Coordinate-difference maps are
continuous, hence Borel under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]]); composition with the Borel
potential preserves measurability
([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]). Finite
sums of the resulting extended-real measurable terms are measurable whenever
defined ([[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]).

$\lfloor x\rfloor$ with $\lfloor x\rfloor\le x<\lfloor x\rfloor+1$.
sections.Proof:
1.1 By [A1] and $\beta>0$, every configuration satisfies
$0\le e^{-\beta U_N}\le e^{\beta BN}$, with the value $0$ when $U_N=+\infty$.

measurable. For every simple minorant of this restricted integrand, [L1]
bounds its integral by the integral of the constant $e^{\beta BN}$ on

$\lambda_d^{\otimes N}(\Lambda_L^N)=L^{dN}$. Thus

$1\le\Xi_L\le\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}(QL^d)^N/N!=e^{QL^d}$; the lower bound is

fm.title: Stationarity and intensity of a periodized empirical field

references.title: H.-O. Georgii, Large deviations and the equivalence of ensembles for Gibbsian particle systems with superstable interaction
references.locator: Section 1, equation (1.1), printed p.172 / PDF p.2: the periodic empirical field is translation invariant.

sections.Statement:
For $L>0$ and a finite configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$ with $N(\omega)=N$, the measure $R_{L,\omega}$ of [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]] is a stationary probability law of finite intensity and
$$\rho(R_{L,\omega})=\frac{N}{L^d}.$$
For any probability law $C_L$ on finite configurations in $\Lambda_L$ with $E_{C_L}N<\infty$, its empirical-field barycenter $\bar C_L$ is also a stationary probability law of finite intensity and $\rho(\bar C_L)=E_{C_L}N/L^d$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The half-open cube $\Lambda_L$, a finite simple configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$, and, when the barycenter is used, a law $C_L$ with $E_{C_L}N<\infty$; use [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]].

[F1] [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]]: $R_{L,\omega}$ averages the translations of the $L\mathbb Z^d$-periodic continuation over one fundamental cube.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]]: stationarity means invariance under every translation and finite intensity means finite expected count in a unit cell.

[F3] [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]], and [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: $\Lambda_L$ has volume $L^d$, translations preserve Lebesgue measure, and nonnegative sums may be integrated termwise.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The hypotheses and definitions in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 By [F1], $R_{L,\omega}$ is the push-forward of normalized Lebesgue probability on $\Lambda_L$, so it is a probability measure. For a bounded measurable local $f$ and $y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$R_{L,\omega}(f\circ T_y)=L^{-d}\int_{\Lambda_L}f(T_{x+y}\omega^{(L)})\,dx.$$
The integrand is $L\mathbb Z^d$-periodic in $x$. The translated cube $\Lambda_L+y$ is another fundamental region for this lattice; partitioning it and $\Lambda_L$ into their finitely many translated intersections and using translation invariance of Lebesgue measure gives equal integrals. Hence $R_{L,\omega}(f\circ T_y)=R_{L,\omega}(f)$ for every $y$, so $R_{L,\omega}$ is stationary. [F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 For bounded Borel $A$, Tonelli's theorem and the periodic continuation give
$$R_{L,\omega}(N_A)=L^{-d}\int_{\Lambda_L}\sum_{q\in\omega}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}\mathbf1_A(q+Lk+x)\,dx.$$
For each fixed $q\in\omega$, the sets $\Lambda_L+Lk$ partition $\mathbb R^d$ up to null boundaries. Translating variables in each integral therefore makes the inner sum of integrals equal to $|A|$. Summing over the $N$ representatives gives $R_{L,\omega}(N_A)=N|A|/L^d$. Taking $A=[0,1)^d$ proves $\rho(R_{L,\omega})=N/L^d$ and finite intensity. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The barycenter $\bar C_L$ is a probability mixture of the stationary laws $R_{L,\omega}$, so it is stationary. By step 2.1 and Tonelli,
$$\rho(\bar C_L)=E_{C_L}[R_{L,\omega}(N_{[0,1)^d})]=E_{C_L}N/L^d<\infty.$$
Thus it belongs to the finite-intensity stationary domain of $\tau_L$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

For any probability law $C_L$ on finite configurations in $\Lambda_L$ with $E_{C_L}N<\infty$, its empirical-field barycenter $\bar C_L$ is also a stationary probability law of finite intensity and $\rho(\bar C_L)=E_{C_L}N/L^d$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The half-open cube $\Lambda_L$, a finite simple configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$, and, when the barycenter is used, a law $C_L$ with $E_{C_L}N<\infty$; use [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]].

[F1] [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]]: $R_{L,\omega}$ averages the translations of the $L\mathbb Z^d$-periodic continuation over one fundamental cube.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]]: stationarity means invariance under every translation and finite intensity means finite expected count in a unit cell.

[F3] [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]], and [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: $\Lambda_L$ has volume $L^d$, translations preserve Lebesgue measure, and nonnegative sums may be integrated termwise.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and definitions in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 By [F1], $R_{L,\omega}$ is the push-forward of normalized Lebesgue probability on $\Lambda_L$, so it is a probability measure. For a bounded measurable local $f$ and $y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$R_{L,\omega}(f\circ T_y)=L^{-d}\int_{\Lambda_L}f(T_{x+y}\omega^{(L)})\,dx.$$
The integrand is $L\mathbb Z^d$-periodic in $x$. The translated cube $\Lambda_L+y$ is another fundamental region for this lattice; partitioning it and $\Lambda_L$ into their finitely many translated intersections and using translation invariance of Lebesgue measure gives equal integrals. Hence $R_{L,\omega}(f\circ T_y)=R_{L,\omega}(f)$ for every $y$, so $R_{L,\omega}$ is stationary. [F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 For bounded Borel $A$, Tonelli's theorem and the periodic continuation give
$$R_{L,\omega}(N_A)=L^{-d}\int_{\Lambda_L}\sum_{q\in\omega}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}\mathbf1_A(q+Lk+x)\,dx.$$
For each fixed $q\in\omega$, the sets $\Lambda_L+Lk$ partition $\mathbb R^d$ up to null boundaries. Translating variables in each integral therefore makes the inner sum of integrals equal to $|A|$. 3.1 The barycenter $\bar C_L$ is a probability mixture of the stationary laws $R_{L,\omega}$, so it is stationary. By step 2.1 and Tonelli,
$$\rho(\bar C_L)=E_{C_L}[R_{L,\omega}(N_{[0,1)^d})]=E_{C_L}N/L^d<\infty.$$
Thus it belongs to the finite-intensity stationary domain of $\tau_L$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

fm.title: Reciprocals of the positive integers decrease to zero

references.title: Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Chapter 1

sections.Statement: In the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$, the sequence $\epsilon_n:=1/(n+1)$, $n\in\mathbb N$, is positive, strictly decreasing, and converges to zero.
sections.Facts & Assumptions: [F1] [[def-complete-ordered-field]]: every nonempty subset of an ordered field that is bounded above has a least upper bound.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** [F1] and the ordered-field laws of $\mathbb R$.

1.1 The natural numbers are nonempty. If they had an upper bound, completeness [F1] would give $s=\sup\mathbb N$. The number $s-1$ cannot be an upper bound, so some $n\in\mathbb N$ satisfies $n>s-1$. Then $n+1>s$, while $n+1\in\mathbb N$, contradicting that $s$ is an upper bound. Thus the natural numbers are unbounded above. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Each $n+1$ is positive, so $\epsilon_n>0$; since $n+2>n+1$, ordered-field division by positive denominators gives $1/(n+2)<1/(n+1)$. Given $\eta>0$, unboundedness from step 1.1 supplies $N\in\mathbb N$ with $N+1>1/\eta$. For all $n\ge N$, $0<\epsilon_n\le1/(N+1)<\eta$, which is the definition of convergence to zero. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

sections.Statement: Let a simple domain and its finite thermal joins satisfy [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. For $0\le\lambda\le1$, write $R_\lambda$ for the compound state $((1-\lambda)x_0,\lambda x_1)$, omitting a zero coefficient at the endpoints. Then there is a unique $\lambda\in(0,1)$ with $R_\lambda\sim x$ in the common accessibility relation.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The compound axioms A1–A6, thermal-join axioms T1–T3 with the equal-state split, strict strip endpoints, and join closure.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: compounds have the preorder, consistency, positive scaling, splitting, and stability assumptions; CH is not part of this definition.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]] and [[lem-tdmath-thermal-scaling-invariance]]: an equal-state split is reversible, thermal equivalence is transitive, and scaling either member of a thermal-equilibrium pair preserves thermal equivalence.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-forward-signed-comparison]] and [[lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellation]]: equal-total signed maps compare by their positive and negative parts; cancellation is valid under A1–A6 without CH.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-sector-nesting]]: every pair of states in each finite join domain is comparable.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F3], and $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$.

1.1 For $0\le\lambda<\mu\le1$, the signed difference $R_\mu-R_\lambda=(\mu-\lambda)(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))$ has positive part $(\mu-\lambda)\mathsf{J}(x_1)$ and negative part $(\mu-\lambda)\mathsf{J}(x_0)$. Since $x_0\prec x_1$, positive scaling and [F2] give $R_\lambda\prec R_\mu$. A reverse comparison would, by [F2] and inverse positive scaling, give $x_1\prec x_0$, contrary to strictness. Thus the reference states are strictly ordered by parameter. [A1, F2, algebra]

1.2 For $0<\lambda<1$, [F1] makes $(1-\lambda)x_0$ and $\lambda x_1$ thermally equivalent. By the definition of thermal equivalence, their compound is reversible with its join state. The equal-state split makes $((1-\lambda)x,\lambda x)$ reversible with its join state and with $x$. Both join states belong to the join of two scaled copies of the same simple domain, so [F3] compares them. The endpoint cases use $R_0=x_0$ and $R_1=x_1$ directly. Hence $R_\lambda$ and $x$ are comparable for every $\lambda\in[0,1]$. [F1, F3, given]

2.1 Let $L=\{\lambda\in[0,1]:R_\lambda\prec x\}$. The strict endpoint comparison $x_0\prec x$ puts $0$ in $L$. Step 1.1 and transitivity make $L$ downward closed. Let $s=\sup L$. If $s>0$, then $s-1/n\in L$ for every sufficiently large $n$. Since $R_{s-1/n}+(1/n)x_1=R_s+(1/n)x_0$, consistency yields $R_s+(1/n)x_0\prec x+(1/n)x_1$. 3.1 If $s<1$, then $s+1/n\notin L$ for every sufficiently large $n$. Step 1.2 gives comparability and the definition of $L$ excludes $R_{s+1/n}\prec x$, so $x\prec R_{s+1/n}$. If $s=1$, the strict strip gives $x\prec R_1$; together with step 2.1 this would imply $x_1\prec x$, contrary to $x\prec\prec x_1$. Thus $s<1$, and step 2.1 and the preceding stability comparison give $R_s\sim x$. [A1, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1]

4.1 The equivalence $R_s\sim x$ also excludes $s=0$, because $R_0=x_0$ and $x_0\not\sim x$, and excludes $s=1$ by strictness of $x\prec\prec x_1$. fm.title: Reference entropy supremum is finite and attained

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Lemmas 2.1 and 2.3

sections.Statement:
Assume [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] on compounds over a nonempty state set $X$, a strict reference pair $x_0\preceq x_1$ with not $x_1\preceq x_0$, and the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. For $x\in X$ define

$$L_x:=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R:R_\lambda\preceq_s e_x\}.$$

Then $L_x$ is nonempty, bounded above, and downward closed. Its supremum $S(x):=\sup L_x$ is a real number and satisfies $R_{S(x)}\sim_s e_x$. Stability is used to prove attainment; no continuity of states or order is assumed.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
[A1] [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]: equal-mass compounds form a preorder with consistency, positive scaling, stability for fixed positive spectators, and CH.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]]: $e_x$ has mass one, compound masses are finite sums, and composition/scaling preserve the stated masses.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] and [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]: signed comparisons are well-defined, translation-invariant, and agree with ordinary comparison on nonnegative compounds.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-reference-order]]: $R_\lambda\preceq_sR_\mu$ exactly when $\lambda\le\mu$.

[F4] [[lem-tdmath-reciprocal-naturals-tend-zero]]: $\epsilon_n:=1/n$ for positive integers $n$ decreases to zero.

[F5] [[def-complete-ordered-field]]: every nonempty bounded-above subset of $\mathbb R$ has a supremum.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** [A1]–[F5], with $x\in X$ fixed.

1.1 Suppose no positive integer $n$ satisfies $(n+1)e_{x_0}\preceq ne_{x_1}+e_x$. Both sides have mass $n+1$, so CH gives $ne_{x_1}+e_x\preceq(n+1)e_{x_0}$. Scale by $1/n$ to obtain $e_{x_1}+n^{-1}e_x\preceq e_{x_0}+n^{-1}e_{x_0}$. Apply stability to the sequence $\epsilon_n=1/n$, with bases $e_{x_1},e_{x_0}$ and spectators $e_x,e_{x_0}$, each of mass one. It yields $x_1\preceq x_0$, contradicting strictness. Thus some $n$ has $(n+1)e_{x_0}\preceq ne_{x_1}+e_x$, which by [F2] is $R_{-n}\preceq_s e_x$; hence $-n\in L_x$. [A1, F1, F2, F4]

1.2 Suppose $L_x$ is unbounded above. For each positive integer $n$, unboundedness supplies $\lambda\in L_x$ with $\lambda>n$; [F3] gives $R_n\preceq_sR_\lambda$, and transitivity gives $n\in L_x$. By [F2], $R_n\preceq_s e_x$ is the compound comparison $e_{x_0}+n e_{x_1}\preceq e_x+n e_{x_0}$. Scaling by $1/n$ gives $e_{x_1}+n^{-1}e_{x_0}\preceq e_{x_0}+n^{-1}e_x$. Stability with bases $e_{x_1},e_{x_0}$ and spectators $e_{x_0},e_x$ now yields $x_1\preceq x_0$, again a contradiction. Therefore $L_x$ is bounded above. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4]

2.1 If $\lambda\in L_x$ and $\mu\le\lambda$, [F3] gives $R_\mu\preceq_sR_\lambda$; signed transitivity and $R_\lambda\preceq_s e_x$ imply $\mu\in L_x$. Thus $L_x$ is downward closed. By steps 1.1 and 1.2 it is nonempty and bounded above, so [F5] supplies the real number $s:=\sup L_x$. [A1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2]

## Statement

Assume [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] on compounds over a nonempty state set $X$, a strict reference pair $x_0\preceq x_1$ with not $x_1\preceq x_0$, and the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. For $x\in X$ define

$$L_x:=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R:R_\lambda\preceq_s e_x\}.$$

Then $L_x$ is nonempty, bounded above, and downward closed. Its supremum $S(x):=\sup L_x$ is a real number and satisfies $R_{S(x)}\sim_s e_x$. Stability is used to prove attainment; no continuity of states or order is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]: equal-mass compounds form a preorder with consistency, positive scaling, stability for fixed positive spectators, and CH.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]]: $e_x$ has mass one, compound masses are finite sums, and composition/scaling preserve the stated masses.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] and [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]: signed comparisons are well-defined, translation-invariant, and agree with ordinary comparison on nonnegative compounds.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-reference-order]]: $R_\lambda\preceq_sR_\mu$ exactly when $\lambda\le\mu$.

[F4] [[lem-tdmath-reciprocal-naturals-tend-zero]]: $\epsilon_n:=1/n$ for positive integers $n$ decreases to zero.

[F5] [[def-complete-ordered-field]]: every nonempty bounded-above subset of $\mathbb R$ has a supremum.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1]–[F5], with $x\in X$ fixed.

1.1 Suppose no positive integer $n$ satisfies $(n+1)e_{x_0}\preceq ne_{x_1}+e_x$. Both sides have mass $n+1$, so CH gives $ne_{x_1}+e_x\preceq(n+1)e_{x_0}$. Scale by $1/n$ to obtain $e_{x_1}+n^{-1}e_x\preceq e_{x_0}+n^{-1}e_{x_0}$. Apply stability to the sequence $\epsilon_n=1/n$, with bases $e_{x_1},e_{x_0}$ and spectators $e_x,e_{x_0}$, each of mass one. It yields $x_1\preceq x_0$, contradicting strictness. Thus some $n$ has $(n+1)e_{x_0}\preceq ne_{x_1}+e_x$, which by [F2] is $R_{-n}\preceq_s e_x$; hence $-n\in L_x$. [A1, F1, F2, F4]

1.2 Suppose $L_x$ is unbounded above. For each positive integer $n$, unboundedness supplies $\lambda\in L_x$ with $\lambda>n$; [F3] gives $R_n\preceq_sR_\lambda$, and transitivity gives $n\in L_x$. By [F2], $R_n\preceq_s e_x$ is the compound comparison $e_{x_0}+n e_{x_1}\preceq e_x+n e_{x_0}$. Scaling by $1/n$ gives $e_{x_1}+n^{-1}e_{x_0}\preceq e_{x_0}+n^{-1}e_x$. Stability with bases $e_{x_1},e_{x_0}$ and spectators $e_{x_0},e_x$ now yields $x_1\preceq x_0$, again a contradiction. Therefore $L_x$ is bounded above. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4]

2.1 If $\lambda\in L_x$ and $\mu\le\lambda$, [F3] gives $R_\mu\preceq_sR_\lambda$; signed transitivity and $R_\lambda\preceq_s e_x$ imply $\mu\in L_x$. Thus $L_x$ is downward closed. By steps 1.1 and 1.2 it is nonempty and bounded above, so [F5] supplies the real number $s:=\sup L_x$. [A1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 For each $n$, $s-1/n$ is not an upper bound of $L_x$, so some $\lambda\in L_x$ has $\lambda>s-1/n$. Downward closure gives $s-1/n\in L_x$. Consistency then gives $R_s+n^{-1}e_{x_0}\preceq_s e_x+n^{-1}e_{x_1}$, because $R_{s-1/n}+n^{-1}e_{x_1}=R_s+n^{-1}e_{x_0}$. Let $K:=R_s^-$. Adding the fixed nonnegative map $K$ to both sides converts this signed comparison into the compound comparisons $R_s^++n^{-1}e_{x_0}\preceq e_x+K+n^{-1}e_{x_1}$. Their bases have equal mass because $m(R_s^+)-m(K)=1$. Stability with spectators $e_{x_0},e_{x_1}$ yields $R_s^+\preceq e_x+K$, that is, $R_s\preceq_s e_x$. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1]

4.1 Since $s$ is an upper bound, $s+1/n\notin L_x$. CH therefore gives $e_x\preceq_s R_{s+1/n}$. Add $n^{-1}e_{x_0}$ to both sides and use $R_{s+1/n}+n^{-1}e_{x_0}=R_s+n^{-1}e_{x_1}$. Adding $K=R_s^-$ converts the result to equal-mass compounds $e_x+K+n^{-1}e_{x_0}\preceq R_s^++n^{-1}e_{x_1}$. Stability with the same positive unit-mass spectators yields $e_x+K\preceq R_s^+$, or $e_x\preceq_sR_s$. Together with step 3.1 this proves $R_s\sim_s e_x$ and the claimed attainment. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

sections.Statement: Let $C$ be a nonempty convex set in a finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space $H$ of dimension $k\ge1$, let $\operatorname{aff}C=H$, and put $K=\overline{C}^{\,H}$. If $z\in\partial_H K$ (that is, $z\in K$ and every relative neighborhood of $z$ meets $H\setminus K$), then there is a nonzero linear functional $\ell$ on the translation space of $H$ such that $\ell(q-z)\le0$ for all $q\in C$. If $C\subset\mathbb R^d$ has affine dimension at most $d-2$, then every $z\in C$ has at least two distinct ambient supporting hyperplanes containing $\operatorname{aff}C$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The stated finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space and convex set.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-closed-convex-separation]]: a point outside a nonempty closed convex Euclidean set is strictly separated from that set by a nonzero linear functional.

[F2] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space are compact.

[F3] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: Euclidean coordinates identify linear functionals with vectors and give the usual unit sphere.
sections.Proof:
1.1 Choose affine coordinates identifying $H$ with $\mathbb R^k$. Convexity of $C$ makes its closure $K$ convex: approximate any two points of $K$ by sequences in $C$ and pass to the limit in each convex combination. Since $z\in\partial_H K$, choose $z_m\notin K$ with $z_m\to z$. By [F1], for each $m$ there are $u_m\ne0$ and $c_m$ with $u_m\cdot q\le c_m<u_m\cdot z_m$ for all $q\in K$. Normalize $u_m$ to unit length; [F3] places these vectors on the compact unit sphere, which is compact by [F2], so a subsequence converges to a unit vector $u$. [F2] and [F3] provide the convergent subsequence. [given, F1, F2, F3, choose]

2.1 For every $q\in K$, the inequalities give $u_m\cdot(q-z_m)<0$. Along the convergent subsequence, continuity of the Euclidean inner product yields $u\cdot(q-z)\le0$. The limit vector has unit length, so its functional is nonzero and supports $K$, hence $C$, at $z$. [step 1.1, F3, algebra]

3.1 If $C\subset\mathbb R^d$ has affine hull $H$ of dimension at most $d-2$, its orthogonal complement has dimension at least two. Choose two nonparallel nonzero normals $n_1,n_2$ orthogonal to the direction space of $H$. For each $j$, the hyperplane $\{q:n_j\cdot(q-z)=0\}$ contains $H$ and therefore supports $C$ at $z$. The two hyperplanes are distinct because their normals are not parallel. [given, F3, algebra] ∎

sections.Statement:
Assume AC. Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on one measurable space and use $D(P\Vert Q)$ as defined in [[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]. Then
$$D(P\Vert Q)=\sup_{\phi\in B_b}\left(P(\phi)-\log Q(e^\phi)\right),$$
where $B_b$ is the set of bounded real measurable functions. In particular $D\geq0$. If $T$ is measurable, then $D(P\circ T^{-1}\Vert Q\circ T^{-1})\leq D(P\Vert Q)$.

For standard-Borel spaces $X,Y$, probability reference measures $Q_X,Q_Y$, and a joint probability $P_{XY}\ll Q_X\otimes Q_Y$ with finite $D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)$, let $P_{Y|X=x}$ be the conditional law supplied by [[thm-conditional-density-formula]]. Then
$$D(P_{XY}\Vert Q_X\otimes Q_Y)=D(P_X\Vert Q_X)+\int_X D(P_{Y|X=x}\Vert Q_Y)\,P_X(dx).$$
More generally, for nested standard-Borel observations $R$ and $S$ with $R$ a measurable function of $S$, and a fixed probability reference $Q_Y$ for a further variable $Y$, the conditional increments
$$G(R):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|R}\Vert Q_Y)\right],\qquad G(S):=E_P\!\left[D(P_{Y|S}\Vert Q_Y)\right]$$
satisfy $0\leq G(R)\leq G(S)$ whenever the joint relative entropy is finite.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** AC, probability measures, standard-Borel observation spaces where conditioning is used, and the exact finite-region relative entropy definition.

[A1] AC supplies Radon–Nikodym densities on these finite measure spaces and is required by the conditional density supplier ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]]).

[F1] For $P\ll Q$, $h=dP/dQ$ is nonnegative, $Q(h)=1$, unique almost everywhere, and $D(P\Vert Q)=Q(h\log h)$ ([[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]).

[F2] A joint density on a product of sigma-finite probability spaces produces an everywhere conditional probability kernel by dividing by its finite positive marginal density; zero and infinite marginal fibers are filled without division ([[thm-conditional-density-formula]]).

[F3] Nonnegative product-measurable functions have measurable section integrals and Tonelli iterated-integral equality ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F4] Dominated and monotone convergence justify the bounded truncation limits in the entropy integrals ([[thm-dominated-convergence]], [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]).

[F5] Natural logarithms turn products into sums and $\log 1=0$ ([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]).
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The hypotheses and exact definitions in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 For $P\ll Q$ with density $h$, the negative part of $h\log h$ is integrable because $-u\log u\leq1/e$ for $0\leq u\leq1$; the density definition is therefore unambiguous. Also $u\log u\geq u-1$ for $u\geq0$, so $D(P\Vert Q)=\int h\log h\,dQ\geq\int(h-1)\,dQ=0$. If $P\not\ll Q$, the defined value is $+\infty\geq0$. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 For bounded $\phi$, let $Q_\phi$ have density $e^\phi/Q(e^\phi)$ relative to $Q$. When $P\ll Q$ and $D(P\Vert Q)<\infty$, the density logarithm identity gives $D(P\Vert Q_\phi)=D(P\Vert Q)-P(\phi)+\log Q(e^\phi)\geq0$ by step 1.1. Thus every variational test is at most $D(P\Vert Q)$; the same upper bound is immediate if $D=+\infty$. If $P\not\ll Q$, choose a measurable $Q$-null set $N$ with $P(N)>0$ and use $\phi=t\mathbf1_N$: then $Q(e^\phi)=1$ and $P(\phi)=tP(N)\to\infty$. [step 1.1, F1, F5, construct]

3.1 In the remaining case $P\ll Q$, let $h=dP/dQ$ and set $\phi_m=\max(-m,\min(m,\log h))$, taking $\phi_m=-m$ on $\{h=0\}$. Then $e^{\phi_m}\to h$ and $e^{\phi_m}\leq1+h$, so [F4] gives $Q(e^{\phi_m})\to1$. The negative part of $h\phi_m$ is bounded by $1/e$, and its positive part increases to $(h\log h)^+$; hence [F4] gives $P(\phi_m)=\int h\phi_m\,dQ\to D(P\Vert Q)$, including when the positive entropy part is infinite. Combining this with step 2.1 proves the variational identity. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, F4, F5]

4.1 If $T$ is measurable, every bounded test $\psi$ on the target pulls back to the bounded test $\psi\circ T$ on the source, and $Q(e^{\psi\circ T})=(Q\circ T^{-1})(e^\psi)$ while $P(\psi\circ T)=(P\circ T^{-1})(\psi)$. Taking suprema in step 3.1 proves the restriction inequality. [step 3.1, F5]

4.2 For a conditioning observation $R$, applying the variational identity pointwise to the conditional density $k_R(r,y)$ shows $$G(R)=\sup_{\phi\in B_b}\left(E_P\phi(R,Y)-E_P\!\left[\log\int e^{\phi(R,y)}Q_Y(dy)\right]\right),$$ where the tests range over bounded measurable functions of $(R,Y)$. The upper bound follows from step 2.1 for each conditional law; the reverse bound follows by using the jointly measurable bounded truncations of $\log k_R$ from step 3.1 and then [F3]–[F4]. When $R$ is a measurable function of $S$, every test depending on $(R,Y)$ is an admissible test depending on $(S,Y)$ with the same objective value, since the $Q_Y$ normalizer still depends only on $R$. Thus $G(R)\leq G(S)$; nonnegativity is step 1.1 applied conditionally. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 Suppose $P_{XY}$ has density $h(x,y)$ relative to $Q_X\otimes Q_Y$. Put $h_X(x)=\int h(x,y)Q_Y(dy)$. By [F3], $h_X$ is a density for $P_X$. Where $0<h_X(x)<\infty$, [F2] supplies the conditional density $k(x,y)=h(x,y)/h_X(x)$ relative to $Q_Y$; elsewhere use its supplied filler. On the full $P_X$-measure set of finite positive $h_X$, $h=h_Xk$ and $\log h=\log h_X+\log k$ $P_{XY}$-almost everywhere. Integrating this identity, with nonnegative conditional entropies and finite total entropy, gives the displayed chain rule. If a restriction entropy is infinite, step 4.1 makes the joint entropy infinite as well, so no subtraction of two infinite terms is used. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 4.1, F5]

6.1 Steps 1.1–1.3 prove nonnegativity and the variational identity, step 4.1 proves restriction monotonicity, step 5.1 proves the product chain rule, and step 4.2 proves monotonicity under additional conditioning. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 4.2] ∎

[A1] AC supplies Radon–Nikodym densities on these finite measure spaces and is required by the conditional density supplier ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]]).

[F1] For $P\ll Q$, $h=dP/dQ$ is nonnegative, $Q(h)=1$, unique almost everywhere, and $D(P\Vert Q)=Q(h\log h)$ ([[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]).

[F2] A joint density on a product of sigma-finite probability spaces produces an everywhere conditional probability kernel by dividing by its finite positive marginal density; zero and infinite marginal fibers are filled without division ([[thm-conditional-density-formula]]).

[F3] Nonnegative product-measurable functions have measurable section integrals and Tonelli iterated-integral equality ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F4] Dominated and monotone convergence justify the bounded truncation limits in the entropy integrals ([[thm-dominated-convergence]], [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]).

[F5] Natural logarithms turn products into sums and $\log 1=0$ ([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and exact definitions in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 For $P\ll Q$ with density $h$, the negative part of $h\log h$ is integrable because $-u\log u\leq1/e$ for $0\leq u\leq1$; the density definition is therefore unambiguous. Also $u\log u\geq u-1$ for $u\geq0$, so $D(P\Vert Q)=\int h\log h\,dQ\geq\int(h-1)\,dQ=0$. If $P\not\ll Q$, the defined value is $+\infty\geq0$. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 For bounded $\phi$, let $Q_\phi$ have density $e^\phi/Q(e^\phi)$ relative to $Q$. When $P\ll Q$ and $D(P\Vert Q)<\infty$, the density logarithm identity gives $D(P\Vert Q_\phi)=D(P\Vert Q)-P(\phi)+\log Q(e^\phi)\geq0$ by step 1.1. Thus every variational test is at most $D(P\Vert Q)$; the same upper bound is immediate if $D=+\infty$. If $P\not\ll Q$, choose a measurable $Q$-null set $N$ with $P(N)>0$ and use $\phi=t\mathbf1_N$: then $Q(e^\phi)=1$ and $P(\phi)=tP(N)\to\infty$. [step 1.1, F1, F5, construct]

3.1 In the remaining case $P\ll Q$, let $h=dP/dQ$ and set $\phi_m=\max(-m,\min(m,\log h))$, taking $\phi_m=-m$ on $\{h=0\}$. Then $e^{\phi_m}\to h$ and $e^{\phi_m}\leq1+h$, so [F4] gives $Q(e^{\phi_m})\to1$. The negative part of $h\phi_m$ is bounded by $1/e$, and its positive part increases to $(h\log h)^+$; hence [F4] gives $P(\phi_m)=\int h\phi_m\,dQ\to D(P\Vert Q)$, including when the positive entropy part is infinite. Combining this with step 2.1 proves the variational identity. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, F4, F5]

4.1 If $T$ is measurable, every bounded test $\psi$ on the target pulls back to the bounded test $\psi\circ T$ on the source, and $Q(e^{\psi\circ T})=(Q\circ T^{-1})(e^\psi)$ while $P(\psi\circ T)=(P\circ T^{-1})(\psi)$. Taking suprema in step 3.1 proves the restriction inequality. [step 3.1, F5]

4.2 For a conditioning observation $R$, applying the variational identity pointwise to the conditional density $k_R(r,y)$ shows $$G(R)=\sup_{\phi\in B_b}\left(E_P\phi(R,Y)-E_P\!\left[\log\int e^{\phi(R,y)}Q_Y(dy)\right]\right),$$ where the tests range over bounded measurable functions of $(R,Y)$. The upper bound follows from step 2.1 for each conditional law; the reverse bound follows by using the jointly measurable bounded truncations of $\log k_R$ from step 3.1 and then [F3]–[F4]. When $R$ is a measurable function of $S$, every test depending on $(R,Y)$ is an admissible test depending on $(S,Y)$ with the same objective value, since the $Q_Y$ normalizer still depends only on $R$. Thus $G(R)\leq G(S)$; nonnegativity is step 1.1 applied conditionally. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 Suppose $P_{XY}$ has density $h(x,y)$ relative to $Q_X\otimes Q_Y$. Put $h_X(x)=\int h(x,y)Q_Y(dy)$. By [F3], $h_X$ is a density for $P_X$. Where $0<h_X(x)<\infty$, [F2] supplies the conditional density $k(x,y)=h(x,y)/h_X(x)$ relative to $Q_Y$; elsewhere use its supplied filler. On the full $P_X$-measure set of finite positive $h_X$, $h=h_Xk$ and $\log h=\log h_X+\log k$ $P_{XY}$-almost everywhere. Integrating this identity, with nonnegative conditional entropies and finite total entropy, gives the displayed chain rule. If a restriction entropy is infinite, step 4.1 makes the joint entropy infinite as well, so no subtraction of two infinite terms is used. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 4.1, F5]

6.1 Steps 1.1–1.3 prove nonnegativity and the variational identity, step 4.1 proves restriction monotonicity, step 5.1 proves the product chain rule, and step 4.2 proves monotonicity under additional conditioning. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 4.2] ∎

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §§III.B–III.C

sections.Statement: Let $C$ be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space $H$. Its relative interior $\operatorname{ri}_H C$ is the interior in $H=\operatorname{aff}C$. Then $\operatorname{ri}_H C$ is nonempty. If $w\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$, $y\in\overline{C}^{\,H}$, and $0\le t<1$, then $(1-t)w+ty\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** A nonempty convex $C\subseteq H$ in finite dimension. Affine dimension is the dimension of its translation space.

[F1] [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]: every finite convex combination of points of $C$ belongs to $C$.
sections.Proof:
1.1 Let $k=\dim(\operatorname{aff}C)$. If $k=0$, then $C$ is a singleton and is open in its affine hull. If $k>0$, the definition of affine hull supplies $k+1$ affinely independent points of $C$ spanning it. Their simplex lies in $C$ by [F1]. Its barycenter has all $k+1$ barycentric coordinates positive; sufficiently small coordinate perturbations preserve positivity and their sum one. Thus a relative neighborhood of that barycenter lies in the simplex, proving $\operatorname{ri}_H C\ne\varnothing$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Fix $w,y,t$ as in the Statement. The case $t=0$ is $w\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$. Suppose $0<t<1$ and put $q=(1-t)w+ty$. Choose $r>0$ so the relative ball $B_H(w,r)$ lies in $C$. Hence $q'=(1-t)w_m(q')+ty_m\in C$ by [F1]. A relative neighborhood of $q$ lies in $C$, so $q\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$. [given, F1, choose, algebra] ∎

fm.title: Every forward sector has nonempty interior

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorem 3.2, pp. 43–45
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, §§4.1 and 7.2–7.3, complete 607-page edition

sections.Statement: Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], every forward sector $A_x$ has nonempty interior in its ambient simple domain $\Gamma_i$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** A1–A7 and S1–S3 on an open convex $\Gamma_i\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d=n_i+1$.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: each sector is supported at every state by exactly one hyperplane, and every state has a strict successor.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-convex-sector-closedness]]: $A_x$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$; if $y\in A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$ by transitivity.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-relative-boundary-support]]: a convex set has a support at its relative boundary in its affine hull, and a set of affine dimension at most $d-2$ has at least two distinct ambient supports through each of its points.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-relative-interior-segment]]: a convex set has nonempty relative interior, and every segment from a relative-interior point to a closure point, except for the closure endpoint, stays in the relative interior.
sections.Proof:
1.1 Suppose $A_x$ has empty ambient interior. If $d=1$, S1 supplies a strict successor $y\ne x$; convexity puts the nondegenerate interval between $x$ and $y$ in $A_x$, contradicting empty interior. Thus take $d\ge2$. The affine hull of $A_x$ has dimension at most $d-1$. If its dimension were at most $d-2$, [F2] would give two distinct supporting hyperplanes at $x$, contradicting S2. Hence its affine hull is a hyperplane $H$; this $H$ supports $A_x$ at every point, including $x$. [A1, F2]

1.2 By S1 choose $y$ with $x\prec\prec y$. Then $y\in A_x$ and $x\notin A_y$. Transitivity gives $A_y\subseteq A_x\subseteq H$. If $A_y$ had affine dimension at most $d-2$, [F2] would again give multiple ambient supports at $y$, contrary to S2. Thus $\operatorname{aff}A_y=H$. [A1, F1, F2]

1.3 Choose $w\in\operatorname{ri}_H A_y$ by [F3]. The segment from $w$ to $x$ is contained in $H\cap\Gamma_i$ by convexity of both sets, starts in $A_y$, and ends outside $A_y$. Its intersection with $A_y$ is closed by relative closedness [F1], so it has a last point $z$ before $x$. Points immediately after $z$ on this segment lie outside $A_y$ and, because $A_y$ is closed in the open set $\Gamma_i$, outside $\overline{A_y}^{\,H}$. Thus $z\in\partial_H\overline{A_y}^{\,H}$. The support statement [F2] supplies a nonzero functional on $H$ whose zero hyperplane supports $A_y$ at $z$. [F1, F2, F3, choose]

2.1 Extend this functional to the ambient Euclidean space by taking its normal vector in the direction space of $H$. Its zero hyperplane contains the within-$H$ support and is not $H$ itself. Since $z\in A_y$, transitivity gives $A_z\subseteq A_y$, so the extended plane supports $A_z$ at $z$; the plane $H$ also supports $A_z$. These are distinct, contradicting S2 at $z$. Therefore $A_x$ has nonempty ambient interior. [A1, F1, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

fm.title: Differential of a smooth partial Legendre transform on a local inverse chart

references.title: Daniel Arovas, Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, Appendix II, §2.15

sections.Statement:
Let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^k\times\mathbb R^m$ be open with $k,m\ge1$, and let $f:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Suppose the map $(u,z)\mapsto(x,z):=(D_u f(u,z),z)$ restricts to a $C^1$ diffeomorphism between open neighborhoods, with inverse $(x,z)\mapsto(g(x,z),z)$. Define

$$\widehat f(x,z):=f(g(x,z),z)-x\cdot g(x,z).$$

Then $\widehat f$ is $C^2$ and

$$d\widehat f=-g\cdot dx+D_z f(g(x,z),z)\cdot dz.$$

This is a local statement. Existence of the inverse chart is a hypothesis; the lemma asserts no global inverse or boundary transform.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** An open domain, a $C^2$ function $f$, and a $C^1$ inverse chart $g$ for $(u,z)\mapsto(D_u f(u,z),z)$.

[F1] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: Differentiating a composition of totally differentiable maps gives the composed derivative.

[F2] [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: A $C^1$ diffeomorphism is a bijection between open neighborhoods whose map and inverse are both $C^1$.

[F3] [[thm-chain-sum-product-and-composition-rules-for-banach-derivatives]]: Differentiation of a bounded-bilinear product obeys the sum of the two product terms.
sections.Proof:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The inverse identity gives $D_u f(g(x,z),z)=x$. By [F1], differentiating the composition in $\widehat f$ gives $d[f(g(x,z),z)]=x\cdot dg+D_z f(g(x,z),z)\cdot dz$. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 Apply [F3] componentwise to the finite scalar products in $x\cdot g$ to obtain $d[x\cdot g]=g\cdot dx+x\cdot dg$. Subtracting this from step 1.1 cancels the $x\cdot dg$ terms and yields the stated differential. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The coefficient functions $g$ and $D_zf(g,z)$ are $C^1$, since $g$ is $C^1$, $f$ is $C^2$, and [F1] applies to their compositions. The first partial derivatives of $\widehat f$ are therefore $C^1$, so $\widehat f$ is $C^2$. [given, F1, F2, step 2.1] ∎

fm.title: Spectator cancellation and signed-order algebra

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorem 2.1 and §II.D

sections.Statement: Under [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]], for equal-mass compounds $A,B,C$, $A+C\preceq B+C$ if and only if $A\preceq B$. The signed relation of [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] is well-defined; on nonnegative equal-mass maps it agrees with $\preceq$, is invariant under adding the same finite-support signed map to both sides, and is transitive and closed under adding two comparisons.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
[F1] [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]]: compounds are finite-support nonnegative maps; their masses are finite sums, additive under composition and homogeneous under positive scaling.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]: $\preceq$ is a preorder, composition-consistent, positively scale-invariant, admits splitting/recombination, satisfies the stated positive-spectator stability axiom, and has CH.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]]: for equal-total finite signed maps $u,v$, the signed comparison is defined by comparing $(v-u)^-$ with $(v-u)^+$.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** [F1], [A1], and [F2].

1.1 For equal-total $u,v$, $d=v-u$ has finite support and total sum zero. Pointwise $d=d^+-d^-$, so finite-sum linearity gives $m(d^+)-m(d^-)=0$; both maps are finite-support and nonnegative. Thus the definition in [F2] compares equal-mass compounds. If $u,v$ are nonnegative, set $k(x)=\min\{u(x),v(x)\}$; then $u=k+(v-u)^-$ and $v=k+(v-u)^+$. [F1, F2]

1.2 Suppose $A+C\preceq B+C$ and $m(C)>0$. For each positive integer $n$, pointwise addition gives $A=n(A/n)$ and $B=n(B/n)$. Scaling the given comparison by $1/n$ gives $A/n+C/n\preceq B/n+C/n$. By composition consistency, replace the $n$ copies of $A/n$ one at a time by $B/n$, keeping the already replaced copies, the remaining copies, and $C/n$ as spectators; after all replacements, $A+C/n\preceq B+C/n$. Apply stability with $Z_0=Z_1=C$ and $\epsilon_n=1/n$ to obtain $A\preceq B$. If $m(C)=0$, nonnegativity implies $C=0$ and the conclusion is the premise itself. Conversely, $A\preceq B$ gives $A+C\preceq B+C$ by consistency. [A1, F1, algebra]

## Statement

Under [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]], for equal-mass compounds $A,B,C$, $A+C\preceq B+C$ if and only if $A\preceq B$. The signed relation of [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] is well-defined; on nonnegative equal-mass maps it agrees with $\preceq$, is invariant under adding the same finite-support signed map to both sides, and is transitive and closed under adding two comparisons.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]]: compounds are finite-support nonnegative maps; their masses are finite sums, additive under composition and homogeneous under positive scaling.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]: $\preceq$ is a preorder, composition-consistent, positively scale-invariant, admits splitting/recombination, satisfies the stated positive-spectator stability axiom, and has CH.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]]: for equal-total finite signed maps $u,v$, the signed comparison is defined by comparing $(v-u)^-$ with $(v-u)^+$.

## Proof

**Given:** [F1], [A1], and [F2].

1.1 For equal-total $u,v$, $d=v-u$ has finite support and total sum zero. Pointwise $d=d^+-d^-$, so finite-sum linearity gives $m(d^+)-m(d^-)=0$; both maps are finite-support and nonnegative. Thus the definition in [F2] compares equal-mass compounds. If $u,v$ are nonnegative, set $k(x)=\min\{u(x),v(x)\}$; then $u=k+(v-u)^-$ and $v=k+(v-u)^+$. [F1, F2]

1.2 Suppose $A+C\preceq B+C$ and $m(C)>0$. For each positive integer $n$, pointwise addition gives $A=n(A/n)$ and $B=n(B/n)$. Scaling the given comparison by $1/n$ gives $A/n+C/n\preceq B/n+C/n$. By composition consistency, replace the $n$ copies of $A/n$ one at a time by $B/n$, keeping the already replaced copies, the remaining copies, and $C/n$ as spectators; after all replacements, $A+C/n\preceq B+C/n$. Apply stability with $Z_0=Z_1=C$ and $\epsilon_n=1/n$ to obtain $A\preceq B$. If $m(C)=0$, nonnegativity implies $C=0$ and the conclusion is the premise itself. Conversely, $A\preceq B$ gives $A+C\preceq B+C$ by consistency. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 For nonnegative $u,v$, step 1.1 gives $u=k+(v-u)^-$ and $v=k+(v-u)^+$. Cancellation from step 1.2 shows $u\preceq v$ exactly when $(v-u)^-\preceq(v-u)^+$, which is $u\preceq_s v$. For general signed maps, adding a common map leaves $v-u$ unchanged, so it leaves signed comparison unchanged. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 If $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s w$, then consistency combines $(v-u)^-\preceq(v-u)^+$ and $(w-v)^-\preceq(w-v)^+$ into a comparison between the sums of their negative and positive parts. The two sums have a common pointwise minimum; cancel it by step 1.2. The remaining maps are precisely $(w-u)^-$ and $(w-u)^+$, so $u\preceq_s w$. The same sum-and-cancel argument applied to two independent signed comparisons proves closure under their addition; reflexivity follows from $0\preceq0$. [A1, F2, step 1.2] ∎
