Require the common meter point masses to satisfy $e_{z_0}\preceq e_{z_1}$ and not $e_{z_1}\preceq e_{z_0}$. These are hypotheses on the comparison algebra, not consequences of separate numerical meter readings.

For positive coefficients $t_{ik}$ on a finite collection of type-$i$ states $x_{ik}$, define $T_i:=\sum_k t_{ik}$ and $T:=\sum_iT_i$. Put $C_0:=\sum_{i,k}t_{ik}e_{a_{i,x_{ik}}}$ and $C:=\sum_{i,k}t_{ik}u_{i,x_{ik}}=C_0+T e_{z_0}$. Thus $C_0$ is the state compound of mass $T$ and $C$ is its fixed-meter encoding of mass $2T$. Empty collections give $T=0$ and $C_0=C=0$. Define

$$\Sigma(C):=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_k t_{ik}\sigma_i(x_{ik}).$$

For two such compounds $C,D$ with the same type-total vector $(T_i)_{i\in I}$, the common comparison satisfies $C\preceq D$ exactly when $\Sigma(C)\le\Sigma(D)$. Equivalently, the same order criterion holds for the state compounds $C_0,D_0$ after canceling their common $T e_{z_0}$. The index family is finite; no arbitrary-index choice or infinite decomposition is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] The common-meter compatibility interface in the Statement: the exact signed substitution for every $u_{i,x}$ holds, finite substitutions compose, equal type totals give the same cancellable reference sum, and the common meter pair is strict.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]] supplies the real normalized product representation, and [[lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds]] supplies $e_{(x,z_0)}\sim_s(1-\sigma_i(x))e_{(r_i,z_0)}+\sigma_i(x)e_{(r_i,z_1)}$ in its unit product-state comparison. The separate mass-two shared substitution is exactly [A1], not an identification of different product and shared tags.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]: finite signed substitutions are additive and common terms can be canceled. [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] and [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] also preserve signed comparison under positive scaling: multiplying the difference by a positive scalar multiplies both its positive and negative parts by that scalar, so the compound scaling axiom applies.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-reference-order]]: for the common strict meter pair, comparison of equal-mass reference expressions is exactly comparison of their $z_1$ coefficients.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1] and [F1]–[F3].

1.1 For each constituent $(i,x_{ik},z_0)$ of $C$, its mass-two shared compound $u_{i,x_{ik}}$ is equivalent by the exact substitution in [A1] to $e_{r_i}+(1-\sigma_i(x_{ik}))e_{z_0}+\sigma_i(x_{ik})e_{z_1}$. Each side has total coefficient two, so this signed substitution is defined. Scale by $t_{ik}>0$ and combine the finitely many comparisons using [A1] and [F2]. The resulting reference-system part is $\sum_iT_i e_{r_i}$, independent of the chosen states. The meter part has coefficients $T-\Sigma(C)$ on $e_{z_0}$ and $\Sigma(C)$ on $e_{z_1}$, where $T:=\sum_iT_i$. Hence $C$ is equivalent to that fixed reference-system compound plus $(T-\Sigma(C))e_{z_0}+\Sigma(C)e_{z_1}$, whose total coefficient is $T+T=2T$. If the collection is empty, both expressions are zero and the equivalence is reflexivity, requiring no order scaling at zero. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The same substitution for $D$ gives the same reference-system compound because its type totals are the same, and the same total meter mass $T$. Cancel the common reference-system terms by [A1] and [F2]. If $T>0$, the remaining meter expressions have total coefficient $T$; positive scaling by $1/T$ turns them into the unit reference maps $R_{\Sigma(C)/T}$ and $R_{\Sigma(D)/T}$. By [F3] these compare exactly when $\Sigma(C)/T\le\Sigma(D)/T$, which is equivalent to $\Sigma(C)\le\Sigma(D)$. Scaling back by $T>0$ proves the reverse comparison equivalence, so no unit-mass reference theorem is applied directly at mass $T$. Reversing the same equivalences proves the converse implication as well. Since $C=C_0+T e_{z_0}$ and $D=D_0+T e_{z_0}$, [F2] also gives $C\preceq D$ exactly when $C_0\preceq D_0$; for $T=0$ all these compounds are empty and the criterion is $0\le0$. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Remarks

The compatibility interface records the compositional assumption needed to move from separate product systems to one shared meter scale. Without it, independent representations need not share a multiplicative calibration. This theorem makes no statement for infinitely many types.

sections.Statement:
Let $\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2$ be simple domains in a family of finite thermal joins satisfying A1–A7, S1–S3, T1–T5, and C1 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Then there are $x_0\prec\prec x_1$ in $\Gamma_1$ and $y_0\prec\prec y_1$ in $\Gamma_2$ such that

$$(x_0,y_1)\sim(x_1,y_0).$$

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-reference-strip-gluing]]: CH holds on every finite scaled product of copies of any simple type in the family.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]]: under that CH, each simple type and its scaled products have an additive extensive entropy representing accessibility.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-thermal-class-dichotomy]]: for each simple join, either every pair of its states is thermally equivalent or one of its adiabats contains two thermally inequivalent states.

[F4] [[thm-tdmath-sector-nesting]] and [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]]: a common adiabat has identical forward sectors; fixed-work accessibility is ordered by energy, and each component adiabat has one state at each work coordinate in its projection.

sections.Proof:
**Given:** [A1]–[A2], [F1]–[F5], and [F8].

1.1 Work in [F8]'s common affine mathematical energy orientation, without redefining any physical energy or calibration. Apply [F1] and [F2] to each simple type, including every finite join, using the positive normalization by its fixed weight in [A1]. Throughout, entropy at a state means its represented-state value: $w_\Gamma$ times its unit-point-mass representation. This normalization preserves order and finite scalar amounts. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] makes each resulting entropy concave, since the comparison of a scaled pair with its convex-combination state translates under the representation to the concavity inequality. By [F4], each entropy is strictly increasing with energy at fixed work coordinates. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F8]

1.2 Use T5 to choose $\bar x\in\Gamma_1$ and $\bar y\in\Gamma_2$ with $\bar x\sim_T\bar y$. Let $\phi=J_{12}(\bar x,\bar y)$ and consider its adiabat $\partial A_\phi$. T2 gives every $Z$ on that adiabat at least one split $Z=J_{12}(x_Z,y_Z)$ with $x_Z\sim_T y_Z$. [A2, F4, choose]

2.1 Suppose a join state $Z$ on $\partial A_\phi$ has two distinct equilibrium splits $(x^{(1)},y^{(1)})$ and $(x^{(2)},y^{(2)})$. By the definition of $\sim_T$, both pairs are reversible with $Z$, hence mutually accessible compounds. Their work coordinates are fixed by $Z$ and their total energies equal its energy. If the first-component energies agreed, both component states in the splits would agree, so distinctness forces unequal first-component energies. If $u_{x^{(1)}}<u_{x^{(2)}}$, fixed-work comparison [F4] gives $x^{(1)}\prec\prec x^{(2)}$; conservation of total energy gives $u_{y^{(2)}}<u_{y^{(1)}}$, hence $y^{(2)}\prec\prec y^{(1)}$. Taking $(x_0,x_1,y_0,y_1)=(x^{(1)},x^{(2)},y^{(2)},y^{(1)})$ gives $(x_0,y_1)\sim(x_1,y_0)$ because both split compounds are reversible with $Z$. If the first energies occur in the opposite order, swap the two splits and obtain the same calibrator form. Therefore, if no calibrator exists, every $Z\in\partial A_\phi$ has a unique equilibrium split. [A2, F4, step 1.2, choose]

3.1 Assume no calibrator exists. For any equilibrium split $(x_Z,y_Z)$ of $Z\in\partial A_\phi$, reversibility with $Z$ and the common adiabat give $(x_Z,y_Z)\sim(\bar x,\bar y)$ as compounds. By [F1], $x_Z$ and $\bar x$ are comparable; [F4] says their sectors coincide exactly when they are equivalent. If $x_Z\prec\prec\bar x$, pair reversibility gives $(\bar x,\bar y)\prec(x_Z,y_Z)$. Consistency adds $\bar y$ to $x_Z\prec\bar x$, and cancellation [F5] gives $\bar y\prec y_Z$. If $y_Z\prec\bar y$, consistency and the pair comparison instead cancel to give $\bar x\prec x_Z$, a contradiction. Thus $\bar y\prec\prec y_Z$, making a calibrator. The case $\bar x\prec\prec x_Z$ is symmetric: it gives $y_Z\prec\prec\bar y$, again a calibrator. Since neither is allowed under the assumption, $x_Z\sim\bar x$. Adding spectators to the two directions and cancelling by [F5] then gives both $\bar y\prec y_Z$ and $y_Z\prec\bar y$, so $y_Z\sim\bar y$. Thus every split on this adiabat has components in the corresponding component adiabats. [A1, A2, F1, F4, F5, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Under the no-calibrator assumption, fix a first-component work coordinate $v_1$ in the projection of $\partial A_{\bar x}$. The boundary-graph result [F4] gives exactly one state $x_*$ on that component adiabat at $v_1$. Every split of a join state on $\partial A_\phi$ with first work coordinate $v_1$ therefore has first component $x_*$. Each split is thermal, so $x_*\sim_T y_Z$ for its second component. T3 makes all such $y_Z$ thermally equivalent, and C1 makes each joined state $J(x_*,y_Z)=Z$ thermally equivalent to $x_*$. Hence all join states on this adiabat over fixed $v_1$ lie in one thermal class. Fixing a second-component work coordinate instead gives the corresponding conclusion for first components. [A2, F4, step 3.1]

5.1 Let $\Omega$ be the open connected work-coordinate projection of $\partial A_\phi$ from [F4]. From any point of $\Omega$, the set reachable by finitely many coordinate-axis segments contained in open boxes in $\Omega$ is relatively open, and its complement is also relatively open; connectedness makes the reachable set all of $\Omega$. Along each such segment, step 4.1 gives equivalence of the corresponding join states; T3 composes these finitely many equivalences. Thus the whole adiabat $\partial A_\phi$ is one thermal class. Since the argument works for every starting join state, every join adiabat is one thermal class. [A2, F4, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Still assuming no calibrator, apply [F3] to each join system. Its alternative with two thermally inequivalent states on one adiabat is excluded by step 5.1, so all states of each join system are thermally equivalent. For any $x,x'\in\Gamma_1$, use T5 with one allowed second work coordinate to choose $y,y'$ with $x\sim_T y$ and $x'\sim_T y'$. C1 relates each component to its joined state, and all join states are in one thermal class; T3 therefore gives $x\sim_T x'$. The same argument gives one thermal class in $\Gamma_2$. Now take $Z=\phi\in\partial A_\phi$ and a split $(x,y)$ supplied by T2. Choose nonzero sufficiently small $\delta$ so $(u_x+\delta,v_1)\in\Gamma_1$ and $(u_y-\delta,v_2)\in\Gamma_2$, possible because the domains are open. These states form a distinct split of the same $Z$. Since the original split has $x\sim_T y$ and each component type is one thermal class, T3 gives thermal equivalence of the changed pair as well. This contradicts uniqueness of the split from step 2.1. Therefore a calibrator exists. [A2, F3, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 5.1, choose]

7.1 Fix a calibrator $x_0\prec\prec x_1$, $y_0\prec\prec y_1$, whose existence is step 6.1. Choose same-type entropy representatives $S_1,S_2$ from [F2], with positive gaps $h_1=S_1(x_1)-S_1(x_0)$ and $h_2=S_2(y_1)-S_2(y_0)$. Normalize $\widetilde S_i=S_i/h_i$, so both calibrator increments are one, and put $s(x)=\widetilde S_1(x)-\widetilde S_1(x_0)$ and $t(y)=\widetilde S_2(y)-\widetilde S_2(y_0)$. Write $u=\mathsf{J}(x_0)+\mathsf{J}(y_1)$ and $v=\mathsf{J}(x_1)+\mathsf{J}(y_0)$. The calibrator says $u\sim v$, so $v-u=(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))-(\mathsf{J}(y_1)-\mathsf{J}(y_0))$ is equivalent to zero; translation and cancellation [F5] give $(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))\sim_s(\mathsf{J}(y_1)-\mathsf{J}(y_0))$. For any state $x$, the signed map $d_x=\mathsf{J}(x)-(1-s(x))\mathsf{J}(x_0)-s(x)\mathsf{J}(x_1)$ has total mass and $\widetilde S_1$-value zero. Its positive and negative parts have equal mass and entropy, so [F2] makes them equivalent. Hence $\mathsf{J}(x)\sim_s(1-s(x))\mathsf{J}(x_0)+s(x)\mathsf{J}(x_1)$; the same argument applies to states of the second type. These are formal signed maps when a coefficient lies outside $[0,1]$. [F2, F5, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 For a state pair $(x,y)$, put $\lambda=(s(x)+t(y))/2$ and $\delta=(s(x)-t(y))/2$. Adding the signed reductions from step 7.1 makes the pair equivalent to $(1-\lambda)(\mathsf{J}(x_0)+\mathsf{J}(y_0))+\lambda(\mathsf{J}(x_1)+\mathsf{J}(y_1))$ plus $\delta[(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))-(\mathsf{J}(y_1)-\mathsf{J}(y_0))]$. The calibrator increment equivalence from step 7.1 makes the latter term equivalent to zero for either sign of $\delta$. Thus each pair reduces to its reference map at parameter $\lambda$. For any finite compound $A$ with amounts $M_1,M_2$ of the two types, add and scale these single-state reductions. Writing $q_1(A),q_2(A)$ for the amount-weighted sums of $s(x),t(y)$, respectively, gives $A\sim_s(M_1-q_1(A))\mathsf{J}(x_0)+q_1(A)\mathsf{J}(x_1)+(M_2-q_2(A))\mathsf{J}(y_0)+q_2(A)\mathsf{J}(y_1)$. Using $(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))\sim_s(\mathsf{J}(y_1)-\mathsf{J}(y_0))$, this is equivalent to $M_1\mathsf{J}(x_0)+M_2\mathsf{J}(y_0)+Q(A)(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))$, where $Q(A)=q_1(A)+q_2(A)$. If the total mass is zero, both compounds are empty and reflexivity compares them. Otherwise, for same-composition $A,B$, their base terms agree. If $Q(A)<Q(B)$, the positive and negative parts of the reference-map difference are $(Q(B)-Q(A))\mathsf{J}(x_1)$ and $(Q(B)-Q(A))\mathsf{J}(x_0)$, so $x_0\prec x_1$ and positive scaling compares the maps forward. If the Q values agree the maps coincide; if $Q(A)>Q(B)$ the reverse comparison holds. Translation, addition, and ordinary-order compatibility [F5] transfer the result to $A,B$. This proves CH for every fixed finite composition of the two types and their scaled copies. [A1, F2, F5, step 7.1, algebra] ∎
sections.Remarks: The proof uses C1 in steps 4.1 and 6.1 and T5 in steps 1.2 and 6.1. It does not establish the calibrator from the bare set-valued join formula or from T1–T4 alone. All conclusions remain conditional mathematical consequences of the listed hypotheses.

Write $u=\mathsf{J}(x_0)+\mathsf{J}(y_1)$ and $v=\mathsf{J}(x_1)+\mathsf{J}(y_0)$. The calibrator says $u\sim v$, so $v-u=(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))-(\mathsf{J}(y_1)-\mathsf{J}(y_0))$ is equivalent to zero; translation and cancellation [F5] give $(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))\sim_s(\mathsf{J}(y_1)-\mathsf{J}(y_0))$. For any state $x$, the signed map $d_x=\mathsf{J}(x)-(1-s(x))\mathsf{J}(x_0)-s(x)\mathsf{J}(x_1)$ has total mass and $\widetilde S_1$-value zero. Its positive and negative parts have equal mass and entropy, so [F2] makes them equivalent. Hence $\mathsf{J}(x)\sim_s(1-s(x))\mathsf{J}(x_0)+s(x)\mathsf{J}(x_1)$; the same argument applies to states of the second type. These are formal signed maps when a coefficient lies outside $[0,1]$. [F2, F5, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 For a state pair $(x,y)$, put $\lambda=(s(x)+t(y))/2$ and $\delta=(s(x)-t(y))/2$. Adding the signed reductions from step 7.1 makes the pair equivalent to $(1-\lambda)(\mathsf{J}(x_0)+\mathsf{J}(y_0))+\lambda(\mathsf{J}(x_1)+\mathsf{J}(y_1))$ plus $\delta[(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))-(\mathsf{J}(y_1)-\mathsf{J}(y_0))]$. The calibrator increment equivalence from step 7.1 makes the latter term equivalent to zero for either sign of $\delta$. Thus each pair reduces to its reference map at parameter $\lambda$. For any finite compound $A$ with amounts $M_1,M_2$ of the two types, add and scale these single-state reductions. Writing $q_1(A),q_2(A)$ for the amount-weighted sums of $s(x),t(y)$, respectively, gives $A\sim_s(M_1-q_1(A))\mathsf{J}(x_0)+q_1(A)\mathsf{J}(x_1)+(M_2-q_2(A))\mathsf{J}(y_0)+q_2(A)\mathsf{J}(y_1)$. Using $(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))\sim_s(\mathsf{J}(y_1)-\mathsf{J}(y_0))$, this is equivalent to $M_1\mathsf{J}(x_0)+M_2\mathsf{J}(y_0)+Q(A)(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))$, where $Q(A)=q_1(A)+q_2(A)$. If the total mass is zero, both compounds are empty and reflexivity compares them. Otherwise, for same-composition $A,B$, their base terms agree. If $Q(A)<Q(B)$, the positive and negative parts of the reference-map difference are $(Q(B)-Q(A))\mathsf{J}(x_1)$ and $(Q(B)-Q(A))\mathsf{J}(x_0)$, so $x_0\prec x_1$ and positive scaling compares the maps forward. If the Q values agree the maps coincide; if $Q(A)>Q(B)$ the reverse comparison holds. Translation, addition, and ordinary-order compatibility [F5] transfer the result to $A,B$. This proves CH for every fixed finite composition of the two types and their scaled copies. [A1, F2, F5, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The proof uses C1 in steps 4.1 and 6.1 and T5 in steps 1.2 and 6.1. It does not establish the calibrator from the bare set-valued join formula or from T1–T4 alone. All conclusions remain conditional mathematical consequences of the listed hypotheses.

sections.Statement:
Fix dimension $d\ge1$, particle mass $m>0$, action reference $h>0$, inverse energy $\beta>0$, and positive cube volumes $V_N$ with $N/V_N\to\rho\in(0,\infty)$. For $N$ indistinguishable classical noninteracting particles in a cube of volume $V_N$, use the phase-space reference $dq\,dp/(N!h^{dN})$ and Hamiltonian $H_N(q,p)=\sum_{i=1}^N|p_i|^2/(2m)$. Define $\lambda_\beta=h\sqrt{\beta/(2\pi m)}$. Then the dimensionless partition integral and free-energy limits are
$$Z_N=\frac{V_N^N}{N!\lambda_\beta^{dN}},\quad\frac{-\beta^{-1}\log Z_N}{N}\longrightarrow\beta^{-1}[\log(\rho\lambda_\beta^d)-1],\quad\frac{-\beta^{-1}\log Z_N}{V_N}\longrightarrow\beta^{-1}\rho[\log(\rho\lambda_\beta^d)-1].$$
There is also the following finite-momentum-block limit. Let $M=dN$, let $G_1,\ldots,G_M$ be independent standard normal variables, set $A_N=M^{-1}\sum_{a=1}^MG_a^2$, and define canonical momenta $P_a^{\rm can}=\sqrt{m/\beta}\,G_a$ and shell-prepared momenta $P_a^{\rm sh}=\sqrt{m/\beta}\,G_a/\sqrt{A_N}$. The shell-prepared vector has exactly energy $dN/(2\beta)$, and for every fixed $r$ and bounded continuous $\psi:\mathbb R^r\to\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb E\psi(P_1^{\rm sh},\ldots,P_r^{\rm sh})\longrightarrow\mathbb E\psi(P_1^{\rm can},\ldots,P_r^{\rm can}).$$
This is weak convergence for each fixed block in this free-particle model. The shell preparation is the stated normalized-Gaussian construction, and no finite-width shell or interacting-gas equivalence is asserted.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The free-particle Hamiltonian, phase-space normalization, and normalized-Gaussian shell preparation.

[A1] $d,N\ge1$, $m,h,\beta,V_N>0$, $N/V_N\to\rho\in(0,\infty)$, and the $N$-particle Hamiltonian is additive kinetic energy in a cubic position box.

[A2] For the block limit, the $G_a$ are independent with density $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ and $r$ is fixed while $N\to\infty$.

[F1] [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]: the phase-space integrals are Lebesgue integrals, and integrability/Fubini hypotheses are stated for the displayed densities.

[F2] [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] and [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]: finite products of the Lebesgue factors carry the rectangular product measure.

[F3] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] and [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: nonnegative product integrals factor by Tonelli; integrable products may be evaluated iteratively.

[F4] [[thm-gaussian-integral]]: $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi$.

[F5] [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]] and [[thm-of-square-roots]]: the scaling substitution $u=\sqrt c\,x$ is valid for $c>0$, so $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-cx^2}\,dx=\sqrt{\pi/c}$.

[F6] [[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]], and [[cor-integral-logarithm-is-strictly-increasing]]: the library natural logarithm equals the integral logarithm and is strictly increasing on positive reals.

[F7] [[thm-integration-by-parts]]: on each finite interval, differentiable factors with integrable derivatives obey the ordinary integration-by-parts identity.

[F8] [[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]]: $R^k e^{-R^2/2}\to0$ for each fixed nonnegative integer $k$, by setting $x=R^2/2$ and bounding $x^{k/2}$ by a larger integer power.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** [A1] and, for the second conclusion, [A2].

1.1 The integrand is nonnegative, so [F3] factors the position and momentum integrals: $$Z_N=\frac1{N!h^{dN}}\int_{\Lambda_N^N}\int_{\mathbb R^{dN}} e^{-\beta\sum_i|p_i|^2/(2m)}\,dp\,dq =\frac{V_N^N}{N!h^{dN}}\left(\int_\mathbb R e^{-\beta p^2/(2m)}\,dp\right)^{dN}.$$ By [F4]–[F5] the one-coordinate integral is $\sqrt{2\pi m/\beta}$, proving the stated exact formula with $\lambda_\beta=h\sqrt{\beta/(2\pi m)}$. The dimensions are consistent: $\lambda_\beta$ is a length, so $V_N^N/\lambda_\beta^{dN}$ and $Z_N$ are dimensionless. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5]

1.2 Let $G$ have the density in [A2]. By [F4]–[F5], it is normalized. Apply [F7] on $[-R,R]$ first with $u(x)=x$, $v'(x)=xe^{-x^2/2}$, and then with $u(x)=x^3$, $v'(x)=xe^{-x^2/2}$. In each case $v(x)=-e^{-x^2/2}$. Letting $R\to\infty$, the endpoint terms vanish by [F8], giving $\mathbb E G^2=1$ and $\mathbb E G^4=3$. Thus $\mathbb E(G^2-1)=0$ and $\mathbb E(G^2-1)^2=2$. Product measure and [F3] make distinct coordinates independent, so expanding the square and factoring cross integrals gives $$\mathbb E(A_N-1)^2=M^{-2}\sum_{a=1}^M2=2/M.$$ For any $\eta>0$, $\eta^2\mathbf1_{\{|A_N-1|>\eta\}}\le(A_N-1)^2$, so integration proves $P(|A_N-1|>\eta)\le2/(M\eta^2)\to0$. Hence $A_N\to1$ in probability. [A2, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F7, F8, algebra]

2.1 Monotonicity of $\log$ from [F6] gives $\int_1^N\log x\,dx\le\log N!\le\int_1^{N+1}\log x\,dx$, hence $\log N!=N\log N-N+O(\log(N+1))$. Substituting the exact $Z_N$ yields $$N^{-1}\log Z_N=\log(V_N/N)+1-d\log\lambda_\beta+o(1)\to-\log\rho+1-d\log\lambda_\beta.$$ Multiplication by $-\beta^{-1}$ proves the per-particle limit; multiplying by $N/V_N\to\rho$ proves the per-volume limit. [A1, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Since $A_N>0$ almost surely, the shell-prepared variables are defined. Algebra gives $$\sum_{a=1}^{dN}\frac{(P_a^{\rm sh})^2}{2m} =\frac1{2\beta A_N}\sum_aG_a^2=\frac{M}{2\beta}=\frac{dN}{2\beta}.$$ This exact energy constraint holds on every outcome where $A_N>0$, an event of probability one since the joint Gaussian density assigns zero mass to the origin. [A2, step 1.2]

2.3 For fixed $r$, the scalar multiplier $A_N^{-1/2}$ tends to $1$ in probability by continuity at $1$ and step 1.2. Therefore $(P_1^{\rm sh},\ldots,P_r^{\rm sh})-(P_1^{\rm can},\ldots,P_r^{\rm can})$ tends to zero in probability: restrict first to the event $\sum_{a=1}^rG_a^2\le R^2$, where its norm is at most $\sqrt{m/\beta}R|A_N^{-1/2}-1|$, and then bound the complement by $P(\sum_{a=1}^rG_a^2>R^2)\le r/R^2$ using the second moment. For bounded continuous $\psi$, choose $R$ so this tail is small, use uniform continuity of $\psi$ on the compact ball of radius $2\sqrt{m/\beta}R$, and then use convergence in probability of the difference. On the complement the expectation difference is at most $2\|\psi\|_\infty$. Sending first $N\to\infty$ and then $R\to\infty$ proves the claimed expectation limit. [A2, F1, F3, step 1.2]

3.1 If positions are included, choose them independently and uniformly in the same cube under both preparations. After coordinatewise rescaling by the side length, every fixed position block already has the same uniform law in both models and is independent of the momentum vector. The same bounded-continuous test argument as in 2.3, first on compact sets and then on their small tails, proves the joint fixed-block limit. This does not change the energy computation because the Hamiltonian has no position dependence. [A1, A2, F1, step 2.3] ∎

sections.Statement:
Assume AC, the ultrafilter extension principle, DC, and HB. Let $\phi$ be superstable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], and fix $z,\beta>0$. For stationary finite-intensity configuration laws, let $I(P)$ be relative entropy density with respect to the independent unit-intensity Poisson law, $\rho(P)=E_PN_{[0,1)^d}$, and $\Phi(P)$ the limiting positional energy density. The existence and lower semicontinuity of $\Phi$ under these hypotheses are part of the proof below. For free and periodic cubes define
$$Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}\!\left[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,bc}}\right],\qquad bc\in\{\mathrm{free},\mathrm{per}\}.$$
Then the limit $p_Q(z,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}$ exists, is independent of $bc$, and
$$p_Q(z,\beta)=-\min_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
The minimizer set is nonempty and compact in the local-tame topology $\tau_L$. This theorem concerns positional configurations only. If $\Xi_{L,z,\beta}$ is instead normalized against Lebesgue measure with $1/N!$, then $\Xi_{L,z,\beta}=e^{L^d}Z_{L,z,\beta,\mathrm{free}}$, so its logarithmic rate is $p_Q+1$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** AC, the ultrafilter extension principle, DC, HB, a superstable regular pair potential, $z,\beta>0$, and the unit-intensity Poisson reference.

[A1] The choice assumptions are carried explicitly because [[thm-tdmath-local-tame-entropy-compactness]] uses AC, the ultrafilter extension principle, DC, and HB for compactness and sequential compactness.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]: superstable means a stable part plus a nonnegative repulsive core, regularity supplies the decreasing integrable lower and upper tail, and $Z_Q$ uses normalized unit-intensity Poisson measure.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-superstable-cell-energy-bound]]: there are $A>0,B\geq0$ such that $H_\phi(\omega)\geq A\sum_iN_{C_i}(\omega)^2-BN(\omega)$.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-local-tame-entropy-compactness]]: for every finite $c$, the laws with $I(P)\leq c$ are compact and sequentially compact in $\tau_L$ under the assumptions in [A1].

[F4] [[thm-tdmath-spatial-mean-information]]: if a stationary law is ergodic under all translations and has finite $I(P)=\gamma$, then $L^{-d}\log(dP_{\Lambda_L}/dQ_{\Lambda_L})\to\gamma$ in $L^1(P)$.

[F5] [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]]: $\tau_L$ is convergence of expectations of every measurable local observable bounded by a constant times $1+N_A$ on some bounded set $A$.

[F6] [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]: for the regular tail class here, the free-cube grand partition is finite and its free pressure limit exists.

Assume the superstable regular model of [[thm-tdmath-periodic-fixed-n-limit]], an interior density $N_L/L^d\to\rho$, and differentiability of $\beta\mapsto F_\beta(\rho)$ at $\beta>0$. Put $e=-\partial_\beta F_\beta(\rho)$. Suppose the grand variational minimizer at a supporting activity $z>0$ is a singleton $P_*$. Let $R_{L,\omega}$ be the periodized empirical field of [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]]. There exists a specified sequence $\delta_L\downarrow0$ such that the uniform positional shell law
$$Q_{\Lambda_L}\!\left(\,\cdot\ \middle|\ N=N_L,\ \left|H_{L,\mathrm{per}}/L^d-e\right|\leq\delta_L\right)$$
is eventually defined, and its empirical field converges in probability in $\tau_L$ to $P_*$. The free and periodic exact-$N$ canonical empirical fields and the matching periodic grand-canonical empirical field converge in probability to the same limit. The energy width $2\delta_LL^d=o(L^d)$; no arbitrary prescribed width or zero-width surface measure is asserted.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The interaction, density, differentiability, supporting activity, and singleton minimizer stated above.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-periodic-fixed-n-limit]]: periodic exact-$N$ log partitions converge to $F_\beta(\rho)$, and their empirical fields have exponentially small probability outside every neighborhood of the supporting minimizer set.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-fixed-n-local-ensemble-equivalence]]: free exact-$N$ empirical fields concentrate exponentially near the supporting grand minimizer set.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-continuum-variational-pressure]]: the grand variational minimizer set is compact in $\tau_L$.

[F4] [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]] and [[lem-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field-stationary-density]]: periodized empirical fields are stationary laws with intensity $N_L/L^d$.

[L1] Georgii's Theorem 2 (1994, Sections 3–5) gives the good $\tau_L$ large-deviation principle for periodized empirical fields under the periodic grand-canonical law, with zero set equal to its stationary variational minimizers. The complete proof was read.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The assumptions and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Let $C_L$ be the periodic exact-$N_L$ canonical law. For $|t|<\beta$, $$ E_{C_L}e^{tH_{\mathrm{per}}} =Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta-t)/Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta). $$ By [F1], the normalized log moment generating function converges to $F_{\beta-t}(\rho)-F_\beta(\rho)$, whose derivative at zero is $e$. For any fixed $\epsilon>0$, choose small positive and negative $t$ so the Chernoff exponents for $H/L^d\geq e+\epsilon$ and $H/L^d\leq e-\epsilon$ are strictly negative. Hence the canonical probability outside the fixed $\epsilon$-window tends to zero. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Choose increasing thresholds $L_k$ so that for every $L\geq L_k$ the probability outside the $1/k$ window is at most $1/k$. Set $k(L)=\max\{k:L_k\leq L\}$ and $\delta_L=1/k(L)$. Then $\delta_L\downarrow0$ and the canonical probability of the selected shell tends to one. Positivity of the canonical weight on the shell implies positive Poisson reference measure, so the shell law is defined eventually. [step 1.1, choose]

3.1 Let $U$ be any open $\tau_L$ neighborhood of $P_*$ and let $S_L$ be the selected shell event. On $S_L$, the periodic canonical density relative to the uniform positional law lies between $e^{-\beta L^d(e+\delta_L)}$ and $e^{-\beta L^d(e-\delta_L)}$. Hence
$$Q_{\Lambda_L}(R_{L,\omega}\notin U\mid S_L)\leq\frac{e^{2\beta\delta_L L^d}}{C_L^{\mathrm{per}}(S_L)}\,C_L^{\mathrm{per}}(R_{L,\omega}\notin U).$$

4.1 The free exact-$N$ empirical field converges in probability by [F2]. The periodic grand empirical fields obey the good LDP [L1]; its unique zero is $P_*$ by [F3], so the probability outside each neighborhood of $P_*$ tends to zero. Let $\phi$ be stable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], with stability constant $B$, and fix $a,\beta>0$. For free-boundary cubes define $\Xi_L(a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$. Then
$$1\leq\Xi_L(a,\beta)\leq\exp(ae^{\beta B}L^d),\qquad p(a,\beta):=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(a,\beta)$$
exists and is finite. This theorem assumes only stability and the decreasing integrable two-sided tail in regularity; it does not assert canonical fixed-density convergence, periodic-boundary equality, or arbitrary-region limits.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** Dimension $d\geq1$, a stable regular pair potential, its stability constant $B$, and fixed numerical length and energy units.

[A1] Stability means $H_\phi(\omega)\geq-BN(\omega)$ for every finite configuration, and the grand partition uses the $1/N!$ normalization in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]].

[F1] [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]: for some nonnegative nonincreasing $\psi$ and $R_0<\infty$, $|\phi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ for $|x|_\infty\geq R_0$, with finite weighted integral $\int_{R_0}^\infty\psi(r)r^{d-1}dr$.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]]: $\sum_{m\geq1}m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq 2^{d-1}g^{-d}\eta(g)$ and there are gaps $g(\ell)$ with $g(\ell)/\ell\to0$ and $(\ell/g(\ell))^d\eta(g(\ell))\to0$.

[F3] [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]] and [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]: $|[0,L)^d|=L^d$ and finite product Lebesgue measure gives $|([0,L)^d)^N|=L^{dN}$.

[F4] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]], [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], and [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]: the nonnegative exponential series sums to $e^x$, $0!=1$, and nonnegative grand terms may be split into a finite partial sum and its tail.

[F5] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: nonnegative sums and product integrals factor over finitely many disjoint regions.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Put $q=ae^{\beta B}$. For every $N$-point configuration, $0\leq e^{-\beta H_\phi}\leq e^{\beta BN}$ by [A1]. Applying [F3] to the finite-volume integral gives $Z(L,N;\beta)\leq(qL^d)^N/N!$. Summing by [F4] yields $\Xi_L\leq e^{qL^d}$; the empty configuration contributes exactly $1$, so $\Xi_L\geq1$. [A1, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Choose $K>eq+1$ and an integer cutoff $n_\ell$ with $K\ell^d<n_\ell\leq K\ell^d+1$. For $N>n_\ell$, $1\leq e^{N-K\ell^d}$, so $$ \sum_{N>n_\ell}Z(\ell,N;\beta)\leq e^{-K\ell^d}\sum_{N\geq0}\frac{(eq\ell^d)^N}{N!}=e^{(eq-K)\ell^d}\leq e^{-\ell^d}. $$ Because $\Xi_\ell\geq1$, the truncated sum $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}=\sum_{N=0}^{n_\ell}Z(\ell,N;\beta)$ satisfies $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}\geq(1-e^{-\ell^d})\Xi_\ell$. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix a core side $\ell$ and a gap $g>2R_0$. Place $M=\lfloor L/(\ell+g)\rfloor^d$ disjoint core cubes of side $\ell$ in $[0,L)^d$ on the lattice of spacing $\ell+g$. Restrict every core to at most $n_\ell$ particles. If two core indices differ by maximum norm $m\geq1$, every pair between them has separation at least $mg$ in maximum norm. The number of offsets in shell $m$ is $(2m+1)^d-(2m-1)^d\leq c_dm^{d-1}$. By [F1], the sum of positive cross-core pair energies is therefore at most $$ D_{L,\ell,g}\leq c_dM n_\ell^2\sum_{m\geq1}m^{d-1}\psi(mg). $$ Negative cross-core energies only increase the Boltzmann weight. Splitting the grand sum by the particle counts in these disjoint cores, Tonelli [F5] and the multinomial coefficient show that the global $N!$ cancels the assignments of labeled coordinates to cores. Thus $$ \Xi_L\geq e^{-\beta D_{L,\ell,g}}(\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut})^M. $$ [F1, F3, F5, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Divide the last inequality by $L^d$ and let $L\to\infty$ with $\ell,g$ fixed. Since $M/L^d\to(\ell+g)^{-d}$, [F2] gives $$ \liminf_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L\geq\left(\frac{\ell}{\ell+g}\right)^d\left[\ell^{-d}\log\Xi_\ell+\ell^{-d}\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})-C_dK_1^2\left(\frac{\ell}{g}\right)^d\eta(g)\right], $$ where $K_1=K+1$ bounds $n_\ell/\ell^d$ for $\ell\geq1$ and $C_d$ absorbs the fixed shell-count constant and $\beta$. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The numbers $p_\ell=\ell^{-d}\log\Xi_\ell$ lie in $[0,q]$ by step 1.1, so choose $\ell_j\to\infty$ with $p_{\ell_j}\to\limsup_{\ell\to\infty}p_\ell$. Set $g=g(\ell_j)$ from [F2]. Then $g/\ell_j\to0$, the volume fraction tends to $1$, the cutoff logarithm divided by $\ell_j^d$ tends to zero, and the cross-core error tends to zero. Step 4.1 therefore yields $\liminf_{L\to\infty}p_L\geq\limsup_{L\to\infty}p_L$. The reverse inequality is automatic for every real sequence, so the limit exists; step 1.1 makes it finite. [F2, step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

sections.Statement: Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to\mathbb C$ be measurable with $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere. Suppose $g\ge0$ is measurable and $\int g\,d\mu<\infty$, and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for every $n$. Then $f$ is integrable, $\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu$, and $\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\to0$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** As stated in the item.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]: integrability, signed/complex integrals, and the reference-measure convention are as defined there.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-fatou]]: for nonnegative measurable functions, the integral of the pointwise liminf is at most the liminf of the integrals.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-monotone-convergence]]: the nonnegative integral is additive and positively homogeneous.

[A1] The functions are measurable, converge almost everywhere, and are dominated almost everywhere by the nonnegative integrable function $g$.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** A measure space, almost-everywhere convergence, and an integrable dominating function $g\ge0$.

1.1 The exceptional convergence and domination sets have a common measurable null superset $N$, by countable subadditivity: disjointifying $N_1,N_2,\ldots$ into successive differences and applying countable additivity gives $\mu(\bigcup_jN_j)\le\sum_j\mu(N_j)=0$. A nonnegative measurable function supported on $N$ has integral zero, since every simple minorant is supported there. Redefine all $f_n$ and $f$ to be zero on $N$; this preserves measurability and their integrals, and now convergence and domination hold everywhere. Also $|f|\le g$ pointwise, hence $f$ is integrable. [F1, A1]

2.1 First take all functions real. The nonnegative functions $f_n+g$ converge pointwise to $f+g$. Fatou gives $\int(f+g)\le\liminf_n\int(f_n+g)=\int g+\liminf_n\int f_n$, so $\int f\le\liminf_n\int f_n$. Applying Fatou to $g-f_n\ge0$ gives $\int(g-f)\le\liminf_n\int(g-f_n)=\int g-\limsup_n\int f_n$, hence $\limsup_n\int f_n\le\int f$. Additivity of integrable signed integrals follows by writing each as a difference of its positive and negative parts and using [F3]. The inequalities imply convergence of integrals. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 For complex $f_n$, apply step 2.1 separately to their real and imaginary parts, each dominated by $g$; their integral limits combine to $\int f$. To prove $L^1$ convergence, apply Fatou to the nonnegative functions $2g-|f_n-f|$, which converge to $2g$; it gives $2\int g\le2\int g-\limsup_n\int|f_n-f|$, so the latter limsup is zero. Therefore $\int|f_n-f|\to0$ as claimed. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to\mathbb C$ be measurable with $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere. Suppose $g\ge0$ is measurable and $\int g\,d\mu<\infty$, and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for every $n$. Then $f$ is integrable, $\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu$, and $\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\to0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** As stated in the item.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]: integrability, signed/complex integrals, and the reference-measure convention are as defined there.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-fatou]]: for nonnegative measurable functions, the integral of the pointwise liminf is at most the liminf of the integrals.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-monotone-convergence]]: the nonnegative integral is additive and positively homogeneous.

[A1] The functions are measurable, converge almost everywhere, and are dominated almost everywhere by the nonnegative integrable function $g$.

## Proof

**Given:** A measure space, almost-everywhere convergence, and an integrable dominating function $g\ge0$.

1.1 The exceptional convergence and domination sets have a common measurable null superset $N$, by countable subadditivity: disjointifying $N_1,N_2,\ldots$ into successive differences and applying countable additivity gives $\mu(\bigcup_jN_j)\le\sum_j\mu(N_j)=0$. A nonnegative measurable function supported on $N$ has integral zero, since every simple minorant is supported there. Redefine all $f_n$ and $f$ to be zero on $N$; this preserves measurability and their integrals, and now convergence and domination hold everywhere. Also $|f|\le g$ pointwise, hence $f$ is integrable. [F1, A1]

2.1 First take all functions real. The nonnegative functions $f_n+g$ converge pointwise to $f+g$. Fatou gives $\int(f+g)\le\liminf_n\int(f_n+g)=\int g+\liminf_n\int f_n$, so $\int f\le\liminf_n\int f_n$. Applying Fatou to $g-f_n\ge0$ gives $\int(g-f)\le\liminf_n\int(g-f_n)=\int g-\limsup_n\int f_n$, hence $\limsup_n\int f_n\le\int f$. Additivity of integrable signed integrals follows by writing each as a difference of its positive and negative parts and using [F3]. The inequalities imply convergence of integrals. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 For complex $f_n$, apply step 2.1 separately to their real and imaginary parts, each dominated by $g$; their integral limits combine to $\int f$. To prove $L^1$ convergence, apply Fatou to the nonnegative functions $2g-|f_n-f|$, which converge to $2g$; it gives $2\int g\le2\int g-\limsup_n\int|f_n-f|$, so the latter limsup is zero. Therefore $\int|f_n-f|\to0$ as claimed. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1] ∎

sections.Statement: Let $I$ be a finite nonempty subsystem state set, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $|E_i|\le L$ for $L\ge0$, and let the dimensionless bath entropy $s_B$ be $C^2$ on an open interval $U$ containing $[u_0-L,u_0+L]$, with $|s_B''(u)|\le M$ on that closed interval for $M\ge0$. Use one energy unit for $E_i,u_0,L$, so $\beta=s_B'(u_0)$ has inverse-energy units and $M$ has inverse-energy-squared units; $\delta=ML^2/2$ is dimensionless. Put $Z:=\sum_{j\in I}e^{-\beta E_j}$ and $q_i:=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$. Suppose the joint shell weights induce the normalized subsystem law $p_i:=e^{s_B(u_0-E_i)}/\sum_{j\in I}e^{s_B(u_0-E_j)}$. Then $|s_B(u_0-E_i)-s_B(u_0)+\beta E_i|\le\delta$ for every $i$, and $\sum_i|p_i-q_i|\le e^{2\delta}-1$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** As stated in the item.

[A1] $I$ is finite and nonempty; $E_i\in\mathbb R$; $L,M\ge0$; $|E_i|\le L$; and $s_B$ is $C^2$ on an open interval U containing $[u_0-L,u_0+L]$ with the stated second-derivative bound. Both laws are normalized on the same state set.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]: for a finite energy list and real $\beta$, $q_i=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$ is the normalized canonical law.

[F2] [[cor-taylor-remainder-bound]]: a bound $|s_B''|\le M$ gives the first-order Taylor error at most $M|E_i|^2/2$.

[F3] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[def-natural-logarithm]], and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: the exponential is positive and logarithms of products are additive.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The finite subsystem, the twice differentiable bath entropy with bounded second derivative, and the stated shell-weight rule.

1.1 Apply [F2] to $s_B$ at $u_0$ with increment $-E_i$. It gives $s_B(u_0-E_i)=s_B(u_0)-\beta E_i+r_i$ where $|r_i|\le M E_i^2/2\le\delta$. [A1, F2]

2.1 The marginal is therefore $p_i=q_i e^{r_i}/C$, where $C:=\sum_jq_je^{r_j}$. The bounds $e^{-\delta}\le e^{r_j}\le e^\delta$ and $\sum_jq_j=1$ imply $e^{-\delta}\le C\le e^\delta$, so $e^{-2\delta}\le p_i/q_i\le e^{2\delta}$. [F1, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 For $x\in[e^{-2\delta},e^{2\delta}]$, $|x-1|\le e^{2\delta}-1$. Thus $\sum_i|p_i-q_i|=\sum_iq_i|p_i/q_i-1|\le(e^{2\delta}-1)\sum_iq_i=e^{2\delta}-1$. The case $\delta=0$ is included and gives equality of the laws. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $I$ be a finite nonempty subsystem state set, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $|E_i|\le L$ for $L\ge0$, and let the dimensionless bath entropy $s_B$ be $C^2$ on an open interval $U$ containing $[u_0-L,u_0+L]$, with $|s_B''(u)|\le M$ on that closed interval for $M\ge0$. Use one energy unit for $E_i,u_0,L$, so $\beta=s_B'(u_0)$ has inverse-energy units and $M$ has inverse-energy-squared units; $\delta=ML^2/2$ is dimensionless. Put $Z:=\sum_{j\in I}e^{-\beta E_j}$ and $q_i:=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$. Suppose the joint shell weights induce the normalized subsystem law $p_i:=e^{s_B(u_0-E_i)}/\sum_{j\in I}e^{s_B(u_0-E_j)}$. Then $|s_B(u_0-E_i)-s_B(u_0)+\beta E_i|\le\delta$ for every $i$, and $\sum_i|p_i-q_i|\le e^{2\delta}-1$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** As stated in the item.

[A1] $I$ is finite and nonempty; $E_i\in\mathbb R$; $L,M\ge0$; $|E_i|\le L$; and $s_B$ is $C^2$ on an open interval U containing $[u_0-L,u_0+L]$ with the stated second-derivative bound. Both laws are normalized on the same state set.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]: for a finite energy list and real $\beta$, $q_i=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$ is the normalized canonical law.

[F2] [[cor-taylor-remainder-bound]]: a bound $|s_B''|\le M$ gives the first-order Taylor error at most $M|E_i|^2/2$.

[F3] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[def-natural-logarithm]], and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: the exponential is positive and logarithms of products are additive.

## Proof

**Given:** The finite subsystem, the twice differentiable bath entropy with bounded second derivative, and the stated shell-weight rule.

1.1 Apply [F2] to $s_B$ at $u_0$ with increment $-E_i$. It gives $s_B(u_0-E_i)=s_B(u_0)-\beta E_i+r_i$ where $|r_i|\le M E_i^2/2\le\delta$. [A1, F2]

2.1 The marginal is therefore $p_i=q_i e^{r_i}/C$, where $C:=\sum_jq_je^{r_j}$. The bounds $e^{-\delta}\le e^{r_j}\le e^\delta$ and $\sum_jq_j=1$ imply $e^{-\delta}\le C\le e^\delta$, so $e^{-2\delta}\le p_i/q_i\le e^{2\delta}$. [F1, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 For $x\in[e^{-2\delta},e^{2\delta}]$, $|x-1|\le e^{2\delta}-1$. Thus $\sum_i|p_i-q_i|=\sum_iq_i|p_i/q_i-1|\le(e^{2\delta}-1)\sum_iq_i=e^{2\delta}-1$. The case $\delta=0$ is included and gives equality of the laws. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

sections.Statement:
Let $m,n\in\mathbb N$ be finite, let $c_j\in\mathbb R^n$ and $h_j\in\mathbb R$ for $0\le j<m$. The finite system

$$c_j\cdot b\ge h_j\qquad(0\le j<m)$$

has a solution $b\in\mathbb R^n$ if and only if every $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$ with $\lambda_j\ge0$ and $\sum_{j<m}\lambda_jc_j=0$ satisfies $\sum_{j<m}\lambda_jh_j\le0$. Dot products and sums are finite. This includes empty rows, empty variables, and an empty inequality family.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
[A1] The finite row data in the Statement: $m,n$ are nonnegative integers, and each row is $(c_j,h_j)$ with real coefficients.

[F1] [[def-complete-ordered-field]] supplies the complete ordered real field; [[def-function-space]] defines $\mathbb R^n$ as functions on $n=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ with pointwise coordinate operations, forming a vector space as in [[def-vector-space]], including the one-element zero space when $n=0$.

[F2] [[def-finite-sum]] and clauses 1 and 2 of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] supply finite-sum additivity and scalar linearity. [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]] supplies bijective reindexing and interchange of finite iterated sums; applied to the additive monoid of $\mathbb R$, these laws justify collecting coefficients in the finite row combinations.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** [A1]–[F2].

1.1 If $b$ solves the system and $\lambda_j\ge0$ with $\sum_j\lambda_jc_j=0$, multiply row $j$ by $\lambda_j$ and add the finitely many inequalities. The left side is $(\sum_j\lambda_jc_j)\cdot b=0$ by [F2]; hence $0\ge\sum_j\lambda_jh_j$. This proves necessity. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 For sufficiency, prove by induction on $n$ the alternative: if the finite system has no solution, there is a nonnegative combination of its rows whose coefficient vector is zero and whose right side is positive. If $n=0$, every row has zero left side; infeasibility means some $h_j>0$, and that single row is the certificate. If $m=0$, the system is feasible, so this case cannot occur under the induction claim's antecedent. [A1, F1]

1.3 Let $n>0$ and assume the alternative for $n-1$ variables. Write $c_j=(a_j,\alpha_j)$ with $a_j\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and split the row indices into $P=\{j:\alpha_j>0\}$, $N=\{j:\alpha_j<0\}$, and $Z=\{j:\alpha_j=0\}$. Retain each row $(a_j,h_j)$ for $j\in Z$. For every $p\in P$ and $q\in N$, add the reduced row $((-\alpha_q)a_p+\alpha_p a_q,\;(-\alpha_q)h_p+\alpha_p h_q)$. Every multiplier used is positive. [A1, F1, algebra]

1.4 The reduced system in $u\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ is feasible exactly when the original is. Indeed, a solution $(u,t)$ implies every retained inequality; adding row $p$ multiplied by $-\alpha_q>0$ to row $q$ multiplied by $\alpha_p>0$ cancels $t$ and gives each pair row. Conversely, if $u$ satisfies the reduced system, rows in $P$ impose finitely many lower bounds $t\ge(h_p-a_p\cdot u)/\alpha_p$, and rows in $N$ impose finitely many upper bounds $t\le(h_q-a_q\cdot u)/\alpha_q$. Each pair row is exactly the inequality that its lower bound is no greater than its upper bound. If both sets are nonempty, their finite maximum lower bound is at most their finite minimum upper bound, so choose $t$ between them. If only lower bounds occur choose their maximum; if only upper bounds occur choose their minimum; if neither occurs choose $t=0$. Thus the original system has a solution. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 If the original system is infeasible, step 1.4 makes the reduced system infeasible. By induction there are nonnegative multipliers on reduced rows with zero combined first $n-1$ coordinates and positive combined right side. Lift each retained zero-row multiplier to its original row; lift each pair-row multiplier $\mu_{pq}$ to coefficients $-\alpha_q\mu_{pq}$ on row $p$ and $\alpha_p\mu_{pq}$ on row $q$. All lifted coefficients are nonnegative. Every pair lift has last coordinate $(-\alpha_q)\alpha_p+\alpha_p\alpha_q=0$; the total first coordinates vanish by the reduced certificate, and its right side remains positive. This is the required certificate for the original system and completes the induction. [A1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4, algebra]

3.1 If the stated multiplier condition holds, the certificate from step 2.1 cannot exist, because it would have zero combined left coefficient and positive combined right side. Therefore the system is feasible. Together with step 1.1 this proves both directions, including the empty-variable base case in step 1.2, the zero/positive/negative sign partition and bound reconstruction in steps 1.3–1.4, and the lifted certificate in step 2.1. [A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4, step 2.1] ∎

sections.Statement: For every fixed $\beta>0$, the sequence $p_L(\beta)$ of [[def-tdmath-bounded-finite-range-lattice]] has a finite limit as $L\to\infty$. If another finite-volume energy $\widetilde H_L$ on the same configurations satisfies $\sup_s|\widetilde H_L(s)-H_L(s)|\le C_bL^{d-1}$ for a constant $C_b$ independent of $L$, define $\widetilde Z_L(\beta):=\sum_{s\in\mathcal A^{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta\widetilde H_L(s)}$ and $\widetilde p_L(\beta):=L^{-d}\log\widetilde Z_L(\beta)$. Then $\widetilde p_L$ has the same limit. The result covers finite-alphabet, bounded, translation-invariant finite-range interactions on cubic boxes; it asserts no continuum-particle or long-range limit.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** As stated in the item.

[A1] The dimension, alphabet, shapes, bounded interaction functions, free-boundary energies, and $\beta>0$ are exactly as in [[def-tdmath-bounded-finite-range-lattice]].

[F1] [[def-tdmath-bounded-finite-range-lattice]]: the alphabet has $q$ states per site, the (possibly empty) interaction list is finite, each term is bounded, and $Z_L$ is the finite partition sum.

[F3] [[thm-division-algorithm-in-z]]: for positive integer $\ell$ and integer $L\ge0$, write $L=k\ell+r$ with integers $k\ge0$ and $0\le r<\ell$.

[F2] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: $\log$ is increasing and converts products to sums.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The bounded finite-range lattice data, $\beta>0$, and (for the boundary comparison clause) the uniform $C_bL^{d-1}$ energy bound.

1.1 Write $V=L^d$ and $J_0=\sum_a\|\Phi_a\|_\infty$. Each configuration satisfies $|H_L(s)|\le J_0V$, so $q^Ve^{-\beta J_0V}\le Z_L\le q^Ve^{\beta J_0V}$. Hence $p_L$ is bounded above and below uniformly in $L$. [A1, F1, F2]

1.2 Fix an integer block length $\ell>2R$ and write $L=k\ell+r$ with $0\le r<\ell$ using [F3]. Partition $\Lambda_L$ into $k^d$ disjoint $\ell$-cubes and an outer remainder. Form $H_{L,\ell}^{\rm cut}$ by retaining only interactions whose entire support lies in one full cube and assigning zero energy to remainder sites. For a fixed shape, every eligible anchor lies in $[1-R,L+R]^d$. If its support crosses an internal block seam, its coordinate normal to that seam lies in at most $2R+1$ integer positions; the other coordinates have at most $(L+2R)^{d-1}$ choices. If it is not in such a seam strip but the interaction is omitted, its support meets the outer remainder, so its anchor lies within $\ell+2R+1$ layers of one of the $d$ outer faces. Counting at most $d(k-1)$ internal seams and $d$ outer faces bounds the omitted anchors per shape by $d(2R+1)(L/\ell)(L+2R)^{d-1}+d(\ell+2R+1)(L+2R)^{d-1}$. Therefore $\sup_s|H_L(s)-H_{L,\ell}^{\rm cut}(s)|\le J_0d[(2R+1)(L/\ell)+\ell+2R+1](L+2R)^{d-1}$. [A1, F1, F3]

2.1 If two energies on a finite state set differ pointwise by at most $D$, their partition sums satisfy $e^{-\beta D}Z'\le Z\le e^{\beta D}Z'$, so their log partition sums differ by at most $\beta D$ using [F2]. The cut energy factorizes over the cubes and has zero-energy remainder, hence $Z_{L,\ell}^{\rm cut}=Z_\ell^{k^d}q^{L^d-k^d\ell^d}$. Divide the comparison by $L^d$ and let $L\to\infty$ with $\ell$ fixed; the remainder fraction tends to zero, $k^d/L^d\to\ell^{-d}$, and the energy error has limsup at most $2^{d-1}\beta J_0d(2R+1)/\ell$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.2]

3.1 It follows for every $\ell>2R$ that $\limsup_L p_L\le p_\ell+2^{d-1}\beta J_0d(2R+1)/\ell$ and $\liminf_L p_L\ge p_\ell-2^{d-1}\beta J_0d(2R+1)/\ell$. Thus $0\le\limsup_Lp_L-\liminf_Lp_L\le2^d\beta J_0d(2R+1)/\ell$ for every such $\ell$. Letting $\ell\to\infty$ makes the difference zero; boundedness from step 1.1 then gives a finite limit. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 For $\widetilde H_L$, the finite-state comparison of step 2.1 gives $|L^{-d}\log\widetilde Z_L-p_L|\le\beta C_b/L$, which tends to zero. Its limit is therefore the same. [A1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

fm.title: Forward orientation and the Lipschitz boundary graph

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorems 3.3–3.5, pp. 45–47

sections.Statement:
Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], each simple domain has one orientation sign $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$, constant across the domain, such that at fixed work coordinate $v$, $x\prec y$ exactly when $\varepsilon_i(u_y-u_x)\ge0$. In coordinates oriented so $\varepsilon_i=1$, for each $x\in\Gamma_i$ the projection $\rho_x$ of $\partial_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ onto work coordinates is open and connected; the boundary is the graph $(u_x(v),v)$ of a $C^1$ function with locally Lipschitz derivative

$$Du_x(v)=-P_i(u_x(v),v).$$

If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y=A_x$ and their boundary graphs agree.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** A1–A7 and S1–S3 on an open convex simple domain $\Gamma_i$.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: each $A_x$ is supported at $x$ by a unique finite-slope plane; $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-convex-sector-closedness]]: $A_x$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$, and its collinear order implications hold.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-sector-interior]]: every $A_x$ has nonempty ambient interior.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-relative-boundary-support]]: a convex set has a support at each relative boundary point of its closure in its affine hull.

[F4] [[lem-tdmath-unique-support-inward-ray]]: at a full-dimensional convex set's boundary point with a unique support, every direction strictly toward the supporting half-space's interior enters the set's interior for all sufficiently small positive steps.

[F5] [[lem-tdmath-convex-function-local-lipschitz]]: every finite convex function on an open convex set is locally Lipschitz.

[F6] [[lem-tdmath-integral-zero-uniqueness]]: a nonnegative continuous function bounded by a constant times its zero-start integral is identically zero.

[F7] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space are compact.

[F8] [[thm-chain-rule]]: the derivative of a composition of differentiable maps is the composition of their derivatives.

[F9] [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]: a continuous function on a closed interval, differentiable in its interior with an integrable derivative extension, has endpoint increment equal to the integral of that derivative.

[F10] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: a continuous real function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** [A1] and [F1]–[F10]. Write a support plane's inward unit normal with energy component nonzero, as ensured by its finite-slope form.

1.1 For fixed $x=(u_x,v_x)$, the vertical section $I_x:=\{u:(u,v_x)\in A_x\}$ is a relatively closed convex interval by [F1]. The support plane at $x$ confines it to one side of $u_x$. Its inward normal has nonzero energy component, so [F4] gives a nontrivial interior vertical segment on that side. [A1, F1, F4]

1.2 The fiber orientation is locally constant in $v$. At any $x$, choose one vertical point just inside the supported half-space and one just outside; by [F4] the inside point can be chosen in $\operatorname{int}A_x$. Openness of $\Gamma_i$ and of the interior and exterior regions preserves these memberships on nearby fibers. Each such fiber therefore meets $\partial A_x$ between these two energy values. A support of $A_x$ at that boundary point also supports the point's own sector and so has its S2 orientation; the inside/outside placement fixes that orientation. Thus nearby fibers have the same sign as the fiber through $x$. Since $\Gamma_i$ is convex, it is connected; a locally constant two-valued sign is constant. [A1, F2, F3, F4]

1.3 Let $u,w$ be two $C^1$ graph solutions of $Dq=-P_i(q,v)$ on a common open domain, and suppose $u(v_0)=w(v_0)$. Since $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz, choose a convex neighborhood of $(u(v_0),v_0)$ on which one Lipschitz constant $L$ works. Continuity of $u,w$ lets us choose a convex ball about $v_0$ whose closure lies in the common domain and whose two graph images stay in that neighborhood; take any $v$ in a smaller concentric ball. Put $d=v-v_0$ and $\gamma(t)=v_0+td$ for $0\le t\le1$. By [F8], $r(t)=u(\gamma(t))-w(\gamma(t))$ is $C^1$ and
$r'(t)=[-P_i(u(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))+P_i(w(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))]\cdot d.$
The local Lipschitz bound for $P_i$ gives $|r'(t)|\le L\|d\||r(t)|$. The derivative is continuous, hence integrable by [F10]; [F9] gives $r(t)=\int_0^t r'(s)\,ds$; hence $h(t):=|r(t)|\le L\|d\|\int_0^t h(s)\,ds$. Apply [F6] on $[0,1]$ to obtain $h=0$. Thus $u=w$ near $v_0$. Along any polygonal path in the common open domain, the set of path parameters at which equality holds is closed by continuity and open by this local result; since the path interval is connected and the set is nonempty, equality holds along the whole path. Every open connected subset of Euclidean space is polygonally connected: points reachable from a fixed point by finitely many segments in small balls form a nonempty relatively open and relatively closed set. Therefore equality extends throughout each common connected domain. [A1, F6, F8, F9, F10, given, construct]

2.1 The convex, relatively closed interval $I_x$ contains a nontrivial segment on the inward side by step 1.1 and [F4]. Suppose it does not contain the whole open $\Gamma_i$-fiber on that side. Its endpoint $b$ toward that side then lies inside $\Gamma_i$; relative closedness puts $b$ in $I_x$, so the interval from $x$ to $b$ is a compact nondegenerate interval by [F7]. Let $x_1$ be its midpoint. Since $x_1\in A_x$, transitivity gives $A_{x_1}\subseteq A_x$. The supporting plane of $A_{x_1}$ has nonzero energy coefficient, so its vertical section lies wholly on one side of $x_1$; being contained in $I_x$, it lies in one half of $[x,b]$ and has at most half its length. It is nonempty and closed relative to $[x,b]$, hence compact. Repeat: take the midpoint $x_{k+1}$ of the current compact interval $I_{x_k}$; then $x_k\prec x_{k+1}$, so the next section is nested inside the current one and again has at most half its length. The nested compact intervals have a common limit point $x_\infty\in\Gamma_i$ by [F7], and their lengths tend to zero. Relative closedness puts $x_\infty$ in every $A_{x_k}$, hence $A_{x_\infty}\subseteq A_{x_k}$ by transitivity. Its vertical section is therefore only $\{x_\infty\}$, contradicting the nontrivial interior vertical segment at $x_\infty$ supplied by [F4]. Thus $I_x$ contains the whole open fiber on its inward side. [A1, F1, F4, F7, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 All states on a fixed work-coordinate fiber have the same orientation. If $x$ is oriented upward and a state $z$ above it were oriented downward, the full upward section from step 2.1 gives $x\prec z$, and the full downward section from $z$ gives $z\prec w$ for a state $w$ below $x$, contradicting the support at $x$. If a state $y$ below an upward $x$ were oriented downward, choose $z$ above $x$ with $x\prec z$; the first collinear implication in [F1], applied to $x$ between $y$ and $z$, gives $y\prec x$, contradicting the downward support at $y$. The reversed argument handles a downward $x$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Adopt the coordinate convention $\varepsilon_i=1$. Step 2.1 and the common orientation give $x\prec y$ exactly for $u_y\ge u_x$ at fixed $v$, with strict comparison for $u_y>u_x$. [step 3.1, step 1.2, algebra]

5.1 Put $\rho_x=\pi_v(\partial A_x)$. At a boundary point $z\in\partial A_x$, [F3] supplies a support to $A_x$. Because $A_z\subseteq A_x$, that plane also supports $A_z$ and equals its unique S2 plane. Its finite slope gives a nonvertical inward direction; [F4] supplies nearby vertical points inside $A_x$, while the opposite side is outside by the support. Neighborhoods of one inside and one outside point show every nearby work fiber meets $\partial A_x$. Hence $\rho_x$ is open. It is connected because S3 makes $\partial A_x$ arcwise connected and projection is continuous. By step 4.1, every vertical fiber over $\rho_x$ has exactly one boundary energy; call it $u_x(v)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 4.1]

6.1 For $v,v'\in\rho_x$, convexity of $A_x$ puts every convex combination of their boundary states in $A_x$. On any sufficiently small convex ball in $\rho_x$, the unique-boundary property and upward orientation make $u_x$ the least energy in each fiber. Therefore $u_x(tv+(1-t)v')\le t u_x(v)+(1-t)u_x(v')$, so $u_x$ is finite and convex there. It is locally Lipschitz by [F5]. The inward support at $(u_x(v),v)$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\ge -P_i(u_x(v),v)\cdot(v'-v).$
The support at $(u_x(v'),v')$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\le -P_i(u_x(v'),v')\cdot(v'-v).$
Local Lipschitz continuity of $u_x$ and $P_i$ makes the difference between these linear bounds $O(\|v'-v\|^2)$. Thus $u_x$ is differentiable with derivative $-P_i(u_x(v),v)$, and that derivative is locally Lipschitz. Hence $u_x\in C^1$ with locally Lipschitz derivative. [A1, F1, F5, step 5.1]

7.1 If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$. The boundary graphs agree at $v_y$ and solve the same differential equation. The set of $v\in\rho_y$ where $v\in\rho_x$ and $u_y(v)=u_x(v)$ is nonempty, open by step 1.3, and closed by continuity and relative closedness of $\partial A_x$. Connectedness of $\rho_y$ makes it all of $\rho_y$. This shows $\rho_y\subseteq\rho_x$. The same argument, using relative closedness of $\partial A_y$, shows $\rho_y$ is relatively closed in connected $\rho_x$; it is relatively open because both projections are open. Hence $\rho_x=\rho_y$ and the boundary graphs agree. In particular $x\in\partial A_y$, so $y\prec x$; together with $y\in A_x$ and transitivity this gives $A_x=A_y$. [A1, F1, step 6.1, step 1.3] ∎
