2.1 The convex, relatively closed interval $I_x$ contains a nontrivial segment on the inward side by step 1.1 and [F4]. Suppose it does not contain the whole open $\Gamma_i$-fiber on that side. Its endpoint $b$ toward that side then lies inside $\Gamma_i$; relative closedness puts $b$ in $I_x$, so the interval from $x$ to $b$ is a compact nondegenerate interval by [F7]. Let $x_1$ be its midpoint. Since $x_1\in A_x$, transitivity gives $A_{x_1}\subseteq A_x$. The supporting plane of $A_{x_1}$ has nonzero energy coefficient, so its vertical section lies wholly on one side of $x_1$; being contained in $I_x$, it lies in one half of $[x,b]$ and has at most half its length. It is nonempty and closed relative to $[x,b]$, hence compact. Repeat: take the midpoint $x_{k+1}$ of the current compact interval $I_{x_k}$; then $x_k\prec x_{k+1}$, so the next section is nested inside the current one and again has at most half its length. The nested compact intervals have a common limit point $x_\infty\in\Gamma_i$ by [F7], and their lengths tend to zero. Relative closedness puts $x_\infty$ in every $A_{x_k}$, hence $A_{x_\infty}\subseteq A_{x_k}$ by transitivity. Its vertical section is therefore only $\{x_\infty\}$, contradicting the nontrivial interior vertical segment at $x_\infty$ supplied by [F4]. Thus $I_x$ contains the whole open fiber on its inward side. [A1, F1, F4, F7, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 All states on a fixed work-coordinate fiber have the same orientation. If $x$ is oriented upward and a state $z$ above it were oriented downward, the full upward section from step 2.1 gives $x\prec z$, and the full downward section from $z$ gives $z\prec w$ for a state $w$ below $x$, contradicting the support at $x$. If a state $y$ below an upward $x$ were oriented downward, choose $z$ above $x$ with $x\prec z$; the first collinear implication in [F1], applied to $x$ between $y$ and $z$, gives $y\prec x$, contradicting the downward support at $y$. The reversed argument handles a downward $x$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Adopt the coordinate convention $\varepsilon_i=1$. Step 2.1 and the common orientation give $x\prec y$ exactly for $u_y\ge u_x$ at fixed $v$, with strict comparison for $u_y>u_x$. [step 3.1, step 1.2, algebra]

5.1 Put $\rho_x=\pi_v(\partial A_x)$. At a boundary point $z\in\partial A_x$, [F3] supplies a support to $A_x$. Because $A_z\subseteq A_x$, that plane also supports $A_z$ and equals its unique S2 plane. Its finite slope gives a nonvertical inward direction; [F4] supplies nearby vertical points inside $A_x$, while the opposite side is outside by the support. Neighborhoods of one inside and one outside point show every nearby work fiber meets $\partial A_x$. Hence $\rho_x$ is open. It is connected because S3 makes $\partial A_x$ arcwise connected and projection is continuous. By step 4.1, every vertical fiber over $\rho_x$ has exactly one boundary energy; call it $u_x(v)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 4.1]

6.1 For $v,v'\in\rho_x$, convexity of $A_x$ puts every convex combination of their boundary states in $A_x$. On any sufficiently small convex ball in $\rho_x$, the unique-boundary property and upward orientation make $u_x$ the least energy in each fiber. Therefore $u_x(tv+(1-t)v')\le t u_x(v)+(1-t)u_x(v')$, so $u_x$ is finite and convex there. It is locally Lipschitz by [F5]. The inward support at $(u_x(v),v)$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\ge -P_i(u_x(v),v)\cdot(v'-v).$
The support at $(u_x(v'),v')$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\le -P_i(u_x(v'),v')\cdot(v'-v).$
Local Lipschitz continuity of $u_x$ and $P_i$ makes the difference between these linear bounds $O(\|v'-v\|^2)$. Thus $u_x$ is differentiable with derivative $-P_i(u_x(v),v)$, and that derivative is locally Lipschitz. Hence $u_x\in C^1$ with locally Lipschitz derivative. [A1, F1, F5, step 5.1]

7.1 If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$. The boundary graphs agree at $v_y$ and solve the same differential equation. The set of $v\in\rho_y$ where $v\in\rho_x$ and $u_y(v)=u_x(v)$ is nonempty, open by step 1.3, and closed by continuity and relative closedness of $\partial A_x$. Connectedness of $\rho_y$ makes it all of $\rho_y$. This shows $\rho_y\subseteq\rho_x$. The same argument, using relative closedness of $\partial A_y$, shows $\rho_y$ is relatively closed in connected $\rho_x$; it is relatively open because both projections are open. Hence $\rho_x=\rho_y$ and the boundary graphs agree. In particular $x\in\partial A_y$, so $y\prec x$; together with $y\in A_x$ and transitivity this gives $A_x=A_y$. [A1, F1, step 6.1, step 1.3] ∎

fm.title: Trace-class Gibbs normalization for a semibounded self-adjoint operator

references.title: Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics (work in progress, dated 12 October 2026)
references.locator: Complete 635-page PDF retrieved; ensembles and traces §§4.2–4.6 pp.192–217; Bose/Fermi models §§5.6–5.7 pp.277–303; 1D Ising §6.2.2 pp.330–333.

sections.Statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be self-adjoint with regular Borel projection-valued measure $E$ from [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], with $E((-\infty,a))=0$ for finite $a\in\mathbb R$. For each $\gamma>0$, define the bounded Gibbs operator $K_\gamma:=\Phi_E(f_\gamma)$ using the bounded Borel PVM integral of [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], where $f_\gamma(\lambda)=e^{-\gamma\lambda}$ for $\lambda\ge a$ and $f_\gamma(\lambda)=e^{-\gamma a}$ for $\lambda<a$. Fix $\beta>0$ and suppose $K_\beta$ is trace class in the sense of [[def-trace-class-operator]]. Then $K_\beta$ is injective and has a finite or countable orthonormal basis $(u_j)$ of $\mathcal H$ with $Au_j=E_ju_j$, $E_j\ge a$, and $K_\beta u_j=e^{-\beta E_j}u_j$. Its partition function $Z_\beta:=\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=\sum_j e^{-\beta E_j}$ is positive and finite, and $\rho_\beta:=K_\beta/Z_\beta$ is positive with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_\beta=1$. For every $B\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta B)=\sum_j(e^{-\beta E_j}/Z_\beta)\langle Bu_j,u_j\rangle$ absolutely. Further, let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and suppose that for every compact $C\subset J$ there is a summable family $a_j\ge0$ with $(1+|E_j|^2)e^{-\gamma E_j}\le a_j$ for all $j$ and $\gamma\in C$. Then for each $\gamma\in J$, $K_\gamma$ is trace class with partition function $Z_\gamma:=\operatorname{Tr}K_\gamma=\sum_j e^{-\gamma E_j}$. With $p_j(\gamma):=e^{-\gamma E_j}/Z_\gamma$, define $\bar E_\gamma:=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)E_j$, $\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(E):=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)(E_j-\bar E_\gamma)^2$, and $S_\gamma:=-\sum_jp_j(\gamma)\log p_j(\gamma)$. These quantities are finite and satisfy $-\partial_\gamma\log Z_\gamma=\bar E_\gamma$, $\partial_\gamma^2\log Z_\gamma=\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(E)$, and $S_\gamma=\log Z_\gamma+\gamma\bar E_\gamma$ as in [[thm-tdmath-summable-canonical-differentiation]]. Countable nonnegative sums use the finite-subsum supremum convention of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]].
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** AC, a nonzero complex Hilbert space, a self-adjoint semibounded operator, the specified Borel functional calculus, trace-class $K_\beta$, and a bounded operator $B$.

[A1] The Hilbert space is nonzero; $A$ is self-adjoint with spectral support in $[a,\infty)$; AC is adopted; $\beta>0$; and $K_\beta$ is trace class. For the interval clause, the same list $(E_j)$ has the local summable moment envelope stated in the theorem.

[A2] $B$ is a bounded operator on $\mathcal H$.

[F1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]: under AC a self-adjoint $A$ has a regular PVM $E$, domain $D(A)=\{x:\int\lambda^2dE_x<\infty\}$, and $Ax=\int\lambda dE(\lambda)x$.

[F2] [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]]: for bounded Borel $f$, $K=\Phi_E(f)$ satisfies $\|Kx\|^2=\int|f|^2dE_x$ and nonnegative $f$ gives a positive operator.

[F3] [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-compact-self-adjoint-operators]] and [[cor-orthonormal-eigenbasis-for-a-compact-self-adjoint-operator]]: compact self-adjoint operators have finite-dimensional nonzero eigenspaces whose closed span is $(\ker K)^\perp$; under AC their union has a complete orthonormal eigenbasis when $\ker K=0$.

[F4] [[def-trace-class-operator]] and [[thm-trace-of-a-positive-operator-is-the-sum-of-its-eigenvalues]]: positive trace-class operators are compact and their trace is the sum of their nonnegative eigenvalues with multiplicity.

[F5] [[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]] and [[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]: the trace is basis-independent and linear in trace-class operators, and multiplying a trace-class operator by a bounded operator preserves trace class.

[F6] [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]] and [[thm-tdmath-summable-canonical-differentiation]]: nonnegative countable sums are suprema of finite subsums, and the stated local moment envelope gives a finite partition sum, finite mean and variance, and the canonical derivative and entropy identities.

[F7] [[thm-cyclicity-of-the-trace]]: for trace-class $S$ and bounded $B$, $\operatorname{Tr}(SB)=\operatorname{Tr}(BS)$.

[F8] [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]: the inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second.

[F9] [[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]: for compact $T$, its positive singular values are the positive eigenvalues of the positive operator $|T|=(T^*T)^{1/2}$ counted with multiplicity. In particular, if $T$ is positive then its absolute value equals $T$.

[F10] [[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]: a complete orthonormal family has Parseval equality and its finite-coordinate projections converge in norm to each vector.

[F11] [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] and [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]: the real exponential is continuous, positive, injective, and strictly increasing.

[F12] [[def-natural-logarithm]]: for $x>0$, $\log x$ is the unique real $y$ satisfying $e^y=x$, so $\exp(\log x)=x$ and $\log(\exp y)=y$.

[F13] [[def-integral-of-a-simple-function-against-a-pvm]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], and [[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]: for a simple function $s=\sum_kc_k\mathbf1_{D_k}$ in disjoint normal form, $\int s\,dE=\sum_kc_kE(D_k)$; the PVM satisfies $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ and $E(\mathbb R)=I$, each $E(D_k)$ is self-adjoint with $\langle E(D_k)x,x\rangle=\|E(D_k)x\|^2\ge0$, and $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a positive countably additive measure with $E_x(\mathbb R)=\|x\|^2$.

[F14] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$, so inner products are continuous under norm convergence.

[F15] [[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]] and [[thm-norm-limit-of-compact-operators-is-compact]]: bounded finite-rank operators are compact, and under AC a norm limit of compact operators into the Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ is compact.

[F16] [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]], and [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]]: the nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous for positive scalars, and $\int\mathbf1_C\,d\mu=\mu(C)$ for measurable $C$.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** AC, a nonzero complex Hilbert space, self-adjoint semibounded $A$, its spectral PVM, a parameter $\beta>0$, and trace-class $K_\beta$.

1.1 Since $\beta>0$, $-\beta\lambda\le-\beta a$ for $\lambda\ge a$; strict increase and positivity from [F11] show that $f_\beta$ is bounded and strictly positive. Each branch is continuous and their values agree at $a$, so $f_\beta$ is Borel. For each $n$, partition its bounded range into finitely many intervals of length at most $1/n$ and take their Borel preimages; choosing a nonnegative value in each interval gives a nonnegative real simple $s_n$ converging uniformly to $f_\beta$. By [F13], $T_n:=\int s_n\,dE$ is a finite real linear combination of self-adjoint projections, hence self-adjoint and has nonnegative quadratic form. By [F2], $T_n\to K_\beta$ in operator norm. Therefore $\langle K_\beta x,y\rangle=\langle x,K_\beta y\rangle$ and $\langle K_\beta x,x\rangle\ge0$ by [F14] and passage to the limit, so $K_\beta$ is self-adjoint and positive. If $K_\beta x=0$, [F2] gives $\int f_\beta^2dE_x=0$. For each $n\ge1$, $f_\beta\ge1/n$ on $C_n:=\{\lambda:f_\beta(\lambda)\ge1/n\}$; [F16] gives $0=\int f_\beta^2dE_x\ge n^{-2}E_x(C_n)$, so $E_x(C_n)=0$. The sets $C_n$ increase to $\mathbb R$; set $D_1=C_1$ and $D_n=C_n\setminus C_{n-1}$ for $n>1$. They are disjoint, cover $\mathbb R$, and satisfy $E_x(D_n)\le E_x(C_n)=0$. Countable additivity in [F13] gives $E_x(\mathbb R)=\sum_nE_x(D_n)=0$, hence $\|x\|=0$ and $K_\beta$ is injective. [A1, F1, F2, F11, F13, F14, F16]

2.1 By the trace-class definition [F4], $K_\beta$ is compact; together with step 1.1 it is compact self-adjoint and positive. Apply [F3]: its nonzero eigenspaces have finite multiplicity and span $(\ker K_\beta)^\perp=\mathcal H$, so AC supplies a finite or countable complete orthonormal family $(u_j)$ of eigenvectors with eigenvalues $\kappa_j>0$. By [F4], $Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=\sum_j\kappa_j<\infty$; because $\mathcal H\ne0$ and $K_\beta$ is injective, this sum is positive. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 Fix $j$. To justify the constant shift in the calculus, choose bounded simple $s_n\to f_\beta$ uniformly. By [F13], $\int(s_n-\kappa_j)\,dE=\int s_n\,dE-\kappa_jI$; [F2] passes both uniform limits, so $\Phi_E(f_\beta-\kappa_j)=K_\beta-\kappa_jI$. Applying the norm identity in [F2] to this difference and the eigenvector gives $\int|f_\beta-\kappa_j|^2dE_{u_j}=\|(K_\beta-\kappa_jI)u_j\|^2=0$. For every $n$, [F16] shows that the set where $|f_\beta-\kappa_j|\ge1/n$ has zero $E_{u_j}$-measure; their union is the complement of the level set. Hence $E_{u_j}$ is supported on $f_\beta^{-1}(\kappa_j)\cap[a,\infty)=\{E_j\}$: injectivity of the exponential gives uniqueness, and [F12] gives $E_j=-\beta^{-1}\log\kappa_j\ge a$. Thus $\int\lambda^2dE_{u_j}=E_j^2<\infty$ and [F1] yields $u_j\in D(A)$ and $Au_j=E_ju_j$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F11, F12, F13, F16, step 2.1]

4.1 The spectral measure of each $u_j$ is the unit mass at $E_j$ by step 3.1. Hence $\|(I-E(\{E_j\}))u_j\|^2=E_{u_j}(\mathbb R\setminus\{E_j\})=0$, so $E(\{E_j\})u_j=u_j$; for Borel $D$ not containing $E_j$, $E(D)u_j=E(D)E(\{E_j\})u_j=E(\varnothing)u_j=0$ by [F13]. For every $\gamma>0$, choose nonnegative simple $s_n\to f_\gamma$ uniformly as in step 1.1. In each disjoint normal form, [F13] then gives $(\int s_n\,dE)u_j=s_n(E_j)u_j$; the uniform-limit clause of [F2] yields $K_\gamma u_j=f_\gamma(E_j)u_j=e^{-\gamma E_j}u_j$. Fix $\gamma\in J$ and enumerate that basis; let $P_N$ project onto its first $N$ vectors, taking $P_N=I$ once a finite basis is exhausted. Parseval gives $\|P_Nx\|\le\|x\|$, so $K_\gamma P_N$ is bounded and finite rank. Fix the summable envelope $a_j$ for $\{\gamma\}\subset J$; every finite subsum of $t_j:=e^{-\gamma E_j}$ is at most the corresponding sum of $a_j$, hence $S:=\sum_jt_j<\infty$ by the finite-subsum definition [F6]. This sum is positive because the basis is nonempty and every term is positive. For $\varepsilon>0$, choose a finite set $F$ with $S-\varepsilon<\sum_{j\in F}t_j$; once $N$ contains $F$, every finite tail subsum is at most $S-\sum_{j\in F}t_j<\varepsilon$, so $\sum_{j>N}t_j\to0$. Again by Parseval, $$\|(K_\gamma-K_\gamma P_N)x\|^2=\sum_{j>N}e^{-2\gamma E_j}|\langle x,u_j\rangle|^2\le\Bigl(\sum_{j>N}e^{-\gamma E_j}\Bigr)^2\|x\|^2,$$ so $K_\gamma P_N$ converges to $K_\gamma$ in operator norm. For $t_j=e^{-\gamma E_j}$ its finite diagonal expansion is $K_\gamma P_Nx=\sum_{j\le N}t_j\langle x,u_j\rangle u_j$; orthonormality and [F8] give $\langle K_\gamma P_Nx,y\rangle=\langle x,K_\gamma P_Ny\rangle$ and $\langle K_\gamma P_Nx,x\rangle=\sum_{j\le N}t_j|\langle x,u_j\rangle|^2\ge0$. Thus each truncation is self-adjoint and positive, and [F14] plus operator-norm convergence preserves both properties. It is compact by [F15], since the truncations are bounded finite-rank operators and $\mathcal H$ is Banach. Thus $K_\gamma$ is compact self-adjoint and positive. Its absolute value is $K_\gamma$, by the unique positive square-root definition in [F9]. If $K_\gamma x=\lambda x$, taking coordinates in the complete basis gives $(t_j-\lambda)\langle x,u_j\rangle=0$ for every $j$; thus its eigenvalues and their multiplicities are exactly the diagonal values $t_j$. Hence [F9] identifies its positive singular values, with multiplicity, as the list $(t_j)$. Their finite subsums are bounded by $\sum_j a_j$, so the trace-class definition [F4] applies and gives $\operatorname{Tr}K_\gamma=\sum_j t_j$. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F6, F8, F9, F10, F13, F14, F15, step 1.1, step 3.1]

5.1 At the fixed $\beta$, $\rho_\beta=K_\beta/Z_\beta$ is positive trace class and [F5] gives $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_\beta=Z_\beta^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=1$. For each $\gamma\in J$, $\rho_\gamma=K_\gamma/Z_\gamma$ likewise has trace one; its eigenvalues $p_j=e^{-\gamma E_j}/Z_\gamma$ form the canonical law, so [F6] gives the finite mean, variance, and identity $-\sum_jp_j\log p_j=\log Z_\gamma+\gamma\sum_jp_jE_j$. [A1, F5, F6, step 2.1, step 4.1]

6.1 For bounded $B$, [F5] makes $\rho_\beta B$ and $B\rho_\beta$ trace class and [F7] gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta B)=\operatorname{Tr}(B\rho_\beta)$. Evaluate the second trace in the complete basis $(u_j)$: $\operatorname{Tr}(B\rho_\beta)=\sum_j\langle B\rho_\beta u_j,u_j\rangle=\sum_jp_j\langle Bu_j,u_j\rangle$, where [F8] and real $p_j$ justify pulling the scalar out. This series is absolutely convergent since $|\langle Bu_j,u_j\rangle|\le\|B\|$ and $\sum_jp_j=1$. [A1, A2, F3, F5, F7, F8, step 5.1] ∎

Further, let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and suppose that for every compact $C\subset J$ there is a summable family $a_j\ge0$ with $(1+|E_j|^2)e^{-\gamma E_j}\le a_j$ for all $j$ and $\gamma\in C$. Then for each $\gamma\in J$, $K_\gamma$ is trace class with partition function $Z_\gamma:=\operatorname{Tr}K_\gamma=\sum_j e^{-\gamma E_j}$. With $p_j(\gamma):=e^{-\gamma E_j}/Z_\gamma$, define $\bar E_\gamma:=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)E_j$, $\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(E):=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)(E_j-\bar E_\gamma)^2$, and $S_\gamma:=-\sum_jp_j(\gamma)\log p_j(\gamma)$. These quantities are finite and satisfy $-\partial_\gamma\log Z_\gamma=\bar E_\gamma$, $\partial_\gamma^2\log Z_\gamma=\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(E)$, and $S_\gamma=\log Z_\gamma+\gamma\bar E_\gamma$ as in [[thm-tdmath-summable-canonical-differentiation]]. Countable nonnegative sums use the finite-subsum supremum convention of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]].

## Facts & Assumptions


**Given:** AC, a nonzero complex Hilbert space, a self-adjoint semibounded operator, the specified Borel functional calculus, trace-class $K_\beta$, and a bounded operator $B$.

[A1] The Hilbert space is nonzero; $A$ is self-adjoint with spectral support in $[a,\infty)$; AC is adopted; $\beta>0$; and $K_\beta$ is trace class. For the interval clause, the same list $(E_j)$ has the local summable moment envelope stated in the theorem.

[A2] $B$ is a bounded operator on $\mathcal H$.

[F1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]: under AC a self-adjoint $A$ has a regular PVM $E$, domain $D(A)=\{x:\int\lambda^2dE_x<\infty\}$, and $Ax=\int\lambda dE(\lambda)x$.

[F2] [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]]: for bounded Borel $f$, $K=\Phi_E(f)$ satisfies $\|Kx\|^2=\int|f|^2dE_x$ and nonnegative $f$ gives a positive operator.

[F3] [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-compact-self-adjoint-operators]] and [[cor-orthonormal-eigenbasis-for-a-compact-self-adjoint-operator]]: compact self-adjoint operators have finite-dimensional nonzero eigenspaces whose closed span is $(\ker K)^\perp$; under AC their union has a complete orthonormal eigenbasis when $\ker K=0$.

[F4] [[def-trace-class-operator]] and [[thm-trace-of-a-positive-operator-is-the-sum-of-its-eigenvalues]]: positive trace-class operators are compact and their trace is the sum of their nonnegative eigenvalues with multiplicity.

[F5] [[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]] and [[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]: the trace is basis-independent and linear in trace-class operators, and multiplying a trace-class operator by a bounded operator preserves trace class.

[F6] [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]] and [[thm-tdmath-summable-canonical-differentiation]]: nonnegative countable sums are suprema of finite subsums, and the stated local moment envelope gives a finite partition sum, finite mean and variance, and the canonical derivative and entropy identities.

[F7] [[thm-cyclicity-of-the-trace]]: for trace-class $S$ and bounded $B$, $\operatorname{Tr}(SB)=\operatorname{Tr}(BS)$.

[F8] [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]: the inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second.

[F9] [[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]: for compact $T$, its positive singular values are the positive eigenvalues of the positive operator $|T|=(T^*T)^{1/2}$ counted with multiplicity. In particular, if $T$ is positive then its absolute value equals $T$.

[F10] [[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]: a complete orthonormal family has Parseval equality and its finite-coordinate projections converge in norm to each vector.

[F11] [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] and [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]: the real exponential is continuous, positive, injective, and strictly increasing.

[F12] [[def-natural-logarithm]]: for $x>0$, $\log x$ is the unique real $y$ satisfying $e^y=x$, so $\exp(\log x)=x$ and $\log(\exp y)=y$.

[F13] [[def-integral-of-a-simple-function-against-a-pvm]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], and [[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]: for a simple function $s=\sum_kc_k\mathbf1_{D_k}$ in disjoint normal form, $\int s\,dE=\sum_kc_kE(D_k)$; the PVM satisfies $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ and $E(\mathbb R)=I$, each $E(D_k)$ is self-adjoint with $\langle E(D_k)x,x\rangle=\|E(D_k)x\|^2\ge0$, and $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a positive countably additive measure with $E_x(\mathbb R)=\|x\|^2$.

[F14] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$, so inner products are continuous under norm convergence.

[F15] [[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]] and [[thm-norm-limit-of-compact-operators-is-compact]]: bounded finite-rank operators are compact, and under AC a norm limit of compact operators into the Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ is compact.

[F16] [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]], and [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]]: the nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous for positive scalars, and $\int\mathbf1_C\,d\mu=\mu(C)$ for measurable $C$.



## Proof

**Given:** AC, a nonzero complex Hilbert space, self-adjoint semibounded $A$, its spectral PVM, a parameter $\beta>0$, and trace-class $K_\beta$.

1.1 Since $\beta>0$, $-\beta\lambda\le-\beta a$ for $\lambda\ge a$; strict increase and positivity from [F11] show that $f_\beta$ is bounded and strictly positive. Each branch is continuous and their values agree at $a$, so $f_\beta$ is Borel. For each $n$, partition its bounded range into finitely many intervals of length at most $1/n$ and take their Borel preimages; choosing a nonnegative value in each interval gives a nonnegative real simple $s_n$ converging uniformly to $f_\beta$. By [F13], $T_n:=\int s_n\,dE$ is a finite real linear combination of self-adjoint projections, hence self-adjoint and has nonnegative quadratic form. By [F2], $T_n\to K_\beta$ in operator norm. Therefore $\langle K_\beta x,y\rangle=\langle x,K_\beta y\rangle$ and $\langle K_\beta x,x\rangle\ge0$ by [F14] and passage to the limit, so $K_\beta$ is self-adjoint and positive. If $K_\beta x=0$, [F2] gives $\int f_\beta^2dE_x=0$. For each $n\ge1$, $f_\beta\ge1/n$ on $C_n:=\{\lambda:f_\beta(\lambda)\ge1/n\}$; [F16] gives $0=\int f_\beta^2dE_x\ge n^{-2}E_x(C_n)$, so $E_x(C_n)=0$. The sets $C_n$ increase to $\mathbb R$; set $D_1=C_1$ and $D_n=C_n\setminus C_{n-1}$ for $n>1$. They are disjoint, cover $\mathbb R$, and satisfy $E_x(D_n)\le E_x(C_n)=0$. Countable additivity in [F13] gives $E_x(\mathbb R)=\sum_nE_x(D_n)=0$, hence $\|x\|=0$ and $K_\beta$ is injective. [A1, F1, F2, F11, F13, F14, F16]

2.1 By the trace-class definition [F4], $K_\beta$ is compact; together with step 1.1 it is compact self-adjoint and positive. Apply [F3]: its nonzero eigenspaces have finite multiplicity and span $(\ker K_\beta)^\perp=\mathcal H$, so AC supplies a finite or countable complete orthonormal family $(u_j)$ of eigenvectors with eigenvalues $\kappa_j>0$. By [F4], $Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=\sum_j\kappa_j<\infty$; because $\mathcal H\ne0$ and $K_\beta$ is injective, this sum is positive. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 Fix $j$. To justify the constant shift in the calculus, choose bounded simple $s_n\to f_\beta$ uniformly. By [F13], $\int(s_n-\kappa_j)\,dE=\int s_n\,dE-\kappa_jI$; [F2] passes both uniform limits, so $\Phi_E(f_\beta-\kappa_j)=K_\beta-\kappa_jI$. Applying the norm identity in [F2] to this difference and the eigenvector gives $\int|f_\beta-\kappa_j|^2dE_{u_j}=\|(K_\beta-\kappa_jI)u_j\|^2=0$. For every $n$, [F16] shows that the set where $|f_\beta-\kappa_j|\ge1/n$ has zero $E_{u_j}$-measure; their union is the complement of the level set. Hence $E_{u_j}$ is supported on $f_\beta^{-1}(\kappa_j)\cap[a,\infty)=\{E_j\}$: injectivity of the exponential gives uniqueness, and [F12] gives $E_j=-\beta^{-1}\log\kappa_j\ge a$. Thus $\int\lambda^2dE_{u_j}=E_j^2<\infty$ and [F1] yields $u_j\in D(A)$ and $Au_j=E_ju_j$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F11, F12, F13, F16, step 2.1]

4.1 The spectral measure of each $u_j$ is the unit mass at $E_j$ by step 3.1. Hence $\|(I-E(\{E_j\}))u_j\|^2=E_{u_j}(\mathbb R\setminus\{E_j\})=0$, so $E(\{E_j\})u_j=u_j$; for Borel $D$ not containing $E_j$, $E(D)u_j=E(D)E(\{E_j\})u_j=E(\varnothing)u_j=0$ by [F13]. For every $\gamma>0$, choose nonnegative simple $s_n\to f_\gamma$ uniformly as in step 1.1. In each disjoint normal form, [F13] then gives $(\int s_n\,dE)u_j=s_n(E_j)u_j$; the uniform-limit clause of [F2] yields $K_\gamma u_j=f_\gamma(E_j)u_j=e^{-\gamma E_j}u_j$. Fix $\gamma\in J$ and enumerate that basis; let $P_N$ project onto its first $N$ vectors, taking $P_N=I$ once a finite basis is exhausted. Parseval gives $\|P_Nx\|\le\|x\|$, so $K_\gamma P_N$ is bounded and finite rank. Fix the summable envelope $a_j$ for $\{\gamma\}\subset J$; every finite subsum of $t_j:=e^{-\gamma E_j}$ is at most the corresponding sum of $a_j$, hence $S:=\sum_jt_j<\infty$ by the finite-subsum definition [F6]. This sum is positive because the basis is nonempty and every term is positive. For $\varepsilon>0$, choose a finite set $F$ with $S-\varepsilon<\sum_{j\in F}t_j$; once $N$ contains $F$, every finite tail subsum is at most $S-\sum_{j\in F}t_j<\varepsilon$, so $\sum_{j>N}t_j\to0$. Again by Parseval, $$\|(K_\gamma-K_\gamma P_N)x\|^2=\sum_{j>N}e^{-2\gamma E_j}|\langle x,u_j\rangle|^2\le\Bigl(\sum_{j>N}e^{-\gamma E_j}\Bigr)^2\|x\|^2,$$ so $K_\gamma P_N$ converges to $K_\gamma$ in operator norm. For $t_j=e^{-\gamma E_j}$ its finite diagonal expansion is $K_\gamma P_Nx=\sum_{j\le N}t_j\langle x,u_j\rangle u_j$; orthonormality and [F8] give $\langle K_\gamma P_Nx,y\rangle=\langle x,K_\gamma P_Ny\rangle$ and $\langle K_\gamma P_Nx,x\rangle=\sum_{j\le N}t_j|\langle x,u_j\rangle|^2\ge0$. Thus each truncation is self-adjoint and positive, and [F14] plus operator-norm convergence preserves both properties. It is compact by [F15], since the truncations are bounded finite-rank operators and $\mathcal H$ is Banach. Thus $K_\gamma$ is compact self-adjoint and positive. Its absolute value is $K_\gamma$, by the unique positive square-root definition in [F9]. If $K_\gamma x=\lambda x$, taking coordinates in the complete basis gives $(t_j-\lambda)\langle x,u_j\rangle=0$ for every $j$; thus its eigenvalues and their multiplicities are exactly the diagonal values $t_j$. Hence [F9] identifies its positive singular values, with multiplicity, as the list $(t_j)$. Their finite subsums are bounded by $\sum_j a_j$, so the trace-class definition [F4] applies and gives $\operatorname{Tr}K_\gamma=\sum_j t_j$. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F6, F8, F9, F10, F13, F14, F15, step 1.1, step 3.1]

5.1 At the fixed $\beta$, $\rho_\beta=K_\beta/Z_\beta$ is positive trace class and [F5] gives $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_\beta=Z_\beta^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=1$. For each $\gamma\in J$, $\rho_\gamma=K_\gamma/Z_\gamma$ likewise has trace one; its eigenvalues $p_j=e^{-\gamma E_j}/Z_\gamma$ form the canonical law, so [F6] gives the finite mean, variance, and identity $-\sum_jp_j\log p_j=\log Z_\gamma+\gamma\sum_jp_jE_j$. [A1, F5, F6, step 2.1, step 4.1]

6.1 For bounded $B$, [F5] makes $\rho_\beta B$ and $B\rho_\beta$ trace class and [F7] gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta B)=\operatorname{Tr}(B\rho_\beta)$. Evaluate the second trace in the complete basis $(u_j)$: $\operatorname{Tr}(B\rho_\beta)=\sum_j\langle B\rho_\beta u_j,u_j\rangle=\sum_jp_j\langle Bu_j,u_j\rangle$, where [F8] and real $p_j$ justify pulling the scalar out. This series is absolutely convergent since $|\langle Bu_j,u_j\rangle|\le\|B\|$ and $\sum_jp_j=1$. [A1, A2, F3, F5, F7, F8, step 5.1] ∎

sections.Statement: Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $w:X\to[0,\infty)$ and $X_a:X\to\mathbb R$ ($1\le a\le r$) be measurable, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ be open. For $\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r)$, define $\theta\cdot X(x):=\sum_{a=1}^r\theta_aX_a(x)$. Set $Z(\theta):=\int w\exp(\theta\cdot X)\,d\mu$ and assume $0<Z(\theta)<\infty$ on $U$. Suppose for every compact $K\subset U$ there is an integrable $G_K\ge0$ such that $w e^{\theta\cdot X}(1+\sum_a|X_a|^2)\le G_K$ pointwise for all $\theta\in K$. For the normalized density $p_\theta=w e^{\theta\cdot X}/Z(\theta)$, define $\mathbb E_\theta Y:=\int Yp_\theta\,d\mu$ when integrable and $\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b):=\mathbb E_\theta[(X_a-\mathbb E_\theta X_a)(X_b-\mathbb E_\theta X_b)]$. Then $\partial_a\log Z=\mathbb E_\theta X_a$ and $\partial_b\mathbb E_\theta X_a=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b)$. Thus the Hessian of $\log Z$ is positive semidefinite. This is a mathematical model identity; it assumes no independence or absence of correlations.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** As stated in the item.

[A1] $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ is a measure space; $w$ is finite-valued nonnegative measurable and each $X_a$ is real-valued measurable; $U$ is open, $Z$ is positive finite, and the displayed compact-parameter envelope is integrable.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]: measurable integrals and densities use the fixed reference measure $\mu$.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-dominated-convergence]]: dominated pointwise limits may be passed through the integral.

[F3] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: exponential weights are differentiable, with derivative equal to the exponential.

[F4] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: $\log Z$ differentiates as $Z'/Z$ when $Z>0$.

[F5] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: scalar difference quotients of the exponential are bounded by intermediate derivatives.

[F6] [[thm-chain-rule]] and [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: the parameterized exponential and quotient have the usual derivative rules.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The parameterized measure model and its compact-parameter integrable envelopes.

1.1 For a coordinate direction $a$, the difference quotient of $w e^{\theta\cdot X}$ tends pointwise to $wX_a e^{\theta\cdot X}$. On a compact neighborhood $K'$ of $\theta$, the mean-value theorem [F5] bounds its absolute value by $w|X_a|e^{\eta\cdot X}$ for an intermediate parameter $\eta\in K'$, at most $G_{K'}$. Dominated convergence [F2] therefore gives $\partial_aZ=\int wX_a e^{\theta\cdot X}d\mu$. Applying the same argument to the first-moment numerator gives $\partial_b\int wX_a e^{\theta\cdot X}d\mu=\int wX_aX_b e^{\theta\cdot X}d\mu$; the same envelope controls this quotient because $|X_aX_b|\le(1+\sum_c|X_c|^2)/2$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, F6]

2.1 Divide the first derivative by $Z>0$ and use [F4] to obtain $\partial_a\log Z=\mathbb E_\theta X_a$. The quotient rule for the normalized first moment gives $\partial_b\mathbb E_\theta X_a=\mathbb E_\theta(X_aX_b)-\mathbb E_\theta X_a\mathbb E_\theta X_b$, the covariance. [A1, F1, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 For any $v\in\mathbb R^r$, $v^T(\nabla^2\log Z)v=\mathbb E_\theta[(v\cdot X-\mathbb E_\theta(v\cdot X))^2]\ge0$. This proves positive semidefiniteness without any independence assumption. [A1, step 2.1] ∎

sections.Statement: Let $\Omega_0$ be a nonempty finite set, let $E:\Omega_0\to\mathbb R$, and fix $\beta\in\mathbb R$. Define $Z_1=\sum_{i\in\Omega_0}e^{-\beta E_i}$ and the canonical law $q_i=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z_1$, and define $\bar E:=\sum_iq_iE_i$. For $N\ge1$, on $\Omega_0^N$ define $H_N(i_1,\ldots,i_N)=\sum_{k=1}^NE_{i_k}$ with the product law. Then $Z_N=Z_1^N$, $\mathbb E[H_N/N]=\bar E$, and $\operatorname{Var}(H_N/N)=\operatorname{Var}_q(E)/N$. Consequently, for every $\varepsilon>0$, $\mathbb P(|H_N/N-\bar E|\ge\varepsilon)\le\operatorname{Var}_q(E)/(N\varepsilon^2)$. If $\beta\ne0$, the mathematical free-energy density $-\beta^{-1}N^{-1}\log Z_N$ is exactly $-\beta^{-1}\log Z_1$ for every $N$.

fm.title: Infinite-valued no-sinks Hahn–Banach sandwich and conditional offsets

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §VI.B
MIT 18.102, Introduction to Functional Analysis, complete lecture notes
D. Daners, Introduction to Functional Analysis (2017), Theorem 26.1 and proof
G. Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis, §4.2, Theorem 4.11 and proof

sections.Statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $V$ be a real vector space and $p:V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ satisfy $p(0)=0$, $p(tx)=tp(x)$ for every $t>0$, and $p(x+y)\le p(x)+p(y)$ in extended-real arithmetic. Assume **no sinks**: $p(x)<+\infty$ if and only if $p(-x)<+\infty$. Put $W:=\{x\in V:p(x)<+\infty\}$. Then $W$ is a linear subspace and there exists a real-linear $L:V\to\mathbb R$ such that

$$-p(-x)\le L(x)\le p(x)\qquad(x\in V),$$

with $-\infty\le r\le+\infty$ interpreted in the usual extended order. The result is valid in arbitrary dimension and allows $p=+\infty$ outside $W$.

For the conditional offset application, let $V=V_{\mathcal G}$ from [[def-tdmath-type-offset-vector-space]], let $F:\mathcal G\times\mathcal G\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ satisfy $p([e_\Gamma]-[e_{\Gamma'}])=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$, and define $B(\Gamma):=L([e_\Gamma])$. Then $B(\Gamma\times\Gamma')=B(\Gamma)+B(\Gamma')$, $B(t\Gamma)=tB(\Gamma)$ for $t>0$, and

$$-F(\Gamma',\Gamma)\le B(\Gamma)-B(\Gamma')\le F(\Gamma,\Gamma').$$

For each $\Gamma\in\mathcal G$, let $X_\Gamma$ be a state set and $\sigma_\Gamma:X_\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ a baseline state function. If every admitted transition $(\Gamma,x)\to(\Gamma',y)$, with $x\in X_\Gamma$ and $y\in X_{\Gamma'}$, satisfies $\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)\ge F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$, then $\sigma_\Gamma(x)+B(\Gamma)$ is nondecreasing across those transitions. The existence or properties of such a cost $p$, including no-sinks, are hypotheses and are not proved by this theorem.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: adopt the Axiom of Choice for the Hahn–Banach and basis-extension steps.

[F1] [[def-vector-space]] and [[def-linear-subspace]]: $V$ is a real vector space, and a subset closed under addition and all scalar multiples is a linear subspace.

[F2] [[def-sublinear-functional]]: a real-valued sublinear functional is positively homogeneous and subadditive.

[F3] [[thm-hahn-banach-dominated-extension]]: for real vector spaces, a subspace, a real-valued sublinear functional and a linear functional dominated on that subspace, there is a dominated linear extension to the whole space.

[F4] [[def-complete-ordered-field]]: the real field used in the one-step dominated-extension argument has the least-upper-bound property.

[F5] [[cor-every-vector-space-has-a-basis]] and [[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]]: under the adopted choice strength, a vector space has a basis and an independent subset extends to a basis of the ambient space.

[F6] [[def-linear-independence]] and [[def-linear-basis]]: a basis is an independent spanning set; spanning gives a finite expression for each vector, and independence makes its finite coefficient map unique.

[F7] [[def-tdmath-type-offset-vector-space]] and [[lem-tdmath-type-offset-vector-space-well-defined]]: the quotient is a real vector space with the declared product and positive-scaling relations.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** [A1]–[F6] and the hypotheses on $p$.

1.1 The set $W$ contains $0$ because $p(0)=0$. If $x,y\in W$, subadditivity gives $p(x+y)\le p(x)+p(y)<+\infty$, so $x+y\in W$. For $t>0$, homogeneity gives $p(tx)=tp(x)<+\infty$. If $t<0$, no-sinks gives $-x\in W$, and positive homogeneity applied to $|t|(-x)$ puts $tx$ in $W$; $0x=0\in W$. Thus $W$ is a linear subspace. The restriction $p|_W$ is finite-valued, positively homogeneous and subadditive, so it is a real-valued sublinear functional. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Let $M=\{0\}\subseteq W$ and let $f_0(0)=0$. This is linear and satisfies $f_0(0)=0=p(0)$. The real ordered field is complete by [F4], as used in the one-step interval argument of the published theorem. Apply [F3] to $p|_W$ and $f_0$; it gives a linear $\ell:W\to\mathbb R$ with $\ell(x)\le p(x)$ for every $x\in W$. Applying this at $-x\in W$ yields $-\ell(x)=\ell(-x)\le p(-x)$, so $-p(-x)\le\ell(x)\le p(x)$ on $W$. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 By [F5], choose a basis $B_W$ of $W$ and extend its independent set to a basis $B_V$ of $V$. Assign value $\ell(b)$ to $b\in B_W$ and $0$ to $b\in B_V\setminus B_W$. For any $v\in V$, [F6] gives a finite basis expression; define $L(v)$ as the same finite linear combination of assigned real values. If two expressions represented $v$, subtracting and collecting equal basis vectors would give a finite zero combination; independence in [F6] forces every collected coefficient to be zero. Thus $L(v)$ is well-defined. Concatenating finite expressions proves additivity and scalar homogeneity, and the basis expression of any $w\in W$ uses only $B_W$, so $L|_W=\ell$. [A1, F5, F6, step 2.1]

4.1 For $x\in W$, step 3.1 and step 2.1 give $-p(-x)\le L(x)\le p(x)$. If $x\notin W$, then $p(x)=+\infty$ by the definition of $W$; no-sinks implies $p(-x)=+\infty$ as well, so the extended bounds reduce to $-\infty\le L(x)\le+\infty$. This proves the global sandwich. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 In the type-offset application, linearity of $L$ and the quotient relations in [F7] give $B(\Gamma\times\Gamma')=B(\Gamma)+B(\Gamma')$ and $B(t\Gamma)=tB(\Gamma)$. Apply the sandwich to $e_\Gamma-e_{\Gamma'}$ and its negative, using the assumed values of $p$, to obtain the two displayed bounds for $B(\Gamma)-B(\Gamma')$. For an admitted transition, its real baseline change is at least $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$, so that cost value must be finite. The corrected change equals $[\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)] + B(\Gamma')-B(\Gamma)=[\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)]-L(e_\Gamma-e_{\Gamma'})$. The assumed lower bound on the baseline change and the upper sandwich bound $L(e_\Gamma-e_{\Gamma'})\le F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$ make this at least $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')-F(\Gamma,\Gamma')=0$. This proves only the stated conditional monotonicity. [F7, step 4.1, algebra] ∎
sections.Remarks: The real-valued Hahn–Banach theorem is applied only on the finite domain $W$; the arbitrary-dimensional extension to $V$ uses a basis and its extension under Choice. When $x\notin W$, both sandwich endpoints are infinite by no-sinks. Neither the finite-dimensional strict-extension variant nor a catalyst-chain cost construction is asserted.

sections.Statement:
Assume the superstable regular model and Poisson conventions of [[thm-tdmath-continuum-variational-pressure]]. Let $D\subset[0,\infty)$ be an interval of positive length, let $\nu$ be the supremum of finite-entropy, finite-energy attainable densities, and set $e_0(\rho)=\inf\{\Phi(P):\rho(P)=\rho,\ I(P)<\infty\}$. If $\inf D<\nu$ and $e>\inf_{\rho\in D}e_0(\rho)$, define
$$A_L=\{N_{\Lambda_L}/L^d\in D,\ H_{L,\mathrm{per}}/L^d\leq e\}.$$
Then $A_L$ has positive Poisson probability for all sufficiently large $L$, and
$$\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log Q_{\Lambda_L}(A_L) =-\min\{I(P):\rho(P)\in\overline D,\ \Phi(P)\leq e\}.$$

sections.Proof:
**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Define $m(\rho,e)=\inf\{I(P):\rho(P)=\rho,\Phi(P)\leq e\}$ and $s=-m$. Divide by $|G|$ and use [F4]; the label entropy vanishes, so $I$ is affine on finite mixtures. The expectation $\rho$ and finite-volume energy expectations are affine, hence their limits $\rho,\Phi$ are affine where finite. Mixtures of feasible laws show $m$ is convex and $s$ concave. If $(\rho_n,e_n)\to(\rho,e)$ and $\liminf m(\rho_n,e_n)<\infty$, choose near-minimizers with bounded $I$. Compactness [F2] gives a convergent subsequence; continuity of $\rho$ by [F6] and lower semicontinuity of $\Phi,I$ in [F1] show the limit is feasible with entropy no greater than the liminf. Thus $m$ is lower semicontinuous and $s$ upper semicontinuous; the same compactness argument attains every finite infimum. For strict feasibility, choose $\rho_1$ in the interior of $D$ below $\nu(\phi)$ with a finite-energy, finite-entropy law $R$. The inequality $e>\inf_{\rho\in D}e_0(\rho)$ gives $\rho_2\in D$ and a finite-entropy law $P$ with $\Phi(P)<e$. If $\rho_2$ is at an endpoint of $D$, mix $P$ with a sufficiently small positive amount of $R$; affinity of $\rho,\Phi,I$ keeps the energy below $e$ and moves the density into the interior of $D$. 2.1 For the lower event bound, take a feasible stationary law with strict density and energy inequalities. Approximate it by separated independent blocks: condition each block on a finite-energy, bounded-count event of probability tending to one, separate blocks by a fixed empty corridor, and average the phase. Its entropy per volume tends to $I(P)$; its empirical density and energy converge to $\rho(P)$ and $\Phi(P)$. The spatial likelihood theorem gives Poisson probability at least $\exp[-L^d(I(P)+o(1))]$ for the joint typical event, which lies in $A_L$. If a minimizing law lies on a constraint boundary, mix it with the strict feasible law. The mixture remains feasible for sufficiently small mixing weight and its entropy tends to the boundary law's entropy by the entropy affinity established in step 1.1 and lower semicontinuity. 3.1 For the upper event bound, let $G_L=Q_{\Lambda_L}(\cdot\mid A_L)$. Its exact entropy is $D(G_L\Vert Q_{\Lambda_L})=-\log Q_{\Lambda_L}(A_L)$. 4.1 The tangent-plane argument in [L1] separates the strict-feasibility constraint set in finite dimension [F3]. The objective coefficient is nonzero by strict feasibility, so it can be normalized to one; this does not make the energy coefficient strictly positive. Since $s$ is nondecreasing in the energy allowance, its tangent energy coefficient is $\beta\geq0$, with finite $\alpha=\log z$. Every constrained entropy minimizer then minimizes $I+\beta\Phi-\alpha\rho$ at positive beta. At zero beta the finite-energy feasible laws are hard-admissible; the retained-admissibility extension and separated-block approximation identify the corresponding minimum on $\mathcal K_B$. The finite-volume hard indicator is retained throughout. Theorem 4 and Proposition 7.3 give the conditional-law accumulation conclusion. Proposition 7.4 proves the positive-beta grand conclusion; the zero-beta grand conclusion follows from the retained-admissibility entropy proof in [F9], rather than an extension of that proposition's strictly positive-beta hypothesis. [F1, F3, F9, L1, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For completeness, the empirical concentration is the extension discussed after Theorem 4, not an additional assertion of its printed formula. The Poisson empirical-field upper bound used in [L1], Lemma 7.2 equation (7.4), applies to every closed subset of the constraint set. Outside an open neighborhood of the constrained entropy minimizers its entropy infimum is strictly above the constrained minimum: otherwise compact entropy levels yield a minimizing limit outside that neighborhood. Divide this exponentially smaller numerator by the event probability from steps 2.1–3.1. Thus the conditional empirical field concentrates on the constrained minimizers, hence on their containing grand minimizer set. For zero beta, tilt Poisson measure by $z^N$ and restrict to the closed hard-admissible class. Its upper bound has rate $I-\alpha\rho$; the separated-block lower bound gives its partition minimum. 6.1 The conditional law is torus-invariant and its entropy density is $-L^{-d}\log Q_L(A_L)$, which is bounded by the event limit. The matching grand law is torus-invariant as well. Consequently [F8] applies. Its transfer result converts step 5.1 into convergence of the periodically continued laws for every local tame observable under uniqueness. No zero extension outside the fundamental cube is used. [F1, F5, F8, step 3.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

sections.Statement: Fix $\beta>0$ and $J,h\in\mathbb R$. For $N\ge2$, let $s_i\in\{-1,1\}$, $s_{N+1}=s_1$, $H_N(s)=-J\sum_{i=1}^Ns_is_{i+1}-h\sum_{i=1}^Ns_i$, and $Z_N=\sum_se^{-\beta H_N(s)}$. Define $\cosh x:=(e^x+e^{-x})/2$, $\sinh x:=(e^x-e^{-x})/2$, and $T_{s,t}:=e^{\beta Jst+\beta h(s+t)/2}$. Then $Z_N=\operatorname{tr}(T^N)=\lambda_+^N+\lambda_-^N$, where $\lambda_\pm=e^{\beta J}\cosh(\beta h)\pm\sqrt{e^{2\beta J}\sinh^2(\beta h)+e^{-2\beta J}}$ and $\lambda_+>|\lambda_-|$. Therefore $N^{-1}\log Z_N\to\log\lambda_+$. On every compact subset of $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^2$ in $(\beta,J,h)$, the limit and its derivatives of every fixed finite order converge uniformly. This is a result for the specified one-dimensional periodic two-state model only.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The periodic two-state chain, the transfer matrix in the statement, and parameters $\beta>0$, $J,h\in\mathbb R$.

[A1] Spins are $\{-1,1\}$, the Hamiltonian and periodic boundary condition are as stated, and the hyperbolic functions have the exponential definitions in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-finite-sum]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: finite configuration sums can be regrouped by their indices.

[F2] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]: exponential weights factor according to sums in the exponent.

[F3] [[thm-nth-roots-exist]]: every positive real radicand has a unique positive square root.

[F4] [[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]], and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: exponentials are smooth; positive real powers have the stated derivative; and the logarithm differentiates on positive reals. Repeated chain and product rules may be applied to obtain the higher derivatives used below.

[F5] [[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]]: for $0<\rho<1$ and fixed $k$, $N^k\rho^N\to0$.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The finite periodic chain and its stated parameters.

1.1 For each configuration, the product $\prod_{i=1}^N T_{s_i,s_{i+1}}$ has bond contribution $e^{\beta J\sum_i s_is_{i+1}}$ and field contribution $e^{\beta h\sum_i(s_i+s_{i+1})/2}=e^{\beta h\sum_i s_i}$. These factors equal $e^{-\beta H_N(s)}$. Summing over the finite spin sequences gives $Z_N=\sum_{s_1,\ldots,s_N}T_{s_1s_2}\cdots T_{s_Ns_1}=\operatorname{tr}(T^N)$. [A1, F1, F2]

1.2 In the ordered basis $+1,-1$, $T=\begin{pmatrix}e^{\beta J+\beta h}&e^{-\beta J}\\e^{-\beta J}&e^{\beta J-\beta h}\end{pmatrix}$. Put $A=e^{\beta J}\cosh(\beta h)$ and $B=\sqrt{e^{2\beta J}\sinh^2(\beta h)+e^{-2\beta J}}$. The diagonal entries give $\operatorname{tr}T=2A$; direct multiplication gives $\det T=e^{2\beta J}-e^{-2\beta J}$. Using $\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1$, which follows by expanding their definitions, $A^2-\det T=e^{2\beta J}\sinh^2(\beta h)+e^{-2\beta J}=B^2$. Thus the characteristic polynomial has roots $A\pm B=\lambda_\pm$. Since $A,B>0$, $A+B>|A-B|$, hence $\lambda_+>|\lambda_-|$. [A1, F2, F3]

2.1 For a $2\times2$ matrix $M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, direct multiplication gives $M^2-(a+d)M+(ad-bc)I=0$. Apply this identity to $T$ and multiply by $T^n$; taking traces gives $z_{n+2}=(\operatorname{tr}T)z_{n+1}-(\det T)z_n$, where $z_n=\operatorname{tr}(T^n)$, $z_0=2$, and $z_1=\lambda_++\lambda_-$. The sequence $\lambda_+^n+\lambda_-^n$ has the same recurrence and initial values, so induction gives $Z_N=z_N=\lambda_+^N+\lambda_-^N$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1]

3.1 Set $r=\lambda_-/\lambda_+$. Then $Z_N=\lambda_+^N(1+r^N)$ and $|r|<1$, so $1+r^N>0$. Therefore $N^{-1}\log Z_N=\log\lambda_++N^{-1}\log(1+r^N)$, whose second term tends to zero. For a compact parameter set, continuity and $|r|<1$ give $0<\rho<1$ with $|r|\le\rho$. The positive radicand in $B$ is a smooth positive combination of exponentials; the real-power derivative in [F4] with exponent $1/2$, followed inductively by chain and product rules, makes $B$ and $\lambda_\pm$ smooth. Since $\lambda_+>0$, its reciprocal and logarithm are smooth as well, by the real-power derivative with exponent $-1$ and the logarithm derivative in [F4]. Every fixed finite collection of derivatives of $r$ is therefore bounded on the compact set. ## Statement


Fix $\beta>0$ and $J,h\in\mathbb R$. For $N\ge2$, let $s_i\in\{-1,1\}$, $s_{N+1}=s_1$, $H_N(s)=-J\sum_{i=1}^Ns_is_{i+1}-h\sum_{i=1}^Ns_i$, and $Z_N=\sum_se^{-\beta H_N(s)}$. Define $\cosh x:=(e^x+e^{-x})/2$, $\sinh x:=(e^x-e^{-x})/2$, and $T_{s,t}:=e^{\beta Jst+\beta h(s+t)/2}$. Then $Z_N=\operatorname{tr}(T^N)=\lambda_+^N+\lambda_-^N$, where $\lambda_\pm=e^{\beta J}\cosh(\beta h)\pm\sqrt{e^{2\beta J}\sinh^2(\beta h)+e^{-2\beta J}}$ and $\lambda_+>|\lambda_-|$. Therefore $N^{-1}\log Z_N\to\log\lambda_+$. On every compact subset of $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^2$ in $(\beta,J,h)$, the limit and its derivatives of every fixed finite order converge uniformly. This is a result for the specified one-dimensional periodic two-state model only.

## Facts & Assumptions


**Given:** The periodic two-state chain, the transfer matrix in the statement, and parameters $\beta>0$, $J,h\in\mathbb R$.

[A1] Spins are $\{-1,1\}$, the Hamiltonian and periodic boundary condition are as stated, and the hyperbolic functions have the exponential definitions in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-finite-sum]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: finite configuration sums can be regrouped by their indices.

[F2] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]: exponential weights factor according to sums in the exponent.

[F3] [[thm-nth-roots-exist]]: every positive real radicand has a unique positive square root.

[F4] [[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]], and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: exponentials are smooth; positive real powers have the stated derivative; and the logarithm differentiates on positive reals. Repeated chain and product rules may be applied to obtain the higher derivatives used below.

[F5] [[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]]: for $0<\rho<1$ and fixed $k$, $N^k\rho^N\to0$.



## Proof

**Given:** The finite periodic chain and its stated parameters.

1.1 For each configuration, the product $\prod_{i=1}^N T_{s_i,s_{i+1}}$ has bond contribution $e^{\beta J\sum_i s_is_{i+1}}$ and field contribution $e^{\beta h\sum_i(s_i+s_{i+1})/2}=e^{\beta h\sum_i s_i}$. These factors equal $e^{-\beta H_N(s)}$. Summing over the finite spin sequences gives $Z_N=\sum_{s_1,\ldots,s_N}T_{s_1s_2}\cdots T_{s_Ns_1}=\operatorname{tr}(T^N)$. [A1, F1, F2]

1.2 In the ordered basis $+1,-1$, $T=\begin{pmatrix}e^{\beta J+\beta h}&e^{-\beta J}\\e^{-\beta J}&e^{\beta J-\beta h}\end{pmatrix}$. Put $A=e^{\beta J}\cosh(\beta h)$ and $B=\sqrt{e^{2\beta J}\sinh^2(\beta h)+e^{-2\beta J}}$. The diagonal entries give $\operatorname{tr}T=2A$; direct multiplication gives $\det T=e^{2\beta J}-e^{-2\beta J}$. Using $\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1$, which follows by expanding their definitions, $A^2-\det T=e^{2\beta J}\sinh^2(\beta h)+e^{-2\beta J}=B^2$. Thus the characteristic polynomial has roots $A\pm B=\lambda_\pm$. Since $A,B>0$, $A+B>|A-B|$, hence $\lambda_+>|\lambda_-|$. [A1, F2, F3]

2.1 For a $2\times2$ matrix $M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, direct multiplication gives $M^2-(a+d)M+(ad-bc)I=0$. Apply this identity to $T$ and multiply by $T^n$; taking traces gives $z_{n+2}=(\operatorname{tr}T)z_{n+1}-(\det T)z_n$, where $z_n=\operatorname{tr}(T^n)$, $z_0=2$, and $z_1=\lambda_++\lambda_-$. The sequence $\lambda_+^n+\lambda_-^n$ has the same recurrence and initial values, so induction gives $Z_N=z_N=\lambda_+^N+\lambda_-^N$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1]

3.1 Set $r=\lambda_-/\lambda_+$. Then $Z_N=\lambda_+^N(1+r^N)$ and $|r|<1$, so $1+r^N>0$. Therefore $N^{-1}\log Z_N=\log\lambda_++N^{-1}\log(1+r^N)$, whose second term tends to zero. For a compact parameter set, continuity and $|r|<1$ give $0<\rho<1$ with $|r|\le\rho$. The positive radicand in $B$ is a smooth positive combination of exponentials; the real-power derivative in [F4] with exponent $1/2$, followed inductively by chain and product rules, makes $B$ and $\lambda_\pm$ smooth. Since $\lambda_+>0$, its reciprocal and logarithm are smooth as well, by the real-power derivative with exponent $-1$ and the logarithm derivative in [F4]. Every fixed finite collection of derivatives of $r$ is therefore bounded on the compact set. For a multi-index $\alpha$ of order at most $k$ and $N\ge k$, repeated product differentiation of the $N$ factors gives at most $C_kN^k$ terms; each has at least $N-k$ undifferentiated factors $r$, so $|\partial^\alpha(r^N)|\le C_kN^k\rho^{N-k}$. Put $u=r^N$. Since $1+u\ge1-\rho$, repeated differentiation of $\log(1+u)$ gives finite sums of products of derivatives of $u$ divided by powers of $1+u$. Each term has at least one derivative factor and the product bounds yield $|\partial^\alpha\log(1+u)|\le C'_kN^k\rho^{N-k}$ after enlarging the constant. Divide by $N$; [F5] implies $N^{k-1}\rho^{N-k}\to0$. The zero-order logarithm term also tends uniformly to zero. Hence the correction and every fixed-order derivative vanish uniformly on the compact set. [A1, F4, F5, step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎

sections.Statement: For the lattice models of [[thm-tdmath-finite-range-lattice-pressure-limit]], write $p_L(\gamma)=L^{-d}\log Z_L(\gamma)$ and let $p(\gamma)=\lim_Lp_L(\gamma)$ on an open interval $J\subseteq(0,\infty)$. At finite $L$, use the canonical law $\mathbb P_{\gamma,L}(s):=e^{-\gamma H_L(s)}/Z_L(\gamma)$ and its finite expectation $\mathbb E_{\gamma,L}$. If $p$ is differentiable at $\beta\in J$, then $\mathbb E_{\beta,L}[H_L]/L^d\to e:=-p'(\beta)$. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there are $c>0$ and $L_0$ such that for $L\ge L_0$, $\mathbb P_{\beta,L}(|H_L/L^d-e|\ge\varepsilon)\le2e^{-cL^d}$. No energy-density limit is asserted at a nondifferentiability point.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** As stated in the item.

[A1] $J\subseteq(0,\infty)$ is open; the finite-volume canonical laws use $\mathbb P_{\gamma,L}(s)=e^{-\gamma H_L(s)}/Z_L(\gamma)$; $p_L(\gamma)\to p(\gamma)$ for each $\gamma\in J$; and $p$ is differentiable at the specified $\beta\in J$.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-finite-range-lattice-pressure-limit]]: $p_L(\gamma)$ converges to finite $p(\gamma)$ for every $\gamma\in J$.

[F2] [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]] and [[def-expectation-on-a-finite-probability-space]]: the finite-volume canonical weights define probabilities and expectations as finite sums.

[F3] [[def-variance-and-covariance]]: variance is a nonnegative centered second moment.

[F4] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[def-natural-logarithm]], and [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: finite partition sums are differentiable and $\log$ differentiates on positive values.

[F5] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: derivative monotonicity and convex secant bounds follow from the mean-value theorem.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The finite-volume lattice models, their canonical probabilities, pointwise convergence $p_L\to p$ on $J$, and differentiability of $p$ at $\beta$.

1.1 Differentiating the finite sum gives $p_L'=-L^{-d}\mathbb E_{\beta,L}H_L$ and $p_L''=L^{-d}\operatorname{Var}_{\beta,L}(H_L)\ge0$. Thus $p_L$ is convex. Passing the two-point convexity inequality to the pointwise limit shows that $p$ is convex too. [A1, F2, F3, F4]

1.2 Fix $t>0$ small enough that $\beta\pm t\in J$. For the upper tail, the pointwise inequality $\mathbf1_{\{H_L\ge L^d(e+\varepsilon)\}}\le e^{t(H_L-L^d(e+\varepsilon))}$ and finite summation give $\mathbb P(H_L/L^d\ge e+\varepsilon)\le\exp\{L^d[p_L(\beta-t)-p_L(\beta)-t(e+\varepsilon)]\}$. Differentiability of $p$ and $e=-p'(\beta)$ imply $p(\beta-t)=p(\beta)+te+o(t)$; choose $t$ so the bracket's limit is at most $-3t\varepsilon/4$. Pointwise convergence at $\beta-t$ and $\beta$ then makes the bracket at most $-t\varepsilon/2$ for all sufficiently large $L$. [A1, F1, F2, F4]

2.1 For any small $h>0$ with $\beta\pm h\in J$, convexity and differentiability of $p_L$ give $[p_L(\beta)-p_L(\beta-h)]/h\le p_L'(\beta)\le[p_L(\beta+h)-p_L(\beta)]/h$. Take lower and upper limits in $L$, use [F1], then let $h\downarrow0$; differentiability of $p$ forces $p_L'(\beta)\to p'(\beta)$. The identity in step 1.1 yields the claimed mean limit. [A1, F1, F5, step 1.1]

2.2 For the lower tail use $\mathbf1_{\{H_L\le L^d(e-\varepsilon)\}}\le e^{-t(H_L-L^d(e-\varepsilon))}$; its expectation is $\exp\{L^d[p_L(\beta+t)-p_L(\beta)+t(e-\varepsilon)]\}$. Since $p(\beta+t)=p(\beta)-te+o(t)$, possibly reducing $t$ and increasing $L_0$ makes this at most $e^{-L^dt\varepsilon/2}$. Adding both tail bounds yields the result with $c=t\varepsilon/2$. [A1, F1, F2, F4, step 1.2]

3.1 Steps 1.2–2.2 bound the two tails whose union is $\{|H_L/L^d-e|\ge\varepsilon\}$; the theorem is conditional on differentiability of $p$ and does not assert convergence of second derivatives or equivalence for arbitrary observables. [A1, step 1.2, step 2.2] ∎

sections.Statement:
Assume AC, the ultrafilter extension principle, DC, and HB. Let
$$\mathcal H_c:=\{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega): I(P)\leq c\},\qquad c\in[0,\infty),$$
where $I$ and the local-tame topology $\tau_L$ are defined by [[thm-tdmath-specific-entropy-density]] and [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]]. Then $\mathcal H_c$ is compact and sequentially compact in $\tau_L$. This is a pure measure-theoretic compactness theorem for simple locally finite configurations relative to the independent unit-intensity Poisson reference; it makes no thermodynamic-limit or physical claim.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** AC, the ultrafilter extension principle, DC, HB, dimension $d\geq1$, and a finite $c\geq0$.

[A1] AC supplies the standard-Borel extension and the choice principles required by the local standard-Borel and Dunford–Pettis suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[A2] The ultrafilter extension principle gives Tychonoff compactness for arbitrary products of compact Hausdorff spaces; DC and HB supply the weak Eberlein–Šmulian equivalence ([[def-ultrafilter-extension-principle]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[def-hahn-banach-extension-principle-relative]]).

[F1] For every integer $m\geq1$, $I(P)=\sup_{m\geq1}m^{-d}D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})$ ([[thm-tdmath-specific-entropy-density]]).

[F2] Relative entropy is nonnegative, decreases under restriction, and obeys its variational formula ([[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]], [[lem-tdmath-relative-entropy-variational-and-chain-rules]]).

[F3] On a finite measure space, a uniformly integrable family in real $L^1$ is relatively weakly compact, and relative weak compactness is equivalent to relative weak sequential compactness under the named choice hypotheses ([[thm-dunford-pettis-for-l-one-on-a-finite-measure-space]], [[thm-eberlein-smulian]]).

[F4] A product of compact Hausdorff spaces is compact under the ultrafilter extension principle, and consistent finite-dimensional laws on standard-Borel coordinate spaces extend to a unique probability law under AC ([[thm-compact-hausdorff-tychonoff-from-the-ultrafilter-lemma]], [[def-standard-borel-space]], [[thm-kolmogorov-extension-for-standard-borel-coordinate-spaces]]).

[F5] Under $Q$, a bounded-region count is Poisson and has finite exponential moment $E_Qe^{aN_A}=\exp(|A|(e^a-1))$ for every $a>0$ ([[thm-tdmath-poisson-reference-count-properties]], [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]).

[F6] A bounded measurable test defines a bounded linear functional on real $L^1(Q_W)$ by integration, using Hölder; it is therefore weakly continuous by the definition of the weak topology. Such tests separate distinct $L^1$ classes (test a nonzero difference against its measurable sign), so the weak topology is Hausdorff ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], [[def-weak-topology-on-a-normed-space]]).

[F7] Monotone and dominated convergence justify the nonnegative count truncations and the exponential-moment limit used below ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]]).
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Let $W=a+[0,m)^d$ be any integer cube, with $a\in\mathbb Z^d$ and integer $m\geq1$. Translation invariance and [F1] give $D(P_W\Vert Q_W)\leq c|W|$. If $A$ is any bounded Borel set, choose one such cube $W$ containing it; by restriction monotonicity [F2], every $P\in\mathcal H_c$ satisfies $D(P_A\Vert Q_A)\leq C_A:=c|W|$. [A1, F1, F2, construct]

1.2 For any probability density $h$ relative to a probability $Q$ with $D(hQ\Vert Q)\leq C$, and any $K>1$, $$\int_{\{h>K\}}h\,dQ\leq\frac{C+1/e}{\log K}.$$ Indeed, $-u\log u\leq1/e$ on $[0,1]$, while $h\log h\geq h\log K$ on $\{h>K\}$. Split the entropy integral at $h=1$ and combine these bounds. Thus, for each fixed cube $W$, the densities $dP_W/dQ_W$ with $P\in\mathcal H_c$ have $L^1(Q_W)$ norm one and are uniformly integrable. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Fix $W$. By [F3], the weak closure $K_W$ of these densities in real $L^1(Q_W)$ is weakly compact. It is Hausdorff by [F6]. Every $h\in K_W$ remains nonnegative and has integral one: testing against each indicator and against $1$ gives weakly closed conditions by [F6]. Also $D(hQ_W\Vert Q_W)\leq c|W|$, because [F2] expresses $D$ as the supremum of weakly continuous affine functions of $h$, with continuity given by [F6]. Hence all entropy sublevels used below are closed in their local weak topologies. [A1, F2, F3, F6, step 1.2]

3.1 Index all integer cubes $W=a+[0,m)^d$ with $a\in\mathbb Z^d$ and integer $m\geq1$ by their countable set of pairs $(a,m)$, and form the product $K_*:=\prod_WK_W$. It is compact by [A2] and Hausdorff because each weak $L^1$ topology is Hausdorff by [F6]. 4.1 A tuple in $K_{\rm stat}$ defines consistent finite-dimensional laws on the countable standard-Borel cell spaces: for a finite set of cells, choose any integer cube containing it and take that marginal. 6.1 The product compactness in step 3.1 first gives compactness for all bounded local tests. For any tame $f$ supported in $A$ with $|f|\leq b(1+N_A)$, set $f_K=f\mathbf1_{\{N_A\leq K\}}$. ## Statement

Assume AC, the ultrafilter extension principle, DC, and HB. Let

where $I$ and the local-tame topology $\tau_L$ are defined by [[thm-tdmath-specific-entropy-density]] and [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]]. Then $\mathcal H_c$ is compact and sequentially compact in $\tau_L$. This is a pure measure-theoretic compactness theorem for simple locally finite configurations relative to the independent unit-intensity Poisson reference; it makes no thermodynamic-limit or physical claim.

[A2] The ultrafilter extension principle gives Tychonoff compactness for arbitrary products of compact Hausdorff spaces; DC and HB supply the weak Eberlein–Šmulian equivalence ([[def-ultrafilter-extension-principle]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[def-hahn-banach-extension-principle-relative]]).

[F1] For every integer $m\geq1$, $I(P)=\sup_{m\geq1}m^{-d}D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})$ ([[thm-tdmath-specific-entropy-density]]).

[F2] Relative entropy is nonnegative, decreases under restriction, and obeys its variational formula ([[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]], [[lem-tdmath-relative-entropy-variational-and-chain-rules]]).

[F3] On a finite measure space, a uniformly integrable family in real $L^1$ is relatively weakly compact, and relative weak compactness is equivalent to relative weak sequential compactness under the named choice hypotheses ([[thm-dunford-pettis-for-l-one-on-a-finite-measure-space]], [[thm-eberlein-smulian]]).

[F4] A product of compact Hausdorff spaces is compact under the ultrafilter extension principle, and consistent finite-dimensional laws on standard-Borel coordinate spaces extend to a unique probability law under AC ([[thm-compact-hausdorff-tychonoff-from-the-ultrafilter-lemma]], [[def-standard-borel-space]], [[thm-kolmogorov-extension-for-standard-borel-coordinate-spaces]]).

[F5] Under $Q$, a bounded-region count is Poisson and has finite exponential moment $E_Qe^{aN_A}=\exp(|A|(e^a-1))$ for every $a>0$ ([[thm-tdmath-poisson-reference-count-properties]], [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]).

[F6] A bounded measurable test defines a bounded linear functional on real $L^1(Q_W)$ by integration, using Hölder; it is therefore weakly continuous by the definition of the weak topology. Such tests separate distinct $L^1$ classes (test a nonzero difference against its measurable sign), so the weak topology is Hausdorff ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], [[def-weak-topology-on-a-normed-space]]).

[F7] Monotone and dominated convergence justify the nonnegative count truncations and the exponential-moment limit used below ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

sections.Statement: Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $E:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable, and let $J\subset\mathbb R$ be open. Suppose $Z(\beta):=\int e^{-\beta E}\,d\mu$ satisfies $0<Z(\beta)<\infty$ on $J$, and for every compact interval $K\subset J$ there is $G_K\in L^1(\mu)$ with $(1+|E|^2)e^{-\beta E}\le G_K$ pointwise for every $\beta\in K$. Then $Z\in C^2(J)$, $Z'=-\int E e^{-\beta E}d\mu$, $Z''=\int E^2e^{-\beta E}d\mu$, and $-\partial_\beta\log Z=\langle E\rangle_\beta$, $\partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$. The reference-relative entropy $-\int p_\beta\log p_\beta\,d\mu$ is finite and equals $\log Z+\beta\langle E\rangle_\beta$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** As stated in the item.

[A1] $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, $E$, $J$, positivity/finiteness of $Z$, and the local integrable envelope are the hypotheses of this statement.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]: the reference measure integral, integrability, and signed/complex conventions.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-dominated-convergence]]: dominated pointwise limits may be passed through the integral.

[F3] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: the exponential is positive and its derivative is itself.

[F4] [[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]], and [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: logarithms convert positive products to sums, are continuous on positive reals, and differentiate as $1/x$.

[F5] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: scalar difference quotients of the exponential are bounded by intermediate derivatives.

[F6] [[thm-chain-rule]]: the derivative of $e^{-\beta E(x)}$ in the parameter $\beta$ is obtained by composition with the exponential.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** A measure space, a measurable real energy $E$, a positive finite partition function, and the compact-interval envelope.

1.1 For $\beta$ in the interior of a compact interval $K\subset J$, the difference quotient of $e^{-\beta E(x)}$ tends pointwise to $-E(x)e^{-\beta E(x)}$. The mean-value theorem [F5] bounds its absolute value, for small $h$, by $|E|e^{-\theta E}$ for an intermediate $\theta\in K$; this is at most $G_K$ because $|E|\le1+|E|^2$. Dominated convergence [F2] therefore gives $Z'=-\int E e^{-\beta E}d\mu$. Applying the same argument to $-E e^{-\beta E}$, dominated by $G_K$, gives $Z''=\int E^2e^{-\beta E}d\mu$; dominated convergence also gives continuity of both derivatives. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, F6]

2.1 The density $p_\beta$ is nonnegative and integrates to one. The envelope makes its first and second energy moments finite. Differentiating $\log Z$ using [F4] gives $-Z'/Z=\int E p_\beta d\mu$ and $Z''/Z-(Z'/Z)^2=\int E^2p_\beta d\mu-(\int Ep_\beta d\mu)^2$. The latter is the variance by expanding its defining square. [A1, F1, F3, F4, F6, step 1.1]

3.1 Since $\log p_\beta=-\beta E-\log Z$ almost everywhere and $\int |E|p_\beta d\mu<\infty$, the entropy integrand is absolutely integrable. Substitution and normalization yield $-\int p_\beta\log p_\beta d\mu=\beta\langle E\rangle_\beta+\log Z$. This entropy depends on the chosen reference measure $\mu$. [A1, F1, F3, F4, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $E:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable, and let $J\subset\mathbb R$ be open. Suppose $Z(\beta):=\int e^{-\beta E}\,d\mu$ satisfies $0<Z(\beta)<\infty$ on $J$, and for every compact interval $K\subset J$ there is $G_K\in L^1(\mu)$ with $(1+|E|^2)e^{-\beta E}\le G_K$ pointwise for every $\beta\in K$. Define $p_\beta=e^{-\beta E}/Z(\beta)$, $\langle Y\rangle_\beta:=\int Yp_\beta\,d\mu$ for integrable $Y$, and $\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E):=\int(E-\langle E\rangle_\beta)^2p_\beta\,d\mu$. Then $Z\in C^2(J)$, $Z'=-\int E e^{-\beta E}d\mu$, $Z''=\int E^2e^{-\beta E}d\mu$, and $-\partial_\beta\log Z=\langle E\rangle_\beta$, $\partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$. The reference-relative entropy $-\int p_\beta\log p_\beta\,d\mu$ is finite and equals $\log Z+\beta\langle E\rangle_\beta$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** As stated in the item.

[A1] $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$, $E$, $J$, positivity/finiteness of $Z$, and the local integrable envelope are the hypotheses of this statement.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]: the reference measure integral, integrability, and signed/complex conventions.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-dominated-convergence]]: dominated pointwise limits may be passed through the integral.

[F3] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: the exponential is positive and its derivative is itself.

[F4] [[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]], and [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: logarithms convert positive products to sums, are continuous on positive reals, and differentiate as $1/x$.

[F5] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: scalar difference quotients of the exponential are bounded by intermediate derivatives.

[F6] [[thm-chain-rule]]: the derivative of $e^{-\beta E(x)}$ in the parameter $\beta$ is obtained by composition with the exponential.

## Proof

**Given:** A measure space, a measurable real energy $E$, a positive finite partition function, and the compact-interval envelope.

1.1 For $\beta$ in the interior of a compact interval $K\subset J$, the difference quotient of $e^{-\beta E(x)}$ tends pointwise to $-E(x)e^{-\beta E(x)}$. The mean-value theorem [F5] bounds its absolute value, for small $h$, by $|E|e^{-\theta E}$ for an intermediate $\theta\in K$; this is at most $G_K$ because $|E|\le1+|E|^2$. Dominated convergence [F2] therefore gives $Z'=-\int E e^{-\beta E}d\mu$. Applying the same argument to $-E e^{-\beta E}$, dominated by $G_K$, gives $Z''=\int E^2e^{-\beta E}d\mu$; dominated convergence also gives continuity of both derivatives. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, F6]

2.1 The density $p_\beta$ is nonnegative and integrates to one. The envelope makes its first and second energy moments finite. Differentiating $\log Z$ using [F4] gives $-Z'/Z=\int E p_\beta d\mu$ and $Z''/Z-(Z'/Z)^2=\int E^2p_\beta d\mu-(\int Ep_\beta d\mu)^2$. The latter is the variance by expanding its defining square. [A1, F1, F3, F4, F6, step 1.1]

3.1 Since $\log p_\beta=-\beta E-\log Z$ almost everywhere and $\int |E|p_\beta d\mu<\infty$, the entropy integrand is absolutely integrable. **Given:** A measure space and a pointwise increasing sequence $0\le f_n\uparrow f$.

For each $c_j>0$, $A_n\cap B_j\uparrow B_j$; countable additivity, applied to successive disjoint differences, gives $\mu(A_n\cap B_j)\uparrow\mu(B_j)$. ## Statement

**Given:** A measure space, its nonnegative integral, and a pointwise increasing measurable sequence.

[F2] [[def-finite-sum]]: finite sums of simple-function level values can be regrouped.

[F3] [[def-complete-ordered-field]]: bounded nonempty subsets of $\mathbb R$ have suprema.

[A1] Countable additivity of $\mu$ is part of the measure-space definition.

[A2] The sequence is measurable and satisfies $0\le f_n\le f_{n+1}$ and $f_n\to f$ pointwise.

sections.Statement:
Assume the superstable regular interaction of [[thm-tdmath-continuum-variational-pressure]], $\beta>0$, and an interior attainable density $\rho>0$. For integers $N_L$ with $N_L/L^d\to\rho$, let $Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta)$ be the $1/N_L!$-normalized positional partition on the periodized cube, with the image convention of [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. Then
$$L^{-d}\log Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta)\longrightarrow F_\beta(\rho),$$
the same rate as the free cube. Let $C^{\mathrm{per}}_{L,N_L}$ be the periodic exact-$N_L$ canonical law and $R_{L,\omega}$ its periodized empirical field from [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]]. For any finite supporting activity $z>0$ of $F_\beta$ at $\rho$, these empirical fields concentrate in every open $\tau_L$ neighborhood of the minimizer set of $I+\beta\Phi-\rho\log z$. A singleton minimizer gives convergence in probability in $\tau_L$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** A superstable regular even pair potential, positive inverse temperature, and an interior canonical density.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]: stability and regularity give the finite canonical integrals and the stated periodic-image convention.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]]: separated-cell tails are summable and admit gaps with vanishing interaction per volume.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-superstable-cell-energy-bound]]: $H\geq A\sum_iN_{C_i}^2-BN$, with $A>0$.

[F4] [[thm-tdmath-canonical-interior-density-limit]]: the free exact-$N$ cube rate is $F_\beta(\rho)$ at each interior density.

[F5] [[thm-tdmath-canonical-grand-duality]]: the canonical rate and grand pressure are convex duals; a supporting activity realizes equality.

[F6] [[thm-tdmath-continuum-variational-pressure]]: free/periodic grand pressures agree and local grand limits minimize the stationary variational functional.

[F7] [[lem-tdmath-canonical-empirical-field-conditioning]]: for either boundary condition, if the exact-$N$ rate is $F_\beta(\rho)$, its periodized empirical fields concentrate near the grand variational minimizer set.

[F8] [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]: Hölder’s inequality makes the log of a finite positive Laplace integral convex in its scalar parameter.

[F9] [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]] and [[lem-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field-stationary-density]]: a finite configuration determines a stationary empirical field with intensity equal to its particle number divided by volume.

[L1] Georgii, Lemma 4.3, states for an empty corridor of width $k$ that the periodic/free energy discrepancy is bounded by $c_d\delta_k T_L$, where $\delta_k\to0$ is the lattice tail and $T_L=\sum_iN_{C_i}^2$. The complete lemma and proof were read; this is used only under its superstable regular hypotheses.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The assumptions and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 For the upper bound, $e^{\alpha N_L}Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta)\leq\Xi_{\mathrm{per}}(L,e^\alpha,\beta)$ for every real $\alpha$. Divide logarithms by $L^d$, use the free/periodic grand limit [F6], and then take the infimum over $\alpha$. The canonical-grand duality [F5] gives $\limsup L^{-d}\log Z_{\mathrm{per}}\leq F_\beta(\rho)$. [F4, F5, F6, algebra]

1.2 Fix corridor width $k$ larger than the tail cutoff. Restrict the $N_L$ particles to the inner cube of side $L-k$, leaving the corridor empty. The exact-$N_L$ density is still $\rho$. The diagonal-gap supplier [F2] gives the vanishing regular-tail cutoff used here. By [L1], the periodized energy differs from the free inner-cube energy by at most $c_d\delta_kT_{L-k}$. The cell bound [F3] implies $T_{L-k}\leq A^{-1}(H_{L-k}+BN_L)$. Consequently $$ Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta)\geq e^{-\beta c_d\delta_k BN_L/A}\, Z(L-k,N_L;\beta(1+c_d\delta_k/A)). $$ The canonical theorem [F4] applies at the perturbed inverse temperature, giving the corresponding lower rate. [F1, F2, F3, F4, L1, algebra]

2.1 At fixed interior $\rho$, $F_\beta(\rho)$ is finite and convex as a function of $\beta>0$, by Hölder’s inequality [F8], since each finite-volume log partition is convex and the pointwise limit is finite. A finite convex function is continuous on the open interval: on a compact subinterval, its secant slopes are bounded by the slopes to fixed exterior endpoints. Let $L\to\infty$ in step 1.2 and then $k\to\infty$, so $\delta_k\to0$; continuity yields $\liminf\geq F_\beta(\rho)$. [F4, F8, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Step 2.1 established the periodic exact-$N_L$ rate $F_\beta(\rho)$, and [F5] supplies a finite supporting activity. The grand rate in [F6] and the periodized empirical field in [F9] satisfy the hypotheses of [F7] with periodic boundary condition. Hence the periodic empirical fields concentrate near the minimizer set, and concentrate at its singleton when it is unique. [F5, F6, F7, F9, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
