sections.Statement:
Let $C\ge1$ be the number of components and $P\ge1$ the number of phases. Use common positive real coordinates $T,p$, expressed in fixed units if they are given a physical interpretation, and, for each phase $\alpha$, an interior composition vector

$$x^\alpha\in\Omega_C:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},$$

with the convention $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $\Omega_1=\{0\}$. The final component fraction is $1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$. The ambient coordinate domain $U=(0,\infty)^2\times\Omega_C^P$ is open in $\mathbb R^n$, where $n=2+P(C-1)$. For each phase $\alpha$ and component $i$, let $\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)$ be a real-valued $C^1$ coordinate function; these are mathematical maps and no thermodynamic potential or physical realization is assumed.

For $P\ge2$, define the $q=C(P-1)$ coexistence equations

$$F_{i,\alpha}(T,p,x^1,\ldots,x^P)=\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)-\mu_i^1(T,p,x^1)=0\quad(1\le i\le C,\ 2\le\alpha\le P).$$

At a solution $z_*\in U$, assume some $q\times q$ derivative minor of $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is invertible. Then the local solution set is a graph of dimension

$$n-q=2+P(C-1)-C(P-1)=C-P+2.$$

For $P=1$ there are no coexistence equations and the coordinate domain itself has dimension $n=C+1=C-P+2$. In a specified reactive variant with $R\ge1$, let $\nu^1,\ldots,\nu^R\in\mathbb R^C$ be linearly independent dimensionless stoichiometric vectors and add the $R$ affinity equations $A_r=\sum_{i=1}^C\nu_i^r\mu_i^1=0$. If the combined equation map has an invertible $(q+R)\times(q+R)$ derivative minor at a solution and $q+R\le n$, its local zero set has dimension

$$n-q-R=C-P+2-R.$$

These are conditional local dimensions under the displayed nonsingular-minor assumptions. No dimension formula follows at singular solutions, on composition boundaries, or from equation counting alone; no empirical or general physical phase rule is asserted.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The finite integers, open coordinate domain, $C^1$ chemical-potential coordinate functions, coexistence equations, and nonsingular-minor assumptions in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: $C^1$ means total differentiability with continuous derivative-matrix entries.

[L1] [[thm-tdmath-local-implicit-rank]]: a $C^1$ map whose derivative has a specified invertible square minor has a local zero set that is a graph over the remaining coordinates, of dimension ambient dimension minus equation count.

[L2] [[thm-algebra-of-total-derivatives]]: finite sums and differences of $C^1$ real-valued maps are $C^1$.
sections.Proof:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $P\ge2$, $F$ has one scalar component for each pair $(i,\alpha)$ with $1\le i\le C$ and $2\le\alpha\le P$, so it has $q=C(P-1)$ components. Each is a difference of $C^1$ maps and therefore $F$ is $C^1$ on the open set $U$ by [F1, L2]. The assumed minor lets [L1] apply, giving local graph dimension $n-q$. ## Statement

Let $C\ge1$ be the number of components and $P\ge1$ the number of phases. Use common positive real coordinates $T,p$, expressed in fixed units if they are given a physical interpretation, and, for each phase $\alpha$, an interior composition vector

$$x^\alpha\in\Omega_C:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},$$

with the convention $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $\Omega_1=\{0\}$. The final component fraction is $1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$. The ambient coordinate domain $U=(0,\infty)^2\times\Omega_C^P$ is open in $\mathbb R^n$, where $n=2+P(C-1)$. For each phase $\alpha$ and component $i$, let $\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)$ be a real-valued $C^1$ coordinate function; these are mathematical maps and no thermodynamic potential or physical realization is assumed.

For $P\ge2$, define the $q=C(P-1)$ coexistence equations

$$F_{i,\alpha}(T,p,x^1,\ldots,x^P)=\mu_i^\alpha(T,p,x^\alpha)-\mu_i^1(T,p,x^1)=0\quad(1\le i\le C,\ 2\le\alpha\le P).$$

At a solution $z_*\in U$, assume some $q\times q$ derivative minor of $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is invertible. Then the local solution set is a graph of dimension

$$n-q=2+P(C-1)-C(P-1)=C-P+2.$$

For $P=1$ there are no coexistence equations and the coordinate domain itself has dimension $n=C+1=C-P+2$. In a specified reactive variant with $R\ge1$, let $\nu^1,\ldots,\nu^R\in\mathbb R^C$ be linearly independent dimensionless stoichiometric vectors and add the $R$ affinity equations $A_r=\sum_{i=1}^C\nu_i^r\mu_i^1=0$. If the combined equation map has an invertible $(q+R)\times(q+R)$ derivative minor at a solution and $q+R\le n$, its local zero set has dimension

$$n-q-R=C-P+2-R.$$

These are conditional local dimensions under the displayed nonsingular-minor assumptions. No dimension formula follows at singular solutions, on composition boundaries, or from equation counting alone; no empirical or general physical phase rule is asserted.

**Given:** The finite integers, open coordinate domain, $C^1$ chemical-potential coordinate functions, coexistence equations, and nonsingular-minor assumptions in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: $C^1$ means total differentiability with continuous derivative-matrix entries.

[L1] [[thm-tdmath-local-implicit-rank]]: a $C^1$ map whose derivative has a specified invertible square minor has a local zero set that is a graph over the remaining coordinates, of dimension ambient dimension minus equation count.

[L2] [[thm-algebra-of-total-derivatives]]: finite sums and differences of $C^1$ real-valued maps are $C^1$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

Expanding $n=2+P(C-1)$ gives $n-q=2+PC-P-CP+C=C-P+2$. [F1, L1, L2, given, algebra]

1.2 If $P=1$, no phase-equality equations are indexed because there is no $\alpha\ge2$. The local solution set is all of the open domain $U$, which has $n=2+(C-1)=C+1=C-P+2$ coordinates. [given, algebra]

2.1 In the reactive variant, each added affinity is a finite linear combination of $C^1$ coordinate functions and is therefore $C^1$ by [F1, L2]; the combined map has $q+R$ scalar equations. Its stated minor satisfies [L1], so the graph dimension is $n-q-R=2+P(C-1)-C(P-1)-R=C-P+2-R$. Linear independence of the $\nu^r$ identifies $R$ distinct reaction directions, while the full-rank minor remains a separate necessary assumption on the equation derivatives. [F1, L1, L2, given, algebra] ∎

sections.Statement: Assume AC, fix $d\geq1$ and $\lambda>0$, and let $Q_\lambda$ be the configuration law of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. For pairwise disjoint bounded Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_r\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, the restrictions $\omega|_{A_1},\ldots,\omega|_{A_r}$ are independent, each count $N_{A_j}$ has Poisson law with mean $\lambda|A_j|$, and the joint law of counts on any finite disjoint family is the product of those Poisson laws. In particular, $Q_\lambda$ is invariant under every translation $T_x$, and its intensity measure is $\lambda$ times Lebesgue measure.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** AC, dimension $d\geq1$, $\lambda>0$, the cell-product law $Q_\lambda$, and pairwise disjoint bounded Borel sets $A_j$.

[A1] AC is part of the Poisson reference construction and of its countable product existence ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]).

[F1] On each unit cell, the count has law $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ and, conditional on $n$, the points are independent uniform points subsequently sorted. Finite cell families are independent ([[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]).

[F2] The number of length-$n$ label sequences with category counts $(n_0,\ldots,n_s)$ is the multinomial coefficient, and its finite expansion is the multinomial theorem ([[def-multinomial-coefficient]], [[thm-multinomial-theorem]]).

[F3] Exponentials turn sums into products ([[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]).

[F4] The configuration sigma-algebra is generated by bounded-Borel count maps, finite count cylinders form a generating pi-system, and agreement there determines probability laws ([[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]], [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]).
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Fix one unit cell $C_i$ and a finite Borel partition $B_0,\ldots,B_s$ of it. Put $v_j=|B_j|$, so $\sum_jv_j=1$. Conditional on the cell count $N=n$, the $n$ independent uniform points give category-count probability $n!\prod_jv_j^{n_j}/\prod_jn_j!$ for $\sum_jn_j=n$. Multiplying by the Poisson count probability $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ gives $e^{-\lambda}\prod_j(\lambda v_j)^{n_j}/n_j!=\prod_je^{-\lambda v_j}(\lambda v_j)^{n_j}/n_j!$, by [F3]. This factors into the Poisson probabilities of the disjoint cell pieces, including the complement $B_0$; hence their counts are independent Poisson variables with respective means $\lambda v_j$. Zero-volume pieces have count zero almost surely by the same formula. [A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Each bounded $A_j$ intersects only finitely many unit cells. Apply step 1.1 to the partition formed by the sets $A_j\cap C_i$ and their complement in each such cell. Independence within each cell and independence between cell configurations show that all component counts, indexed by both $j$ and $i$, are independent Poisson variables. [A1, step 1.1, F1, construct]

3.1 For fixed $j$, sum the component counts over its finitely many cells. The sum of independent Poisson variables of means $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_q$ has mass at $n$ equal to $e^{-\sum\mu_i}(\sum\mu_i)^n/n!$: expand $(\sum_i\mu_i)^n$ by [F2], then use the product of the component masses. Thus $N_{A_j}$ is Poisson with mean $\lambda\sum_i|A_j\cap C_i|=\lambda|A_j|$. The groups of components for different $j$ are disjoint independent families, so their sums remain independent. [A1, step 2.1, F2, F3, algebra]

4.1 Let $A_1,\ldots,A_r$ be pairwise disjoint and, for each $j$, consider a finite count-cylinder event in the restriction to $A_j$. Refine the finitely many counting sets in each event into their disjoint atoms inside $A_j$. Step 3.1 gives independent Poisson counts on all these atoms across every $j$; the event for each restricted configuration is a measurable function only of its own atom counts. Thus finite cylinder events factor across $j$. The restriction sigma-fields are generated by these cylinders, so repeated pi-lambda extension proves independence of the restrictions themselves. [A1, step 3.1, F4]

5.1 For a finite family of bounded Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_s$, partition their union into the finitely many disjoint Boolean atoms formed by the sets and their complements. Every $N_{A_j}$ is a sum of the counts on these atoms. Translation preserves each atom's volume, so step 3.1 gives the same joint distribution of this whole count vector under $Q_\lambda$ and its translate. Thus the laws agree on every finite count cylinder. These cylinders generate the configuration sigma-algebra by [F4], and pi-lambda uniqueness identifies the laws. The one-set case gives $E_{Q_\lambda}N_A=\lambda|A|$, which is the asserted intensity measure. [A1, step 3.1, F4] ∎

sections.Statement:
Let $A$ be a finite set of reaction channels, let $r\in\mathbb N$, let $\nu_a\in\mathbb R^r$ be the output-minus-input type vector of channel $a$, and let $d_a\in\mathbb R$ be a finite lower bound on its already calibrated entropy change. There exists an offset vector $b\in\mathbb R^r$ satisfying

$$b\cdot\nu_a+d_a\ge0\qquad(a\in A)$$

if and only if every $\lambda\in\mathbb R^A$ with $\lambda_a\ge0$ and $\sum_{a\in A}\lambda_a\nu_a=0$ satisfies $\sum_{a\in A}\lambda_ad_a\ge0$. If an actual transition has entropy change $\Delta\sigma_a\ge d_a$, such a vector guarantees $\Delta\sigma_a+b\cdot\nu_a\ge0$. The criterion is exact for the finite lower-bound inequalities; it does not claim necessity for actual transitions when $d_a$ is only a loose bound.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
[A1] The finite channel data in the Statement, with $d_a$ a lower bound on the calibrated change supplied by [[thm-tdmath-common-meter-calibration]].

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-finite-inequality-alternative]]: $c_j\cdot b\ge h_j$ is feasible exactly when every nonnegative zero-left-side multiplier has nonpositive combined right side.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** [A1] and [F1].

1.1 Apply [F1] to the rows $c_a=
u_a$ and $h_a=-d_a$. The row system $
u_a\cdot b\ge-d_a$ is exactly the required offset system. Its multiplier condition is $\sum_a\lambda_a
u_a=0\Rightarrow\sum_a\lambda_a(-d_a)\le0$, which is equivalent to $\sum_a\lambda_ad_a\ge0$. This proves the if-and-only-if, including $A=\varnothing$ where $b=0$ is feasible and the multiplier condition is vacuous. If $r=0$ and $A$ is nonempty, every $
u_a=0$; testing the coordinate multiplier for each channel makes the criterion equivalent to $d_a\ge0$ for every $a$, and then the unique empty vector $b$ satisfies all rows. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 For any channel with actual change $\Delta\sigma_a\ge d_a$, add $b\cdot
u_a$ to both sides of that bound and use the solved row inequality $b\cdot
u_a\ge-d_a$. Then $\Delta\sigma_a+b\cdot
u_a\ge d_a+b\cdot
u_a\ge0$. This is a sufficient monotonicity conclusion for the stated channels. [A1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $A$ be a finite set of reaction channels, let $r\in\mathbb N$, let $\nu_a\in\mathbb R^r$ be the output-minus-input type vector of channel $a$, and let $d_a\in\mathbb R$ be a finite lower bound on its already calibrated entropy change. There exists an offset vector $b\in\mathbb R^r$ satisfying

$$b\cdot\nu_a+d_a\ge0\qquad(a\in A)$$

if and only if every $\lambda\in\mathbb R^A$ with $\lambda_a\ge0$ and $\sum_{a\in A}\lambda_a\nu_a=0$ satisfies $\sum_{a\in A}\lambda_ad_a\ge0$. If an actual transition has entropy change $\Delta\sigma_a\ge d_a$, such a vector guarantees $\Delta\sigma_a+b\cdot\nu_a\ge0$. The criterion is exact for the finite lower-bound inequalities; it does not claim necessity for actual transitions when $d_a$ is only a loose bound.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] The finite channel data in the Statement, with $d_a$ a lower bound on the calibrated change supplied by [[thm-tdmath-common-meter-calibration]].

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-finite-inequality-alternative]]: $c_j\cdot b\ge h_j$ is feasible exactly when every nonnegative zero-left-side multiplier has nonpositive combined right side.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1] and [F1].

1.1 Apply [F1] to the rows $c_a=\nu_a$ and $h_a=-d_a$. The row system $\nu_a\cdot b\ge-d_a$ is exactly the required offset system. Its multiplier condition is $\sum_a\lambda_a\nu_a=0\Rightarrow\sum_a\lambda_a(-d_a)\le0$, which is equivalent to $\sum_a\lambda_ad_a\ge0$. This proves the if-and-only-if, including $A=\varnothing$ where $b=0$ is feasible and the multiplier condition is vacuous. If $r=0$ and $A$ is nonempty, every $\nu_a=0$; testing the coordinate multiplier for each channel makes the criterion equivalent to $d_a\ge0$ for every $a$, and then the unique empty vector $b$ satisfies all rows. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 For any channel with actual change $\Delta\sigma_a\ge d_a$, add $b\cdot\nu_a$ to both sides of that bound and use the solved row inequality $b\cdot\nu_a\ge-d_a$. Then $\Delta\sigma_a+b\cdot\nu_a\ge d_a+b\cdot\nu_a\ge0$. This is a sufficient monotonicity conclusion for the stated channels. [A1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

For $r=0$ and nonempty $A$, the criterion reduces to $d_a\ge0$ for every channel. Strict increase, infinitely many channels, and lower bounds equal to actual changes are separate conditions and are not inferred here.

fm.title: Reference-strip gluing proves comparison for scaled copies

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, Theorem 4.4 and Lemma 4.1, pp. 54–56

sections.Statement: Assume [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and T1–T4 of [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]] for every finite join. For any one simple type $\Gamma_i$, every two finite compounds of its scaled copies with the same total coefficient mass are comparable. Thus CH holds on all multiple scaled products of that type. No entropy across different material types is asserted here.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The stated forward-sector and thermal-contact hypotheses; every thermal join remains a simple domain with these hypotheses.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: A1–A7, S1–S3, and the tagged finite-compound conventions hold, without an assumed CH.

[A2] [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]: T1–T4 provide simple thermal joins, reversible equilibrium splits, thermal scaling, and a thermal endpoint pair surrounding each state.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-reference-strip-coordinate]]: every state in a strip with strict thermally equivalent endpoints is equivalent to a unique reference mixture with parameter in $(0,1)$.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-sector-nesting]]: one-copy comparisons hold on each finite join domain; strict comparison is interior membership, and forward sectors are nested.

[F3] [[def-tdmath-forward-signed-comparison]] and [[lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellation]]: signed comparison is defined from positive/negative parts; it is translation invariant, additive, and cancellable under A1–A6.

[F4] [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]]: each simple domain has one constant fixed-work energy orientation; arbitrarily close states on a vertical segment are strictly ordered in that orientation.

[F5] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: a closed bounded subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space is compact.
sections.Proof:
1.1 By T4, the open strips $\Sigma(a,b):=\{x:a\prec\prec x\prec\prec b\}$ with $a\prec\prec b$ and $a\sim_T b$ cover $\Gamma_i$. They are open: by [F2], $a\prec\prec x$ is $x\in\operatorname{int}A_a$, and $x\prec\prec b$ is $x\notin A_b$; the latter set is open because $A_b$ is relatively closed. [A1, A2, F2]

1.2 Let $\Sigma(a,b)$ and $\Sigma(c,d)$ overlap. Their intersection is open. Choose two states $e\prec\prec f$ in a small vertical segment contained in the overlap, using [F4]. Let $s_e,s_f$ be their coordinates in the first strip and $t_e,t_f$ in the second, supplied by [F1]. If $s_f<s_e$, the signed difference $R_{s_e}-R_{s_f}=(s_e-s_f)(\mathsf{J}(b)-\mathsf{J}(a))$ and positive scaling and signed compatibility [A1, F3] give $R_{s_f}\prec R_{s_e}$, so $f\prec e$ by the two reference equivalences; if $s_f=s_e$, those references coincide and give $f\sim e$. sections.Statement:
Let $\phi$ be superstable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], and let $B=\{x:\phi(x)=+\infty\}$. For a finite configuration $\omega$, call it admissible when no pair displacement belongs to $B$; for periodic boxes require this also for every periodic image pair. Define the zero-inverse-temperature-parameter continuation (the mathematical $\beta=0$ branch) to be $z^{N(\omega)}\mathbf 1_{\rm admissible}(\omega)$, explicitly retaining the hard exclusion. Then the normalized Poisson free and periodic partition rates exist and equal
$$-\min_{P\in\mathcal K_B}\{I(P)-\rho(P)\log z\},$$
where $\mathcal K_B$ is the set of stationary laws with no forbidden pair almost surely. The minimizer set is nonempty and compact in $\tau_L$. The periodically continued grand laws are relatively compact in $\tau_L$, all their accumulation points are minimizers, and if this minimizer is unique they converge to it for every measurable local observable of at-most-linear count growth. If $B=\varnothing$, this is the Poisson activity-$z$ model. For $B\ne\varnothing$, it is not an unrestricted Poisson law and does not assign a value to the undefined product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** Superstability and regularity, $z>0$, the unit-intensity Poisson reference, and the explicitly defined hard-admissibility beta-zero weight.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]: the interaction is an even measurable superstable pair potential with a decreasing integrable two-sided far-tail envelope, and its normalized Poisson partition uses $1/N!$.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-local-tame-entropy-compactness]]: stationary laws with bounded Poisson specific entropy are compact in $\tau_L$; $I$ is lower semicontinuous.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-spatial-mean-information]]: for stationary laws ergodic under all translations and with finite specific entropy, normalized finite-volume log likelihoods converge in probability to $I(P)$.


[F4] [[lem-tdmath-relative-entropy-variational-and-chain-rules]]: for bounded $f$, $D(P\Vert Q)\geq E_Pf-\log E_Qe^f$, and relative entropy has the conditional chain rule and is nonnegative.

[F5] [[thm-tdmath-continuum-variational-pressure]]: for positive inverse temperature the stationary entropy-energy functional has compact sublevels, its free and periodic pressures agree, and finite-energy stationary laws admit separated-block approximation with the stated entropy and local-tame controls.

[F6] [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]]: $\tau_L$ tests every measurable local observable bounded by a constant times $1+N_A$.

[F7] [[thm-tdmath-poisson-reference-count-properties]] and [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]: the unit-cube Poisson count has exponential moment $E_Qe^{aN_C}=e^{e^a-1}$, and bounded truncations increase to this count test.

[F8] [[lem-tdmath-periodic-law-local-tame-transfer]]: torus-invariant finite-volume laws with bounded entropy density have relatively compact continued laws, uniformly integrable local counts, and limit entropy bounded by the limiting finite-volume entropy density.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Regularity bounds $\phi$ above outside a bounded set, so $B$ is bounded. Define $\chi=+\infty$ on $B$ and $0$ elsewhere. Then $\chi$ is even, stable with constant $0$, and has zero far tail. Its finite-volume beta-zero partition is exactly the specified hard-admissibility partition. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 For each bounded region $A$, the event that $A$ contains a forbidden pair is a bounded measurable local event. Its probability is continuous under $\tau_L$ by [F6]. Exhausting space by countably many bounded cubes shows that $\mathcal K_B$ is $\tau_L$-closed. Apply [F4] to the bounded tests $f_M=a\min(N_C,M)$ and let $M\to\infty$. Monotone convergence and [F7] give $I(P)\geq a\rho(P)-(e^a-1)$, hence $\rho(P)\leq(I(P)+e^a-1)/a$. Choosing $a>2\max(\log z,0)$ makes $I(P)-\rho(P)\log z$ coercive in $I(P)$. By [F2], every finite sublevel is compact and lower semicontinuous, so the infimum on $\mathcal K_B$ is attained whenever the admissible class is nonempty. The empty configuration law gives a finite candidate. [F2, F4, F6, F7, algebra]

1.3 Fix $P\in\mathcal K_B$ with $I(P)<\infty$. Condition its restriction to a cube of side $n$ on configurations whose distinct points have separation at least $1/q$ and whose finite pair energies are at most $q$. As $q\to\infty$, these events increase to probability one because configurations are locally finite, simple, and hard-admissible. Choose $q=q(n)$ so the conditioning probability tends to one. Tile space by these conditioned blocks separated by an empty corridor wider than the range of $B$ and the fixed tail cutoff, take independent copies, then average the lattice phase uniformly. No cross-block pair is forbidden. The conditional entropy inequality $$ D(P(\cdot\mid E)\Vert Q)\leq [D(P\Vert Q)+1]/P(E)-\log P(E) $$ follows by expanding the conditional density $1_E(dP/dQ)/P(E)$ and using $-u\log u\leq1/e$. Additivity on independent blocks and the vanishing corridor fraction give $\limsup I(P_n)\leq I(P)$; local count truncation and finite first moments give $P_n\to P$ in $\tau_L$. Each $P_n$ has finite original energy density. [F1, F2, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 For a finite-volume beta-zero Gibbs law $G_L^b$, direct integration of its density gives $$ -\log Z_{Q,L}=D(G_L^b\Vert Q_L)-(\log z)E_{G_L^b}N_L. $$ Stationarize independent blocks and average their phase. The entropy chain rule bounds the resulting specific entropy by the displayed finite-volume entropy per volume; hard admissibility passes to every local limit. Compactness [F2], lower semicontinuity, and the entropy identity therefore give the pressure upper bound by the negative minimum in the statement. For the reverse bound, use the approximating finite-energy laws from step 1.3. Their independent separated blocks are admissible; the spatial likelihood theorem [F3] supplies typical blocks with likelihood cost $I(P_n)$, while empirical counts converge to $\rho(P_n)$. Changing from Poisson measure to the beta-zero weight gives the lower rate $-I(P_n)+\rho(P_n)\log z$. Let $n\to\infty$ and optimize over $P$. Corridors change the normalized log weight by their vanishing volume fraction, so free and periodic rates agree. [F2, F3, F5, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Put $\alpha=\log z$, $p_L=L^{-d}\log Z_{Q,L}$, and $d_L=L^{-d}D(G_L^{\rm per}\Vert Q_L)$. The exact identity in step 2.1 reads $d_L=\alpha\rho_L-p_L$. For $a>\max(\alpha,0)$, the entropy count inequality gives $d_L\geq a\rho_L-(e^a-1)$; the convergent pressure rates therefore bound both $\rho_L$ and $d_L$. The grand density and periodic hard-admissibility condition are invariant under translations modulo the box, so [F8] gives relatively compact continued laws. Every limit $P$ lies in $\mathcal K_B$ by the bounded local forbidden-pair tests from step 1.2. Along a subsequence realizing the entropy liminf, [F8] and count-tail uniformity give
$$I(P)-\alpha\rho(P)\leq\liminf(d_L-\alpha\rho_L)=-\lim p_L=\min_{\mathcal K_B}(I-\alpha\rho).$$
The opposite inequality is the definition of the minimum. Thus every accumulation point is a minimizer. If there is just one, relative compactness forces convergence of the entire sequence in $\tau_L$, including every stated tame test. [F2, F4, F6, F7, F8, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

Additivity on independent blocks and the vanishing corridor fraction give $\limsup I(P_n)\leq I(P)$; local count truncation and finite first moments give $P_n\to P$ in $\tau_L$. Each $P_n$ has finite original energy density. [F1, F2, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 For a finite-volume beta-zero Gibbs law $G_L^b$, direct integration of its density gives $$ -\log Z_{Q,L}=D(G_L^b\Vert Q_L)-(\log z)E_{G_L^b}N_L. $$ Stationarize independent blocks and average their phase. The entropy chain rule bounds the resulting specific entropy by the displayed finite-volume entropy per volume; hard admissibility passes to every local limit. Compactness [F2], lower semicontinuity, and the entropy identity therefore give the pressure upper bound by the negative minimum in the statement. For the reverse bound, use the approximating finite-energy laws from step 1.3. Their independent separated blocks are admissible; the spatial likelihood theorem [F3] supplies typical blocks with likelihood cost $I(P_n)$, while empirical counts converge to $\rho(P_n)$. Changing from Poisson measure to the beta-zero weight gives the lower rate $-I(P_n)+\rho(P_n)\log z$. Let $n\to\infty$ and optimize over $P$. Corridors change the normalized log weight by their vanishing volume fraction, so free and periodic rates agree. [F2, F3, F5, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Put $\alpha=\log z$, $p_L=L^{-d}\log Z_{Q,L}$, and $d_L=L^{-d}D(G_L^{\rm per}\Vert Q_L)$. The exact identity in step 2.1 reads $d_L=\alpha\rho_L-p_L$. For $a>\max(\alpha,0)$, the entropy count inequality gives $d_L\geq a\rho_L-(e^a-1)$; the convergent pressure rates therefore bound both $\rho_L$ and $d_L$. The grand density and periodic hard-admissibility condition are invariant under translations modulo the box, so [F8] gives relatively compact continued laws. Every limit $P$ lies in $\mathcal K_B$ by the bounded local forbidden-pair tests from step 1.2. Along a subsequence realizing the entropy liminf, [F8] and count-tail uniformity give
$$I(P)-\alpha\rho(P)\leq\liminf(d_L-\alpha\rho_L)=-\lim p_L=\min_{\mathcal K_B}(I-\alpha\rho).$$
The opposite inequality is the definition of the minimum. Thus every accumulation point is a minimizer. If there is just one, relative compactness forces convergence of the entire sequence in $\tau_L$, including every stated tame test. [F2, F4, F6, F7, F8, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

sections.Statement: Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], the sectors are nested: if $y\in A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$; equality holds when $y\in\partial A_x$, and $A_y\subset\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ when $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$. sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** A1–A7 and S1–S3 on a simple domain $\Gamma_i$.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: $A_x$ is defined by $x\prec y$, every state is in its own sector, and each support plane is unique.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-convex-sector-closedness]]: sectors are convex and relatively closed; the collinear implications hold.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-sector-interior]]: every sector has nonempty ambient interior.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]]: if $w\in\partial A_x$, then $A_w=A_x$.

[F4] [[lem-tdmath-relative-interior-segment]]: if $w$ is in the relative interior of a convex set and $q$ lies in its closure, then $(1-t)w+tq$ lies in the relative interior for every $0\le t<1$.
sections.Proof:
1.1 If $y\in A_x$, transitivity gives $A_y\subseteq A_x$. If also $y\in\partial A_x$, [F3] gives equality. Suppose instead $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. If $A_y$ met $\partial A_x$ at $z$, then $z\in A_y$ and [F3] would give $A_z=A_x$. Since $z\in A_y$, transitivity gives $A_z\subseteq A_y\subseteq A_x$, so $A_y=A_x$. But S2 puts $y$ on $\partial A_y$, contradicting $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. Thus $A_y$ avoids $\partial A_x$ and, being a subset of the closed sector $A_x$, lies in $\operatorname{int}A_x$. [A1, F3, algebra]

1.2 Suppose neither $y\in A_x$ nor $x\in A_y$. Choose $z\in\operatorname{int}A_x$ using [F2]. The segment from $y$ to $z$ lies in $\Gamma_i$ and meets $\partial A_x$ at a point $w$ strictly between its endpoints. By [F3], $A_w=A_x$, so $w\prec z$. The collinear implication in [F1], applied to $w=ty+(1-t)z$, gives $y\prec w\prec z$. Hence every $z\in\operatorname{int}A_x$ lies in $A_y$. Reversing $x,y$ gives $\operatorname{int}A_y\subseteq A_x$. [A1, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Because $A_x$ is full-dimensional by [F2], its affine hull is the ambient space. Fix $w\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. For any $q\in A_x$, relative closedness gives $q\in\overline{A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$, and [F4] puts $(1-t)w+tq$ in $\operatorname{int}A_x$ for every $0\le t<1$. Letting $t\uparrow1$ shows $q\in\overline{\operatorname{int}A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$. The reverse inclusion follows because $A_x$ is relatively closed. Hence $A_x=\overline{\operatorname{int}A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$; the same holds for $A_y$. Relative closedness from [F1] therefore extends the two interior inclusions in step 1.2 to $A_x\subseteq A_y$ and $A_y\subseteq A_x$. Equality would put $x\in A_y$, contradicting the supposition. Thus at least one of $x\prec y$ or $y\prec x$ always holds. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.2]

3.1 If $x\prec y$, then $y\in A_x$. If $y$ is a boundary point, step 1.1 gives $A_x=A_y$, hence $x\prec y$ and $y\prec x$. Otherwise step 1.1 gives $A_y\subset\operatorname{int}A_x$, and $x\notin A_y$ because S2 places $x$ on $\partial A_x$. Thus $x\prec\prec y$. Conversely, if $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$, step 1.1 and S2 show $x\notin A_y$, so $x\prec\prec y$. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

sections.Statement:
Assume AC. Let $d\geq1$, let $P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$, with this class defined in [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]], be ergodic under the full translation group $\mathbb R^d$, and suppose its specific relative entropy $I(P)=\gamma$ relative to the unit-intensity Poisson law $Q$ is finite. Ergodic means that every measurable event invariant modulo $P$-null sets under each translation has probability $0$ or $1$. For an integer $N\geq1$, let $\Lambda_N=[0,N)^d$, and let $h_N=dP_{\Lambda_N}/dQ_{\Lambda_N}$, which exists because $D(P_{\Lambda_N}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N})<\infty$. Then
$$\frac{1}{N^d}\log h_N\longrightarrow\gamma\qquad\text{in }L^1(P).$$
Without the full-translation ergodicity hypothesis the proof yields an invariant $L^1(P)$ limit of mean $\gamma$; it need not be constant.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** AC, a stationary finite-intensity law $P$, finite specific relative entropy $\gamma$, and ergodicity under every real translation.

[A1] AC is used by the conditional-density convergence and Hilbert-space mean-ergodic suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[lem-tdmath-conditional-log-density-convergence]], [[thm-von-neumann-mean-ergodic-theorem-in-l-two]]).

[F1] For $P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$, every bounded restriction has finite relative entropy when $I(P)<\infty$, the cube entropy ratio converges to $\gamma$, and the cube ratios are bounded above by $\gamma$ ([[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]], [[thm-tdmath-specific-entropy-density]]).

[F2] The conditional density of a unit cell given its finite past has logarithm with directed $L^1$ limit $Z=\log k_\infty$, where $k_\infty$ is a density relative to $R_0:=P_{F_+}\otimes Q_C$ and $E_PZ=\gamma$ ([[lem-tdmath-conditional-log-density-convergence]]).

[F3] Finite-region densities factor into successive conditional densities relative to the independent Poisson restrictions; the chain rule identifies the expectation of each conditional log density with its conditional relative entropy. If $k$ is a conditional density relative to a probability reference $R$, then $E_P(-\log k)^+=\int_{0<k<1}k(-\log k)\,dR\leq1/e$, because $u(-\log u)\leq1/e$ for $0<u<1$ ([[thm-tdmath-poisson-reference-count-properties]], [[lem-tdmath-relative-entropy-variational-and-chain-rules]]).

[F4] For each measure-preserving transformation, the Cesàro averages on complex $L^2$ converge in norm to the orthogonal projection onto its invariant subspace ([[thm-von-neumann-mean-ergodic-theorem-in-l-two]]).

[F5] On a probability space $L^2$ convergence implies $L^1$ convergence by Hölder, and dominated convergence passes integrable truncations to the limit ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]]).
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Let $S_N=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}^d$ be the cell indices in $\Lambda_N$. For $i\in S_N$, set $A_{i,N}=\{j-i:j\in S_N,\ j<_{\rm lex}i\}$; this is a finite subset of the past of the reference cell. Repeated conditional-density factorization from [F3] gives, $P$-almost surely, $$\log h_N(\omega)=\sum_{i\in S_N}\log k_{A_{i,N}}(T_{-i}\omega).$$ Every finite factor is defined $P$-almost surely because the corresponding local relative entropy is finite by [F1]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 Fix $\varepsilon>0$. By the directed convergence in [F2], choose a finite past $A_*$ such that every finite $B\supseteq A_*$ satisfies $E_P|\log k_B-Z|<\varepsilon$. Put $R=\max\{|a_j|:a\in A_*,1\leq j\leq d\}$, with $R=0$ if $A_*=\varnothing$. Let $S_N^\circ$ consist of cells at least $R$ cells from each face of $S_N$. If $i\in S_N^\circ$, then $A_*\subseteq A_{i,N}$, so by stationarity $E_P|\log k_{A_{i,N}}(T_{-i}\omega)-Z(T_{-i}\omega)|<\varepsilon$. The boundary has $N^d-(N-2R)^d=o(N^d)$ cells (for $N>2R$). For every finite past $B$, $E_P\log k_B=g(B)\leq\gamma$ and $E_P(-\log k_B)^+\leq1/e$, hence $E_P|\log k_B|\leq\gamma+2/e$. For $Z=\log k_\infty$, $E_P(-\log k_\infty)^+=\int_{0<k_\infty<1}k_\infty(-\log k_\infty)\,dR_0\leq1/e$ on its reference probability $R_0=P_{F_+}\otimes Q_C$, so [F2] gives $E_P|Z|\leq\gamma+2/e$ as well. Summing the interior errors and bounding each boundary error by $2(\gamma+2/e)$ yields $$\left\|N^{-d}\log h_N-N^{-d}\sum_{i\in S_N}Z(T_{-i}\cdot)\right\|_{L^1(P)}\longrightarrow0,$$ since $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $j=1,\ldots,d$, the shift $U_jf=f\circ T_{-e_j}$ is a linear isometry on complex $L^2(P)$ by stationarity. Apply [F4] to $N^{-1}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}U_j^n$, obtaining strong convergence to the orthogonal projection $P_j$ onto the $U_j$-invariant subspace. The coordinate shifts commute, so every average for coordinate $j$ commutes with every average for coordinate $k$; taking strong limits shows that the $P_j$ commute with each other and with the other coordinate averages. Since all these operators have norm at most one, a finite telescoping estimate gives strong convergence of the product of the $d$ averages to $P_1\cdots P_d$. This product is the orthogonal projection onto the intersection of the coordinate-invariant subspaces, because the $P_j$ are commuting orthogonal projections. The product averages are exactly the rectangular cube averages $N^{-d}\sum_{i\in S_N}Z_M(T_{-i}\cdot)$, so these converge in $L^2$ for bounded $Z_M$ to a function invariant under every integer shift. [A1, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Since $Z\in L^1(P)$, dominated convergence gives $\|Z-Z_M\|_1\to0$. Cube averages are $L^1$ contractions, so the averages of $Z$ are Cauchy in $L^1$: for large $M$ their distance from the convergent averages of $Z_M$ is at most $\|Z-Z_M\|_1$. Let their $L^1$ limit be $s$. Every cube average has mean $E_PZ=\gamma$, hence $E_Ps=\gamma$. For each coordinate shift $e_j$, the averaging index cube and its translate have symmetric difference of exactly $2N^{d-1}$ indices, so $\|U_j A_NZ-A_NZ\|_1\leq2\|Z\|_1/N$. Passing to the $L^1$ limit gives $U_js=s$. These generators imply invariance under every integer translation. [A1, F2, F5, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Fix $r\in\mathbb R^d$, put $G=\Lambda_N$, $G'=G+r$, and $B=G\cap G'$. For $N>2\|r\|_\infty$, $B$ contains a cube $J$ of side $N-2\|r\|_\infty$. By [F1] and restriction monotonicity, $D(P_G\Vert Q_G)\leq\gamma N^d$ and $D(P_B\Vert Q_B)\geq D(P_J\Vert Q_J)$; the latter divided by $N^d$ tends to $\gamma$. Therefore $N^{-d}(D(P_G\Vert Q_G)-D(P_B\Vert Q_B))\to0$. The conditional chain rule [F3] identifies $\log h_G-\log h_B$ with a conditional log density. Its mean is this entropy difference, and [F3] bounds its negative-part expectation by $1/e$; thus its $L^1(P)$ norm is at most the entropy difference plus $2/e$. The same bound applies to $G'$. Translation covariance gives $\log h_{G'}=(\log h_G)\circ T_{-r}$; thus the normalized information in $G$ and $G'$ have the same $L^1$ limit. Since $N^{-d}\log h_G\to s$, it follows that $s\circ T_{-r}=s$ $P$-almost surely for this $r$. [A1, F1, F3, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Step 5.1 applies to every fixed $r\in\mathbb R^d$. For each rational $q$, the event $\{s\leq q\}$ is therefore invariant modulo null sets under every translation. Full-translation ergodicity makes each such event have probability $0$ or $1$. If $s$ were not almost surely constant, some rational sublevel set would have probability strictly between $0$ and $1$; hence $s$ is constant. Its mean from step 4.1 is $\gamma$, so $s=\gamma$. Combining with step 2.1 proves the asserted $L^1(P)$ limit. [A1, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎

[F4] For each measure-preserving transformation, the Cesàro averages on complex $L^2$ converge in norm to the orthogonal projection onto its invariant subspace ([[thm-von-neumann-mean-ergodic-theorem-in-l-two]]).

[F5] On a probability space $L^2$ convergence implies $L^1$ convergence by Hölder, and dominated convergence passes integrable truncations to the limit ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 Let $S_N=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}^d$ be the cell indices in $\Lambda_N$. For $i\in S_N$, set $A_{i,N}=\{j-i:j\in S_N,\ j<_{\rm lex}i\}$; this is a finite subset of the past of the reference cell. Repeated conditional-density factorization from [F3] gives, $P$-almost surely, $$\log h_N(\omega)=\sum_{i\in S_N}\log k_{A_{i,N}}(T_{-i}\omega).$$ Every finite factor is defined $P$-almost surely because the corresponding local relative entropy is finite by [F1]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 Fix $\varepsilon>0$. By the directed convergence in [F2], choose a finite past $A_*$ such that every finite $B\supseteq A_*$ satisfies $E_P|\log k_B-Z|<\varepsilon$. Put $R=\max\{|a_j|:a\in A_*,1\leq j\leq d\}$, with $R=0$ if $A_*=\varnothing$. Let $S_N^\circ$ consist of cells at least $R$ cells from each face of $S_N$. If $i\in S_N^\circ$, then $A_*\subseteq A_{i,N}$, so by stationarity $E_P|\log k_{A_{i,N}}(T_{-i}\omega)-Z(T_{-i}\omega)|<\varepsilon$. The boundary has $N^d-(N-2R)^d=o(N^d)$ cells (for $N>2R$). For every finite past $B$, $E_P\log k_B=g(B)\leq\gamma$ and $E_P(-\log k_B)^+\leq1/e$, hence $E_P|\log k_B|\leq\gamma+2/e$. For $Z=\log k_\infty$, $E_P(-\log k_\infty)^+=\int_{0<k_\infty<1}k_\infty(-\log k_\infty)\,dR_0\leq1/e$ on its reference probability $R_0=P_{F_+}\otimes Q_C$, so [F2] gives $E_P|Z|\leq\gamma+2/e$ as well. Summing the interior errors and bounding each boundary error by $2(\gamma+2/e)$ yields $$\left\|N^{-d}\log h_N-N^{-d}\sum_{i\in S_N}Z(T_{-i}\cdot)\right\|_{L^1(P)}\longrightarrow0,$$ since $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $j=1,\ldots,d$, the shift $U_jf=f\circ T_{-e_j}$ is a linear isometry on complex $L^2(P)$ by stationarity. Apply [F4] to $N^{-1}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}U_j^n$, obtaining strong convergence to the orthogonal projection $P_j$ onto the $U_j$-invariant subspace. The coordinate shifts commute, so every average for coordinate $j$ commutes with every average for coordinate $k$; taking strong limits shows that the $P_j$ commute with each other and with the other coordinate averages. Since all these operators have norm at most one, a finite telescoping estimate gives strong convergence of the product of the $d$ averages to $P_1\cdots P_d$. This product is the orthogonal projection onto the intersection of the coordinate-invariant subspaces, because the $P_j$ are commuting orthogonal projections. The product averages are exactly the rectangular cube averages $N^{-d}\sum_{i\in S_N}Z_M(T_{-i}\cdot)$, so these converge in $L^2$ for bounded $Z_M$ to a function invariant under every integer shift. [A1, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Since $Z\in L^1(P)$, dominated convergence gives $\|Z-Z_M\|_1\to0$. Cube averages are $L^1$ contractions, so the averages of $Z$ are Cauchy in $L^1$: for large $M$ their distance from the convergent averages of $Z_M$ is at most $\|Z-Z_M\|_1$. Let their $L^1$ limit be $s$. Every cube average has mean $E_PZ=\gamma$, hence $E_Ps=\gamma$. For each coordinate shift $e_j$, the averaging index cube and its translate have symmetric difference of exactly $2N^{d-1}$ indices, so $\|U_j A_NZ-A_NZ\|_1\leq2\|Z\|_1/N$. Passing to the $L^1$ limit gives $U_js=s$. These generators imply invariance under every integer translation. [A1, F2, F5, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Fix $r\in\mathbb R^d$, put $G=\Lambda_N$, $G'=G+r$, and $B=G\cap G'$. For $N>2\|r\|_\infty$, $B$ contains a cube $J$ of side $N-2\|r\|_\infty$. By [F1] and restriction monotonicity, $D(P_G\Vert Q_G)\leq\gamma N^d$ and $D(P_B\Vert Q_B)\geq D(P_J\Vert Q_J)$; the latter divided by $N^d$ tends to $\gamma$. Therefore $N^{-d}(D(P_G\Vert Q_G)-D(P_B\Vert Q_B))\to0$. The conditional chain rule [F3] identifies $\log h_G-\log h_B$ with a conditional log density. Its mean is this entropy difference, and [F3] bounds its negative-part expectation by $1/e$; thus its $L^1(P)$ norm is at most the entropy difference plus $2/e$. The same bound applies to $G'$. Translation covariance gives $\log h_{G'}=(\log h_G)\circ T_{-r}$; thus the normalized information in $G$ and $G'$ have the same $L^1$ limit. Since $N^{-d}\log h_G\to s$, it follows that $s\circ T_{-r}=s$ $P$-almost surely for this $r$. [A1, F1, F3, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Step 5.1 applies to every fixed $r\in\mathbb R^d$. For each rational $q$, the event $\{s\leq q\}$ is therefore invariant modulo null sets under every translation. Full-translation ergodicity makes each such event have probability $0$ or $1$. If $s$ were not almost surely constant, some rational sublevel set would have probability strictly between $0$ and $1$; hence $s$ is constant. Its mean from step 4.1 is $\gamma$, so $s=\gamma$. Combining with step 2.1 proves the asserted $L^1(P)$ limit. [A1, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎

$$D_L:=D(P_{\Lambda_L}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_L}).$$

$$I(P):=\lim_{L\to\infty}\frac{D_L}{L^d}$$
exists in $[0,+\infty]$ and satisfies
$$I(P)=\sup_{m\in\mathbb N,\ m\geq1}\frac{D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})}{m^d}.$$

sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** AC, dimension $d\geq1$, a stationary finite-intensity configuration law $P$, and the unit-intensity reference $Q$.

[F1] For independent Poisson reference restrictions on disjoint bounded sets, the finite-region relative entropy is nonnegative, obeys the conditional chain rule, and does not increase under restriction ([[thm-tdmath-poisson-reference-count-properties]], [[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]], [[lem-tdmath-relative-entropy-variational-and-chain-rules]]).

[F2] The domain $\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$ consists of translation-invariant laws with finite unit-cell count, and stationarity of $P$ and $Q$ gives $D(P_{G+x}\Vert Q_{G+x})=D(P_G\Vert Q_G)$ for every bounded Borel $G$ and translation $x$ ([[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]], [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], [[thm-tdmath-poisson-reference-count-properties]]).

[F3] If a cube restriction has finite relative entropy, then every bounded subregion has no larger relative entropy ([[lem-tdmath-relative-entropy-variational-and-chain-rules]], claim 2).
sections.Proof:
**Given:** AC, $P$, and $Q$ as in the Statement.

1.1 If $G_1,G_2$ are disjoint bounded Borel sets, [F1] decomposes $D(P_{G_1\cup G_2}\Vert Q_{G_1}\otimes Q_{G_2})$ into $D(P_{G_1}\Vert Q_{G_1})$ plus the mean conditional relative entropy of $G_2$ given $G_1$. That conditional increment is at least $D(P_{G_2}\Vert Q_{G_2})$ by the conditioning monotonicity in [F1], comparing observation by $G_1$ with no observation. Thus relative entropy is superadditive over disjoint regions; if the left side is infinite the inequality is immediate, and otherwise all terms in the chain rule are finite. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 Fix an integer $m\geq1$ and let $q_N=\lfloor N/m\rfloor$. Tile $[0,q_Nm)^d$ by $q_N^d$ disjoint translates of $\Lambda_m$, leaving the Borel remainder $\Lambda_N\setminus[0,q_Nm)^d$. Iterating step 1.1 and using nonnegativity on the remainder gives $$D(P_{\Lambda_N}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N})\geq q_N^dD(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m}),$$ because stationarity gives the same entropy for each translated $m$-cube. If $D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})=+\infty$, this forces $D(P_{\Lambda_N}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N})=+\infty$ for every $N\geq m$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Put $s=\sup_{m\geq1}m^{-d}D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})$. If $s=+\infty$, step 2.1 makes the liminf of $N^{-d}D_N$ exceed every finite bound, so the integer-cube limit is $+\infty=s$. If $s<+\infty$, step 2.1 gives $$\liminf_{N\to\infty}N^{-d}D_N\geq m^{-d}D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})$$ for every $m$, since $q_N^d/N^d\to m^{-d}$. Taking the supremum gives liminf at least $s$, while the definition of $s$ gives $N^{-d}D_N\leq s$ for every integer $N$. Hence the integer-cube limit exists and equals $s$. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For real $L\to\infty$, let $N=\lfloor L\rfloor$. The inclusions $\Lambda_N\subseteq\Lambda_L\subseteq\Lambda_{N+1}$ and [F3] give $D_N\leq D_L\leq D_{N+1}$. Since $N/L\to1$ and $(N+1)/L\to1$, step 3.1 squeezes $L^{-d}D_L$ to the same extended limit $s$; if some integer-cube entropy is infinite, monotonicity gives the same conclusion directly. [F2, F3, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If $I(P)<\infty$ and $A$ is bounded, choose an integer cube $\Lambda_N+x$ containing $A$. **Given:** AC, $P$, and $Q$ as in the Statement.

1.1 If $G_1,G_2$ are disjoint bounded Borel sets, [F1] decomposes $D(P_{G_1\cup G_2}\Vert Q_{G_1}\otimes Q_{G_2})$ into $D(P_{G_1}\Vert Q_{G_1})$ plus the mean conditional relative entropy of $G_2$ given $G_1$. 2.1 Fix an integer $m\geq1$ and let $q_N=\lfloor N/m\rfloor$. Tile $[0,q_Nm)^d$ by $q_N^d$ disjoint translates of $\Lambda_m$, leaving the Borel remainder $\Lambda_N\setminus[0,q_Nm)^d$. 3.1 Put $s=\sup_{m\geq1}m^{-d}D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})$. If $s=+\infty$, step 2.1 makes the liminf of $N^{-d}D_N$ exceed every finite bound, so the integer-cube limit is $+\infty=s$. fm.title: No-sinks cost offsets give a weak global entropy

references.title: Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §VI.B, pp. 76–80

sections.Statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $F$ be the decorated cost of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]], and assume the **no-sinks condition**

$$F(\Gamma,\Gamma')<+\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F(\Gamma',\Gamma)<+\infty$$

for every type pair. Let $V_F$ be the real difference space of [[def-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space]]. Then there is an additive extensive offset $B:\mathcal G\to\mathbb R$ such that

$$-F(\Gamma',\Gamma)\le B(\Gamma)-B(\Gamma')\le F(\Gamma,\Gamma').$$

If every admitted cross-type transition $x\prec y$ from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma'$ satisfies the calibrated cost inequality of [[thm-tdmath-unattained-cost-entropy-inference]], then $\sigma_\Gamma(x)+B(\Gamma)$ is nondecreasing across every such transition. Only this weak inequality is asserted; no-gap equalities and strict extensions are not concluded.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** The no-sinks condition, A1–A6 for cross-type transitions, the finite-chain costs, and the Axiom of Choice.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: adopt AC for the Hahn–Banach dominated-extension and basis-extension steps in the vector-space supplier.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space]] and [[lem-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space-well-defined]]: $V_F$ is a real vector space of formal type differences, with composition additive and positive scaling homogeneous.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-decorated-cost-algebra]]: $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$, $F$ is translation-invariant, positively homogeneous and subadditive, finite reverse witnesses bound forward costs, and costs have no negative cycles.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-infinite-no-sinks-sandwich]]: under AC, a sublinear $p:V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ with $p(0)=0$ and symmetric finite domain admits a linear $L$ with $-p(-v)\le L(v)\le p(v)$.

[F4] [[thm-tdmath-unattained-cost-entropy-inference]]: every admitted transition $x\prec y$ satisfies $\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)\ge F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F4], and the no-sinks condition.

1.1 If $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')<+\infty$, no-sinks gives a finite reverse witness of some real cost $c$. Concatenating it with any forward witness makes a closed chain, so [F2] gives forward cost at least $-c$. Thus $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')>-\infty$ whenever it is finite; all cost values are in $\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. [A1, F2, given]

2.1 For a pair class $v=[\Gamma,\Gamma']\in V_F$, define $p(v):=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$. Suppose $(\Gamma,\Gamma')\equiv(\Lambda,\Lambda')$ via $C$, so $P=\Gamma\times\Lambda'\times C\approx_0 Q=\Lambda\times\Gamma'\times C$. Put $D=\Gamma'\times\Lambda'\times C$. Since $P\approx_0 Q$, the triangle inequality gives $F(P,D)\le F(Q,D)$ and $F(Q,D)\le F(P,D)$; the costs have no $-\infty$ by step 1.1, so these inequalities imply equality. Catalyst invariance from [F2] gives $F(P,D)=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$ and $F(Q,D)=F(\Lambda,\Lambda')$. Therefore $p$ is independent of the pair representative. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The identity $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$ gives $p(0)=0$. Homogeneity of $F$ gives $p(tv)=tp(v)$ for $t>0$, and its product subadditivity gives $p(v+w)\le p(v)+p(w)$. The no-sinks condition says $p(v)<+\infty$ exactly when $p(-v)<+\infty$. By step 1.1, $p$ has no $-\infty$ value. [F1, F2, given, step 1.1]

3.1 Apply [F3] to $V_F$ and $p$. It gives a real-linear $L:V_F\to\mathbb R$ with $-p(-v)\le L(v)\le p(v)$ for all $v$. Put $B(\Gamma)=L([\Gamma,1])$, where $1$ is the empty unit type. Since $[\Gamma\times\Gamma',1]=[\Gamma,1]+[\Gamma',1]$, $B$ is additive. Since $[t\Gamma,1]=t[\Gamma,1]$ (the unit type satisfies $t1=1$), $B(t\Gamma)=tB(\Gamma)$ for $t>0$. Also $[\Gamma,\Gamma']=[\Gamma,1]-[\Gamma',1]$, so applying the sandwich to this pair gives the displayed two-sided cost bound. [A1, F1, F3, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 For an admitted transition, [F4] gives $\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)\ge F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$, while step 3.1 gives $B(\Gamma)-B(\Gamma')\le F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$. Subtracting the latter from the former yields
$[\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)+B(\Gamma')]-[\sigma_\Gamma(x)+B(\Gamma)]\ge0.$
Thus the offset entropy is nondecreasing across every admitted transition. [F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
sections.Remarks: The no-sinks condition is an explicit hypothesis about cross-type reachability. AC is used by [[thm-tdmath-infinite-no-sinks-sandwich]] and is carried here. The result does not assert a no-gap condition, a unique offset, or an exact entropy principle for all transitions.

**Given:** The no-sinks condition, A1–A6 for cross-type transitions, the finite-chain costs, and the Axiom of Choice.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: adopt AC for the Hahn–Banach dominated-extension and basis-extension steps in the vector-space supplier.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space]] and [[lem-tdmath-cost-offset-difference-space-well-defined]]: $V_F$ is a real vector space of formal type differences, with composition additive and positive scaling homogeneous.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-decorated-cost-algebra]]: $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$, $F$ is translation-invariant, positively homogeneous and subadditive, finite reverse witnesses bound forward costs, and costs have no negative cycles.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-infinite-no-sinks-sandwich]]: under AC, a sublinear $p:V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ with $p(0)=0$ and symmetric finite domain admits a linear $L$ with $-p(-v)\le L(v)\le p(v)$.

[F4] [[thm-tdmath-unattained-cost-entropy-inference]]: every admitted transition $x\prec y$ satisfies $\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)\ge F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F4], and the no-sinks condition.

1.1 If $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')<+\infty$, no-sinks gives a finite reverse witness of some real cost $c$. Concatenating it with any forward witness makes a closed chain, so [F2] gives forward cost at least $-c$. Thus $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')>-\infty$ whenever it is finite; all cost values are in $\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. [A1, F2, given]

2.1 For a pair class $v=[\Gamma,\Gamma']\in V_F$, define $p(v):=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$. Suppose $(\Gamma,\Gamma')\equiv(\Lambda,\Lambda')$ via $C$, so $P=\Gamma\times\Lambda'\times C\approx_0 Q=\Lambda\times\Gamma'\times C$. Put $D=\Gamma'\times\Lambda'\times C$. Since $P\approx_0 Q$, the triangle inequality gives $F(P,D)\le F(Q,D)$ and $F(Q,D)\le F(P,D)$; the costs have no $-\infty$ by step 1.1, so these inequalities imply equality. Catalyst invariance from [F2] gives $F(P,D)=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$ and $F(Q,D)=F(\Lambda,\Lambda')$. Therefore $p$ is independent of the pair representative. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The identity $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$ gives $p(0)=0$. Homogeneity of $F$ gives $p(tv)=tp(v)$ for $t>0$, and its product subadditivity gives $p(v+w)\le p(v)+p(w)$. The no-sinks condition says $p(v)<+\infty$ exactly when $p(-v)<+\infty$. By step 1.1, $p$ has no $-\infty$ value. [F1, F2, given, step 1.1]

3.1 Apply [F3] to $V_F$ and $p$. It gives a real-linear $L:V_F\to\mathbb R$ with $-p(-v)\le L(v)\le p(v)$ for all $v$. Put $B(\Gamma)=L([\Gamma,1])$, where $1$ is the empty unit type. Since $[\Gamma\times\Gamma',1]=[\Gamma,1]+[\Gamma',1]$, $B$ is additive. Since $[t\Gamma,1]=t[\Gamma,1]$ (the unit type satisfies $t1=1$), $B(t\Gamma)=tB(\Gamma)$ for $t>0$. Also $[\Gamma,\Gamma']=[\Gamma,1]-[\Gamma',1]$, so applying the sandwich to this pair gives the displayed two-sided cost bound. [A1, F1, F3, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 For an admitted transition, [F4] gives $\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)\ge F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$, while step 3.1 gives $B(\Gamma)-B(\Gamma')\le F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$. Subtracting the latter from the former yields
$[\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)+B(\Gamma')]-[\sigma_\Gamma(x)+B(\Gamma)]\ge0.$
Thus the offset entropy is nondecreasing across every admitted transition. [F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
## Remarks

The no-sinks condition is an explicit hypothesis about cross-type reachability. AC is used by [[thm-tdmath-infinite-no-sinks-sandwich]] and is carried here. The result does not assert a no-gap condition, a unique offset, or an exact entropy principle for all transitions.

fm.title: Finite free-cube grand pressure for stable power-tempered pair potentials

references.title: Stefan Adams, Mathematical Statistical Mechanics, MPI Lecture Note 30, §5.2
M. E. Fisher and J. L. Lebowitz, Asymptotic Free Energy of a System with Periodic Boundary Conditions, §§II–III, VI

sections.Statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let $d\ge1$. Let $\phi$ be a stable,
power-tempered pair potential as in
[[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]], with constants
$B,C,R,\epsilon$ as there. Fix activity $a>0$ and inverse-energy parameter
$\beta>0$ in fixed reference units. Use the free-boundary grand partition sums
$\Xi_L(a,\beta)$ defined in
[[lem-tdmath-particle-exponential-cutoff]]. For $L\ge1$, put
$$p_L(a,\beta):=L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(a,\beta).$$
Then the limit
$$p(a,\beta):=\lim_{L\to\infty}p_L(a,\beta)$$
exists as a finite real number. The assertion is for cubes with free boundary
and the displayed power-tail hypothesis.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, $d\ge1$, a stable power-tempered pair
potential, $a,\beta>0$, and the free-cube partitions in
[[lem-tdmath-particle-exponential-cutoff]].

[F1] [[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]] defines $U_N$,
stability, and the two-sided power-tail bound.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-particle-exponential-cutoff]] gives the exact grand
partition definition, $1\le\Xi_L\le e^{QL^d}$, and the particle-cutoff lower
bound, where $Q=ae^{\beta B}$.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-separated-cube-tail-bound]] gives the uniform bound
$D\le(C/2)Mn^2S_{d,\epsilon}g^{-d-\epsilon}$ on all cross-cube energies.

[F4] [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] defines the local nonnegative integral as
the supremum over simple minorants; that current batch-11 carrier is a draft
definition with its interface inspected. The local bridge
[[lem-tdmath-measure-integral-agrees-with-root-lebesgue-integral]] proves that
this integral agrees with the shared nonnegative Lebesgue integral. This is the
interface needed to apply the published Tonelli theorem to the partition
integrals.

[F5] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] states that for
sigma-finite measure spaces and a nonnegative product-measurable function, the
product integral equals either iterated integral. The Euclidean product Borel
theorem [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]] ensures
the finite-configuration integrand is product-measurable.

[F6] [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]
supplies the rectangle formula and uniqueness for the finite product measures;
the Lebesgue factors are sigma-finite by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]].

[F7] [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]
preserves each cube integral under a common translation of its particle
coordinates. The corresponding finite product measure is translation-invariant
by the rectangle formula and uniqueness in [F6].

[F8] [[def-countable-choice]] is the exact $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ assumption
used by the Lebesgue-measure suppliers
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]] and
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]. No full
arbitrary-index choice is used in the block construction.

[F9] Positive real powers obey the exponent laws and are continuous on positive
bases ([[def-real-power]], [[thm-real-power-laws]],
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]). The natural logarithm is
continuous, strictly increasing and onto $\mathbb R$ on $(0,\infty)$
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]); together with
[[thm-exponential-limits-and-range]], this gives $\ell^\gamma\to0$ for every
$\gamma<0$ and $\ell^\gamma\to\infty$ for every $\gamma>0$.

[F10] [[lem-integer-part]] gives an integer $m$ with $m\le x<m+1$ for every
real $x$.

[F11] Factorials satisfy $0!=1$ and the recursion
$(N+1)!=(N+1)N!$ ([[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]).

[A1] Since $p_L$ is defined for $L\ge1$, write
$$\limsup_{L\to\infty}p_L:=\inf_{T\ge1}\sup_{L\ge T}p_L,\qquad \liminf_{L\to\infty}p_L:=\sup_{T\ge1}\inf_{L\ge T}p_L.$$
These are finite because [F2] bounds $p_L$ in $[0,Q]$.
sections.Proof:
1.1 Set $\alpha:=\frac12\bigl(1+d/(d+\epsilon)\bigr)$ and
$g_\ell:=\ell^\alpha$. Then $d/(d+\epsilon)<\alpha<1$ and
$\ell^d g_\ell^{-d-\epsilon}=\ell^{d-\alpha(d+\epsilon)}\to0$ while
$g_\ell/\ell\to0$. Fix a sufficiently large $\ell\ge1$ so that
$g_\ell\ge R$. For $L\ge\ell+g_\ell$, set
$m_L:=\lfloor L/(\ell+g_\ell)\rfloor$. Since $L/(\ell+g_\ell)\ge1$, [F10]
gives $m_L\ge1$ and
$m_L(\ell+g_\ell)\le L<(m_L+1)(\ell+g_\ell)$. Place $M_L=m_L^d$ cubes
$$C_j=(\ell+g_\ell)j+[0,\ell]^d,\qquad j\in\{0,\ldots,m_L-1\}^d.$$
They lie inside $[0,L]^d$ and have pairwise gaps at least $g_\ell$.
[given, F9, F10, construct]

2.1 Fix occupancies $0\le N_j\le n_\ell$ with total $N=\sum_jN_j$. The
ordered configurations in the disjoint cubes with exactly these occupancies
are partitioned by assignments of the $N$ particle labels to cubes. The number
of assignments is $N!/(\prod_jN_j!)$: order all $N$ labels, then note that
each assignment occurs exactly $\prod_jN_j!$ times from within-cube reorderings.
Particle-permutation symmetry of $U_N$ and invariance of the finite product
measure (rectangle formula and uniqueness in [F6]) make the assignment
integrals equal. [F1, F6, F11, given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Restrict the grand partition sum in $[0,L]^d$ to configurations with no
particles outside these cubes and at most $n_\ell$ particles in each cube,
where $n_\ell$ is the cutoff from [F2]. If two cubes have index difference
$k\ne0$, the coordinate gap in a coordinate attaining $\|k\|_\infty$ is at
least $\|k\|_\infty g_\ell$; [F3] therefore bounds the total absolute
inter-cube energy by
$$D_L\le\frac C2M_Ln_\ell^2S_{d,\epsilon}g_\ell^{-d-\epsilon}.$$
Thus $U_N=\sum_jU_{N_j}^{(j)}+U_{\mathrm{cross}}$ with
$U_{\mathrm{cross}}\le D_L$, and
$e^{-\beta U_N}\ge e^{-\beta D_L}\prod_j e^{-\beta U_{N_j}^{(j)}}$;
this remains true when an internal energy is $+\infty$, since both sides then
vanish. [F1, F2, F3, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 On each assignment domain from step 2.1, the pointwise lower bound in
step 2.2 factors into nonnegative within-cube integrands. Repeated application
of [F5] and the rectangle formula in [F6] factors their integral into the
product of the translated one-cube integrals; [F7] identifies each with its
origin-centered value. Multiplying by $a^N/N!$ cancels the label count from
step 2.1, leaving $e^{-\beta D_L}\prod_j Z_{\ell,N_j}$. Summing over the
finitely many occupancy vectors and expanding the finite product of cutoff
sums from [F2] gives
$$\Xi_L\ge e^{-\beta D_L}(\Xi_\ell^{\mathrm{cut}})^{M_L}.$$
[F2, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The integer-part bounds in step 1.1 give
$L/(\ell+g_\ell)-1<m_L\le L/(\ell+g_\ell)$, so
$m_L/L\to(\ell+g_\ell)^{-1}$ and $M_L/L^d\to(\ell+g_\ell)^{-d}$.
By [F2], $\Xi_\ell^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge(1-e^{-\ell^d})\Xi_\ell$, so
$\log\Xi_\ell^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge\ell^dp_\ell+\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})$.
Taking logarithms in step 3.1, dividing by $L^d$, and using step 2.2 gives
$$p_L\ge\frac{M_L}{L^d}\left(\ell^dp_\ell+\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})-\frac{\beta C}{2}n_\ell^2S_{d,\epsilon}g_\ell^{-d-\epsilon}\right).$$
Taking the lower limit and using the volume ratio above yields the same bound
with $M_L/L^d$ replaced by $(\ell+g_\ell)^{-d}$. The cutoff definition [F2]
and $\ell\ge1$ give
$n_\ell\le K\ell^d+1\le(K+1)\ell^d$. Factoring
$(\ell/(\ell+g_\ell))^d$ and using this estimate in the negative error term
therefore gives
$$\liminf_{L\to\infty}p_L\ge\left(\frac{\ell}{\ell+g_\ell}\right)^d\left[p_\ell+\ell^{-d}\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})-\frac{\beta C}{2}(K+1)^2S_{d,\epsilon}\ell^dg_\ell^{-d-\epsilon}\right].$$
[A1, F2, F9, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 As $\ell\to\infty$, the prefactor tends to $1$. Also
$e^{-\ell^d}\to0$, so continuity of $\log$ at $1$ gives
$\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})\to0$; since $\ell^{-d}\to0$, their product
$\ell^{-d}\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})$ tends to zero. The cross-energy error tends to
zero because $d-\alpha(d+\epsilon)<0$ by step 1.1. The replacement of the
prefactor times $p_\ell$ by $p_\ell$ has error at most
$Q\bigl[1-(\ell/(\ell+g_\ell))^d\bigr]\to0$ by [F2]. Thus for every
$\eta>0$ there is $T$ such that every $\ell\ge T$ makes the right side of
step 4.1 at least $p_\ell-\eta$. [F2, F9, step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Let $\overline p=\limsup_{\ell\to\infty}p_\ell$. By [A1], for every
$\eta>0$ and every $T\ge1$ there is an $\ell\ge T$ with
$p_\ell>\overline p-\eta$; otherwise the tail supremum from $T$ onward would
be at most $\overline p-\eta$, contradicting the infimum defining
$\overline p$. Choose $T$ large enough for step 5.1. Then
$\liminf_{L\to\infty}p_L\ge\overline p-2\eta$. Letting $\eta\downarrow0$
shows $\liminf p_L\ge\limsup p_L$. [A1, step 5.1, choose, algebra]

7.1 For any $S,T\ge1$, choose $L\ge\max(S,T)$. Then
$\inf_{x\ge S}p_x\le p_L\le\sup_{x\ge T}p_x$. Taking the supremum over $S$
and then the infimum over $T$ proves
$\liminf p_L\le\limsup p_L$ by [A1]. Together with step 6.1, the two finite
tail bounds equal a number $p$. For every $\eta>0$, their definitions give
tail thresholds with $\inf_{L\ge T_-}p_L>p-\eta$ and
$\sup_{L\ge T_+}p_L<p+\eta$; hence $|p_L-p|<\eta$ for all sufficiently large
$L$. The limit is finite by [F2]. This proves existence for the specified
free-cube reduced grand pressure. [A1, F2, step 6.1, algebra] ∎
sections.Remarks:
The proof uses fixed free-boundary cubes. It does not establish a canonical
fixed-density limit, arbitrary-boundary independence, or the corresponding
result for every decreasing integrable tail. In particular, stability alone
does not enter as a claim about arbitrary van Hove shapes; those are separate
interfaces with additional hypotheses. The displayed pressure is per reference
volume and is the reduced pressure (the classical pressure multiplied by
$\beta$). If $L$ is measured in units of a reference length $\ell_0$ and
$\beta$ is the numerical inverse temperature in units $E_0^{-1}$, then the
physical pressure is $P=E_0p/(\beta\ell_0^d)$. Without that specified
classical interpretation, this theorem asserts only the mathematical
existence of the reduced limit.

sums from [F2] gives
$$\Xi_L\ge e^{-\beta D_L}(\Xi_\ell^{\mathrm{cut}})^{M_L}.$$
[F2, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The integer-part bounds in step 1.1 give
$L/(\ell+g_\ell)-1<m_L\le L/(\ell+g_\ell)$, so
$m_L/L\to(\ell+g_\ell)^{-1}$ and $M_L/L^d\to(\ell+g_\ell)^{-d}$.
By [F2], $\Xi_\ell^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge(1-e^{-\ell^d})\Xi_\ell$, so
$\log\Xi_\ell^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge\ell^dp_\ell+\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})$.
Taking logarithms in step 3.1, dividing by $L^d$, and using step 2.2 gives
$$p_L\ge\frac{M_L}{L^d}\left(\ell^dp_\ell+\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})-\frac{\beta C}{2}n_\ell^2S_{d,\epsilon}g_\ell^{-d-\epsilon}\right).$$
Taking the lower limit and using the volume ratio above yields the same bound
with $M_L/L^d$ replaced by $(\ell+g_\ell)^{-d}$. The cutoff definition [F2]
and $\ell\ge1$ give
$n_\ell\le K\ell^d+1\le(K+1)\ell^d$. Factoring
$(\ell/(\ell+g_\ell))^d$ and using this estimate in the negative error term
therefore gives
$$\liminf_{L\to\infty}p_L\ge\left(\frac{\ell}{\ell+g_\ell}\right)^d\left[p_\ell+\ell^{-d}\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})-\frac{\beta C}{2}(K+1)^2S_{d,\epsilon}\ell^dg_\ell^{-d-\epsilon}\right].$$
[A1, F2, F9, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 As $\ell\to\infty$, the prefactor tends to $1$. Also
$e^{-\ell^d}\to0$, so continuity of $\log$ at $1$ gives
$\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})\to0$; since $\ell^{-d}\to0$, their product
$\ell^{-d}\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})$ tends to zero. The cross-energy error tends to
zero because $d-\alpha(d+\epsilon)<0$ by step 1.1. The replacement of the
prefactor times $p_\ell$ by $p_\ell$ has error at most
$Q\bigl[1-(\ell/(\ell+g_\ell))^d\bigr]\to0$ by [F2]. Thus for every
$\eta>0$ there is $T$ such that every $\ell\ge T$ makes the right side of
step 4.1 at least $p_\ell-\eta$. [F2, F9, step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Let $\overline p=\limsup_{\ell\to\infty}p_\ell$. By [A1], for every
$\eta>0$ and every $T\ge1$ there is an $\ell\ge T$ with
$p_\ell>\overline p-\eta$; otherwise the tail supremum from $T$ onward would
be at most $\overline p-\eta$, contradicting the infimum defining
$\overline p$. Choose $T$ large enough for step 5.1. Then
$\liminf_{L\to\infty}p_L\ge\overline p-2\eta$. Letting $\eta\downarrow0$
shows $\liminf p_L\ge\limsup p_L$. [A1, step 5.1, choose, algebra]

7.1 For any $S,T\ge1$, choose $L\ge\max(S,T)$. Then
$\inf_{x\ge S}p_x\le p_L\le\sup_{x\ge T}p_x$. Taking the supremum over $S$
and then the infimum over $T$ proves
$\liminf p_L\le\limsup p_L$ by [A1]. Together with step 6.1, the two finite
tail bounds equal a number $p$. For every $\eta>0$, their definitions give
tail thresholds with $\inf_{L\ge T_-}p_L>p-\eta$ and
$\sup_{L\ge T_+}p_L<p+\eta$; hence $|p_L-p|<\eta$ for all sufficiently large
$L$. The limit is finite by [F2]. This proves existence for the specified
free-cube reduced grand pressure. [A1, F2, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The proof uses fixed free-boundary cubes. It does not establish a canonical
fixed-density limit, arbitrary-boundary independence, or the corresponding
result for every decreasing integrable tail. In particular, stability alone
does not enter as a claim about arbitrary van Hove shapes; those are separate
interfaces with additional hypotheses. The displayed pressure is per reference
volume and is the reduced pressure (the classical pressure multiplied by
$\beta$). If $L$ is measured in units of a reference length $\ell_0$ and
$\beta$ is the numerical inverse temperature in units $E_0^{-1}$, then the
physical pressure is $P=E_0p/(\beta\ell_0^d)$. Without that specified
classical interpretation, this theorem asserts only the mathematical
existence of the reduced limit.

sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** As stated in the item.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]: $Z$, $p_i$, expectation, variance and $H_g$ have the definitions and domains stated there.

[F2] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: $\exp$ is positive and differentiable with $\exp'=\exp$.

[F3] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: $\log$ is defined on positive reals and $(\log u)'=u'/u$ for differentiable $u>0$.

[F4] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: a function continuous on a closed interval and differentiable in its interior has a point where its secant slope equals its derivative.

[A1] For every compact $K\subset J$ there is a nonnegative summable sequence $(a_i)$ such that $g_i(1+|E_i|^2)e^{-\beta E_i}\le a_i$ for all $i$ and $\beta\in K$; the tail $\sum_{i>N}a_i$ tends to zero.

[F5] [[thm-chain-rule]]: differentiating $e^{-\beta E_i}$ with respect to $\beta$ uses the one-variable chain rule.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The countable canonical model and the local summable envelope in the statement.

1.1 On a compact interval $K\subset J$, let $Z_N$, $D_N$, and $Q_N$ be the first $N$ partial sums of $\sum_i g_i e^{-\beta E_i}$, $-\sum_i g_iE_ie^{-\beta E_i}$, and $\sum_i g_iE_i^2e^{-\beta E_i}$. Since $|E_i|^r\le1+|E_i|^2$ for $r=0,1,2$, each tail is bounded uniformly on $K$ by the corresponding tail of $\sum_i a_i$, which tends to zero [A1]. Thus all three sequences converge uniformly; call their limits $Z,D,Q$. Each finite partial sum has the displayed derivatives by the chain rule [F5] and the exponential derivative [F2]. Each partial sum is continuous, so the uniform limits are continuous by the $\varepsilon/3$ definition of continuity. [F1, A1, F2, F5]

2.1 For an interior $\beta$ and sufficiently small $h\ne0$, apply [F4] to $Z_N$ on the interval with endpoints $\beta$ and $\beta+h$: its difference quotient is $D_N(\xi_{N,h})$ for some intermediate $\xi_{N,h}$. Choose $N=N(h)$ so that $\sup_K|Z_N-Z|<h^2$ and $\sup_K|D_N-D|<|h|$. The difference quotient for $Z$ then differs from $D(\beta)$ by at most $2|h|+|h|+\sup_{|t-\beta|\le|h|}|D(t)-D(\beta)|$, which tends to zero by continuity of $D$. Hence $Z'=D$. Applying the same argument to $D_N$ and $Q_N$ proves $D'=Q$, so the displayed derivatives hold. [F2, F4, F5, step 1.1]

3.1 The summands of $Z$ are positive and at least one is present, hence $0<Z<\infty$ on $K$; summing the definition of $p_i$ gives $\sum_i p_i=1$. ## Statement

3.1 The summands of $Z$ are positive and at least one is present, hence $0<Z<\infty$ on $K$; summing the definition of $p_i$ gives $\sum_i p_i=1$. sections.Statement:
Assume a superstable regular pair potential as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]] and the van Hove definition [[def-tdmath-van-hove-sequence]]. For every van Hove sequence $(\Omega_k)$, the free-wall physical grand pressure satisfies
$$|\Omega_k|^{-1}\log\Xi_{\Omega_k}(z,\beta)\longrightarrow p(z,\beta),$$
the free-cube limit from [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. The extra superstability hypothesis is essential to this proof's uniform cell-occupation bound; no arbitrary-shape theorem under stability alone is claimed.
sections.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** A stable, regular, superstable interaction, $z,\beta>0$, and a bounded measurable van Hove sequence.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]: the pair interaction has a summable lower-tail envelope and a stable grand-canonical normalization.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-van-hove-sequence]]: every fixed-width boundary layer has volume $o(|\Omega_k|)$.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-superstable-cell-energy-bound]]: the energy dominates a positive cell-square sum minus a linear count.

[F4] [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]: the free-cube pressure limit exists and is finite.

[F5] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: nonnegative configuration-sector sums and integrals may be interchanged over the sigma-finite product reference.

[L1] Ruelle Proposition 2.6 states that finite-volume Gibbs correlation densities of a superstable lower-regular interaction satisfy $\rho_m(x_1,\dots,x_m)\leq\xi^m$ uniformly in every bounded measurable region. The original statement and proof were visually checked on printed pp.140–141; the claim is used only under those hypotheses.
sections.Proof:
**Given:** The hypotheses and suppliers in Facts & Assumptions.

1.1 First take a finite union $\mathcal R$ of unit cells and its free Gibbs law. By [L1] and Tonelli [F5],
$$E N_i^2=E N_i+E[N_i(N_i-1)] \leq \xi |C_i\cap\mathcal R|+\xi^2|C_i\cap\mathcal R|^2 \leq M:=\xi+\xi^2.$$
Let the cells be partitioned into boxes of side $\ell$. For each cell $i$, let $e_i$ be the sum of the lower-regular lattice envelope over cells $j$ in other boxes. The negative cross-box energy obeys $W^-\leq\tfrac12\sum_i e_iN_i^2$, because $N_iN_j\leq(N_i^2+N_j^2)/2$. Therefore $E W^-\leq(M/2)\sum_i e_i$. If $\sum_i e_i>0$, then $P(W^->M\sum_i e_i)\leq E W^-/(M\sum_i e_i)\leq1/2$; if the sum is zero, $W^-=0$ almost surely. Thus the event $W^-\leq M\sum_i e_i$ has probability at least $1/2$. [F1, F3, F5, L1, algebra]

2.1 For each $\Omega_k$, let $\mathcal R_k$ be the union of unit cells meeting $\Omega_k$. Then $\Xi_{\Omega_k}\leq\Xi_{\mathcal R_k}$ by domain monotonicity, and $|\mathcal R_k|/|\Omega_k|\to1$ by the van Hove boundary condition. Partition $\mathcal R_k$ into boxes of $\ell$ unit cells per side. The probability event from step 1.1 has full Gibbs probability at least $1/2$; on it, $H_{\mathrm{total}}\geq H_{\mathrm{in}}-M\sum_i e_i$, where $H_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the sum of within-box energies. Therefore
$$\Xi_{\mathcal R_k}/2\leq e^{\beta M\sum_i e_i}\prod_B\Xi_{\mathcal R_k\cap B}.$$
Indeed, $\Xi_{\mathcal R_k}\mu_{\mathcal R_k}(E)=\int_Ee^{-\beta H_{\mathrm{total}}}d\Pi\leq e^{\beta M\sum_i e_i}\int_Ee^{-\beta H_{\mathrm{in}}}d\Pi$, and the last integral is bounded by the unrestricted product over boxes. Each partial-box partition is at most the full $\ell$-cube partition. For one full box, $E_\ell=\sum_{i\in B,j\notin B}\Psi(|i-j|)$ satisfies $E_\ell/\ell^d\to0$: cells within fixed distance $R$ of the boundary are $O_R(\ell^{d-1})$; all other cells contribute at most the summable tail beyond $R$. Thus
$$\limsup_k|\Omega_k|^{-1}\log\Xi_{\Omega_k} \leq\ell^{-d}\bigl[\log\Xi_{\Lambda_\ell}+\beta M E_\ell\bigr].$$
Let $\ell\to\infty$ and use [F4]. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, L1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For the lower bound, fix core side $\ell$ and gap $g$, and retain every whole $(\ell+g)$-cell whose core lies in $\Omega_k$. By the van Hove property [F2], the retained count divided by $|\Omega_k|$ tends $(\ell+g)^{-d}$. Restrict each core to at most $K\ell^d$ particles. Exact $N!$ cancellation factorizes their grand weights. The lattice-shell count and [F1] bound positive cross energy per core by $C K^2(\ell/g)^d\eta(g)$, with $\eta(g)\to0$ from the integrable tail. This gives the same separated-core lower bound as the free-cube packing proof. First let $k\to\infty$, then choose $g=g(\ell)$ from [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]] and let $\ell\to\infty$; packing fraction tends one and the cross penalty vanishes. The resulting liminf is at least the cube pressure [F4]. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

3.1 For the lower bound, fix core side $\ell$ and gap $g$, and retain every whole $(\ell+g)$-cell whose core lies in $\Omega_k$. 2.1 Put $\delta_n=1/n$. In one finite compound type form
